BY THE POOL. t&t.... Surely he took the hard first prize In suffering's bitter school, Who lay for eight-and-thirty years, By Bethesda's wonderful pool; • Who watched for eight-and-thirty years Of desperate struggle and prayer, Till strife to dull quiescence:sank, And hope died to despair, So often the rush of the miracle Proved Faith's best dreaming true; $o often the merciful angel's wings Cleft down the Syrian blue, And swept the placid waters, Till they ruffled and flashed in light, And of all the halt and plague-struck there, ' Just one might prove its might. And there was never a kindly grasp, To raise or succour him; sever a strong true hand to help, As he dragged him close tothe brim; So very near to the healing wave, The crippled form had been, And always, just as he reached it, Had someone stepped between. What throes of mortal anguish, What bitter, helpless wad, What bursts of hard, defiant wrath, ! Had known each effort fail! Ere conquered pain won patience, And quietly he said : "Sir, there is none to help me," To the Lord of quick and dead. So many lie in impotence reath sorrow's heavy rod; So many wait, and watch, and pray, For the descending God. One day, when hope has soared to faith, And the spirit owned its rule, The words" Rise up and walk" will come, As erst besidefthe pool. —.All the Year Round.

A DEWDROP IN NOVEMBEP Flash and glitter, dewdrop, In the meadows lone, Blazed thy rubied splendour On thy emerald throne, Like a fairy monarch Dropt from Ilesper's zone. But the eye--; wherewith I viewed thee When, in my youth, morn strewed thee On the vernal grass before me, are o'er changed and shadowed quite. For the days are growing colder, And my heart is growing older, And the stars that lit my morning are declining into night. Topaz of Oberon, Gl3riana's tear! Thou hast less of splendour And less beauty every yelr ! When will the old eyes open— Childhood's morn draw near? Ah ! I know now that for ever Glides the last down Time's dark river, That the birds that cheered our morning never at our noon can sing; That no more will dawn the sweetness Of youth's fairylike completeness' For the sere leaf of November hath no freshness of the Spring. Dewdrop, gentle dewdrop! Magian of the grass! Diamond of Aurora! Mystic wizard's glass! Like thee, me the swift sunbeams Shall wither as they pass. Yet within my spirit's embers Dwells the warmth of past Novembers, A deep4heart adoration for all lowly things like thee; For though gone for e'er the lightness Of morn's most seraphic brightness, nod thedusk of evening shadows burns the twilight • still for me.

Art. thou gleaming, dewdrop, On the pathway still? Thou wilt pass, 0! starlike! Pass and slumber chill, When Winter's homeless snowflakes Fall down upon the hill; Yet I still would have thee quiver Like a',bubble on a river nsleath the shadows, sunlight rifted, like a pearl whirled o'er and o'er, Bringing back the past before me, My lost childhood's impulse o'er me; It ;gives hope to see the lighthouse, though we never touch the:shore.
CHARLES J. O'MA.LLEY.

A farmer and his wife went into a dentist's. "How much do you charge for fillin' teeth?" asked the farmer. From ten shillings to one pound." "And for pullin'?" "Two shillings and sixpence." " Mariar," he said, turning to his wife, "you'd better get it pulled." Smith keep a savage dog on his premises, and near its kennel a board is displayed with the warning in large letters, "Beware of the dog." "I suppose," said Jones, pointing to the words,:" you have painted that sign in large letters so that 'he who runs may read." "so," said Smith," but that he who reads may run." Edmund About once wrote in a feuilleton that Alboni's singing (she was very stout) was "like a nightingale piping out of a lump of suet." The indignant prima donna sent him a goose-quill through the agency of a Marquis. About received the pen with his most charm- ing smile, and said—" I regret, sir, that Madame Alboni should have plucked you for my sake !" A doctor was visiting a lady who was in the habit of sending for him constantly without being ill in any way, B,nd she was entertaining him with a full and particular account of her maladies, the list of which was as long as her glove. "Au, madam," said he, with a look of ad- miration, "what robust health you must enjoy in order to be able to stand all these complaints!" A Clerk in the Corporation offices of a small provincial town desired promotion, and sent in a written applica- tion which contained the following passage :—" During the late war and the consequent disturbed state of the conntry, I displayed such activity that I frequently slept at the office, for which reason I think myself entitled to faldifrable consideration." "I will put your picture in the window, but I must insist that you paint your name on it in large, plain letters," said the proprietor of the art shop to a local amateur artist. "Why should I do that ?" asked the artist, somewhat surprised. "Because I am conscien- tious about this matter. Ido not want an unjust sus- picion to fall on an innocent person." Payment to singers has sometimes taken an odd form. When Mdlle. Zelie, a vocalist from the Theatre Lyrique at Paris, was making a professional tour round the world some years since, she gave a concert at the Society Islands. She agreed to sing an air from " Norma " and a few other songs, and was to receive in exchange a third part of the receipts. When counted, the prima donna's shale was found to consist of three pigs, twenty- three turkeys, and forty-four chickens, five-thousand cocoaenutS, besides considerable quantities of bananas, lemons, and oranges. An English lord who visited America was at a dinner given in his honour. A little daughter of his host who was too well bred to stare, but who eyed him covertly as the occasion presented itself, finally ventured to remark, " And you are really and truly an English lord?" "Yes," be answered pleasantly, "really and truly." "I have often thought I would like to see an English lord," she went on, "and—and—" "And now you are satisfied at last ?" he put in laughingly. "N-o," replied the truthful little girl, "I'm not satisfied. I'm a good deal disappointed !" An invitation to dinner among the middle or upper classes of Japan frequently commences about as follows: —" I beg pardon for thus insulting you in begging your company at my house to dinner. The house is small, and very dirty. Our habits are rude and you may not get anything fit to eat; and yet I hope that you will condescend to be present with us at six o'clock on the ninth of December." Upon arriving at the house you find it spotlessly clean, tasty in arrangement, and the host and hostess affable indeed. The bill of fare consists of ten or fifteen courses, the best the market can afford. All the self-humiliation of the hostis the method adopted to pay you honour. When the late Lord Kaimes went to Aberdeen as a Judge upon circuit, he took up his quarters at a good tavern;and being fatigued and pensive after dinner, he 'inquired of the landlord if there was any learned man in the neighbourhood who could favour him with his com- pany over a glass of wine. The landlord answered that the Professor of Mathematics lived close by; and the Lord of Sessions sent his compliments. The professor was not only eminent in his science, but of various and lively conversation, though he had the defect of La Fontaine and many great men—that of a stupid and dull appearance before it became enlivened by wine or com- papy. After a respectful bow, he took his seat and looked at the fire, quite immersed in some problem he had left. Two glasses of wine were filled and drunk in complete silence. Lord Kaimes, to begin the conver- sation, said, "I have just passed over your new bridge. It is a truly magnificent piece of architecture. What may have been the cost?" "Can't say," was the dry answer of the mathematician, who still looked at the fire. The Judge, surprised and piqued, said, "I saw a board put up of all the tolls to be paid by carriages and animals. Will you be so good as to inform me what is the toll on an ass?" The professor: "I do not pretend to know, but when your Lordship rePasses, the toll- gatherer cannot fail to inform you." The learned Judge, starting and taking him by the hand, exclaimed, "You are my man !" and they began a long and animated con- versation. A man in Monticello, 111., placed some giant powder in, a stove to blow the soot from the pipe. The neighbours all say that it is a pity he couldn't have lived long enough to see how thoroughly the soot was cleared out. All great men have some eccentric habit, and now that Sitting Bull is becoming civilised, he is no exception. Wherever the great chief appears at dinner, be carefully unfolds his napkin, spreads it upon a chair, and sits upon it. "is --our master in?" inquired a collector, with a look on his face which would remind a person of "dun" e, cry time he glanced at it. "He is not, sorr," replied \ the newly-engaged footman of Hibernian descent. "About what time will he be back ?" said the disap- pointed collector. "Irrdade, sorr, when he sends me downstairs to say he's out, I can niver tell for surtin," answered the footman, with a confidential air. A traveller recently returned from India, was relating his travelling impressions. "What a country that is !" he exclaime7l. "There everybody keeps dozens of ser- vants. I had four whose sole business was to look after my pipe. One brought it to me, another filled it, a third lighted it for me—" "And the fourth ?" "The fourth smoked it for me. Tobacco never agreed with me." A teacher in one of the American Indian schools gives the following illustration of an Indian boy's quick thought:—" He had asked the meaning of the word 'miss.' To miss,' I told him, 'is the same as to fail. You shoot at a bird or at a mark, and do not hit it; you miss it. You go to a tailor's for a coat, and your coat firs badly; it is a misfit. You hope to enter the middle class next year; but you cannot pass the examination, and so you miss the promotion.' His face wore a puzzled air, and he shook his head. 'Then,' said I, 'there is another meaning. of "miss." We call a married woman "madam," but an unmarried woman " miss." ' His face brightened; lie smiled and nodded. ' Ah, I see!' said lie, 'she has missed her man." The following amusing story is given in Ned Stafford's Experiences in United States :—As Ned was hurrying back through the broad, well-lit hall of the hotel to re- join his friend, a well-dressed gentleman who was stand- ing on the threshold of a sleeping-apartment accosted him with, "Say, mister, do you understand these new- fangled lights in this hyar hotel?" "Do you refer to the : gaslights?" asked Ned. "We], yes! I reckon it is called gas; hut me and my wife hey bin tryin' ter git a light for I dunno how long, and can't manage ter git a sputter nohow." Ned followed the man into the room, where he observed a lady who was striking matches and ap- plying them to every part of the gas-fittings. "Allow me to see if I can manage it," said Ned. He struck a match, turned the tap, and, to his surprise, lit the gas. "There is nothing wrong that I see,'.' said Ned. " Wal, I'm darned !" ejaculated the man as he stared at the brilliant light. "How on airth did yer do it ?" "Why," said Ned, laughing heartily, "you had forgotten to turn on the gas! How could you expece to get a light ?" "Why," replied the man, "we hey struck a hull box of matches tryin' to find the wick! We are jest down hyar from North Carolina, and I'll swar I never seed such a fixin' as thet in all my born days—no wick nor nothin' ! Show us agin how yer do it t" THE MauSa's Baialrte.—Very Many yeArs ago, when I was living as a boy in a country vicarage in Yorkshire, I heard my mother say that a bank-note, which she had laid on a shelf in the storeroom, always kept locked by herself, had suddenly vanished. Our servants were quite above suspicion, and, on the other hand, the facts that the note had been laid in that particular place, and had disappeared, admitted of no doubt whatever. After some search in the storeroom, and the removal of some of the things in it, it was noticed that there was a mouse- hole in the corner of the floor. A happy thought sug- gested itself, that this should be explored. Accordingly a carpenter was sent for, and I have a very vivid recol- lection of standing by while a board was taken up, and the man's arm extended beneath it up to the shoulder. Immense quantities—l remember two large jars being quite filled—of minute bits of paper were drawn out, the accumulation, probably, of very many years. Strange to say, in one corner of the heap he got hold of a nest of young mice, and brought them out lying on the bank- note! It was wholly uninjured, except from a slight strain; not the smallest portion had been nibbled away, and it was absolutely the only piece of paper left entire lin all that heap. It Happened, then, that the mouse had I carried the note, folded up as it was, through its hole, I and then unfolded and spread it out as a lining to its I nest, and had used it as a blanket, evidently conscious of 'its softness and flexibility. The really wonderful part of the story is the leaving of this one piece of paper entire, apparently because it was a different texture from I the rest. i "SMALL Pox."—The correspondent of a Boston journal ' I writes:—" One of our railroads runs by the County- buildings. Prisoners, paupers, and the deceased are often transported thither on the street cars to save ex- pense. This practice creates great indignation' but so far all protests have been in vain. The other day the conductor was collecting fares from a crowded load. A foreign person, poorly dressed, and with eruptive face, handed up his money. In answer to the question, 'Do you go through ?'—which means, Do you go beyond the city line ?—he said. 'I have got the smallpox do!' 'Have you got the smallpox?' said the astonished con- , ductor. 'Yes I have got the smallpox do.' The pas- sengers came to their feet; women screamed, and their excitement was intense. 'Come, get out of this car; you can't ride here,' said the official. The unfortunate made for the front platform. He was hustled out of the I car, and nearly pitched headlong into the street. He re- covered himself, and started for the front of the car. The driver took the car-hook and threatened 'to brain' him if lie got on. The poor fellow kept up with the horses, shouting 'l'll go; give me my small pox,' pointing I to a two-foot-square chest standing on end behind tne I driver. The mystery was explained. The honest Ger- ' man wanted to pay for his small box on the car as well as his own fare. The conductor apologised, and a seat was offered to the man. But he had had enough of that company. He refused all invitations to ride, shouldered. his 'small pox,' and trudged on foot to the almshouse. Such is one of the consequences of speaking broken English." 1 A REMARKABLE DOG. —A solemn man recently entered 1 a restaurant, followed by his dog, seated himself, and called for a bill of fare. It was given him. "What would you like to have sir ?" asked the waiter, flipping the table with his napkin. The dog meanwhile had climbed upon a chair on the other side of the table, and was gravely regarding his master. "Well," said the solemn man, reflectively, "gimme some ox-tail soup." "Gimme the same," said the dog. The waiter's face assumed the colour of cold boiled veal. "Cup of coffee and plenty of milk," went on the solemn man. "Gimme the same," said the dog. The waiter shuddered, and turning, fled for the kitchen_ A man with a squint at an adjoining table was much interested in the scene. He had observed it closely, and finally spoke to the solemn man—" It must be a fearful lot o' work to teach that dog to talk, mister." "It was," said the solemn man. "I should think so," said the dog. "What 'ud you take for him, naw ?" said the man with a squint. "Wouldn't sell him," said the solemn man. "You'd better not," said the dog. The man with a squint was much impressed. He began making wild offers, and when he reached 200 dollars the solemn man relented. "Well, said he, "I can't refuse that. I hate to part with him, but you can have hint" "He'll be sorry for it," said the dog. The man with the squint drew a cheque for the amount, which he gave to the solemn man. The man was about leaving when the dog cried again—" Never mind, I'll get even. I'll never speak again." He never did. The gentleman with the squint was proprietor of a show. The solemn man was a professional ventriloquist. A QUESTION OF RELIGIOUS DISABILITY.— The other story belonging to James Allan Park, and still floating about the York and Lancaster law courts when I first went round the circuit as marshal, is certainly a strange one, but barrister after barrister so solemnly assured me that it was really true, and that it had been repeated to me without any measurable exaggeration, as to leave me no choice except to believe it. Here it is. Some York- shire footpad (perhaps partly for the fun of the thing) robbed a Chinese pedlar near Leeds. An orthodox churchman, by his own account, he was quite ready to kiss the book and go through all preliminary forms as a Christian, but a terrible doubt fell upon the mind of Park, the presiding judge. He insisted on having the Celestial pedlar's religious views thoroughly ascertained. Ask him," he said, sternly putting aside the prosecuting, counsel's general assurances, "where he was baptised ?" , The obedient interpreter started at once; Hubble Bubble, &c., out came the answer in the same dialect. "My lord," explained the interpreter, "he says he is baptised in every town he comes to." This fact, as far as it went, was undoubtedly creditable to the Chinaman, but it did not absolutely chime in with the thirty-nine articles, or satisfy the exacting piety of the judge. "Oh dear, oh dear," he said, "Ask him where he expects to go after death." The Hubble Bubble process resorted to again brought out this reply in English, "that he expected to go back to Pekin." The judge, completely upset, applied to David Dundas, in these words: "My -dear young friend you have heard what has happened • pray go over to the other court, and ask my brother Holroyd what I had better do." Away went Dundas as directed. Now this brother Holroyd happened to be a very tough hard Yorkshirernan, who had forced his way to the front of his profession by sheer strength rather than by any special cultivation or grace of manner. Dundas found him stripped to the waist, sponging and soaping himself all over (the weather being then very hot), before he started on his walk before dinner. " What," he shouted out from the middle of his basin, "has Park caught a tartar? What an ass he must be to hesitate about the matter! Go back and tell him from me, that the man's evidence is clearly inadmissable." "But, my lord," meekly suggested Dundas, "the fellow says he is a Chris- tian." "He a Christian ! " roared out Hol-royd, resuming his ablutions with redoubled vigour. "Ho be damned; he is no more a Christian than I am." This was the answer that David Dundas had to carry back. Not that I I suppose Holroyd meant more than to reinforce his statement as emphatically as possible, only the soap and water, in which he kept plunging about like a walrus, prevented him from picking and choosing his words with perfect discretion. At any rate, not being under examination, the precise attitude he took up towards the head of the Church, however it might operate against him in the futura, was of no present importance.— Reminiscences of Sir Francis Hastings Doyle.l WHAT Is ROMP° ? THE EXAMINER SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 209 1886 • NOTES ON AGBIOULTURE HORTI THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. " C ULTURE. kc. THE SELECTION OF BREEDING STOCK. The whole question of the selection of breeding stock is full of the greatest interest, and is at once most im- portant to everyone who desires to improve the quality of his animals or birds. In fact, we know of no subject which has so many attractions as that which relates to the selection, natural or otherwise, of the various races of domestic animals. But of course the subject is far too great to be dealt with here, and all that we can do is to show a few of the leading principles—those which are most likely to be of the greatest service to the ordinary poultry breeder, who will be well repaid by the attention he gives to this matter. Perhaps the first question that should be asked is, what are the limitations in this matter of breeding? That is, what restrictions are there to the unlimited power of the breeder? For that there are many re- strictions is indisputable. On this point Darwin says:— "From a remote period, in all parts of the world, man has subjected many animals and plants to domestication and culture. Man has no power of altering the absolute conditions of life; he cannot change the climate of any country; he adds no new element to the soil; but he can remove an animal or plant from one climate to , another, and give it food on which it did not subsist in its natural state. It is an error to speak of man tam- pering with nature' and causing variability. . . . If organic beings had not possessed an inherent tendency to vary, man could have done nothing. He unintention- ally exposes his animals and plants to various conditions of life, and variability supervenes, which he cannot even prevent or check." From this it will be seen that there are defined limits outside which nothing can be done, but these limits are wide enough for the majority of breeders. There is, however, another limitation which is not mentioned in the quotation just made from the great naturalist, but which we may more fully refer to later on, namely, the sterility of hybrids. This is one of the few limitations against which the spirit of the breeder always seems to rebel, for the attempt is constantly being made to break down the naturally imposed barrier. That is a matter, however, we shall leave on one side for the present. To this variability we owe all the many breeds of poultry we have. In the articles on the origin of the domestic fowl, which appeared some time ago, we showed that all these breeds have been derived' from one or at most two sources, a fact that of itself shows what selection will do. The fact is that there is an almost in- exhaustible field for the skill of the breeder within his limitations. Turning again to the late Professor Darwin, we find that on this question he says :—" Although man does not mice variability and cannot even prevent it, he can select, preserve, and accumulate the variations given to him by the hand of nature almost in any way which he chooses; and thus he can certainly produce a great result. Selection may be followed either methodically and intentionally, or unconsciously and unintentionally. Man may select and preserve each successive variation, with the distinct intention of improving and altering a breed, in accordance with a preconceived idea; and by thus adding up variation, 9.f.t?ri Ele slight fts to be im- perceptible by an uneducated eye, he has effected Won- derful i changes and improvements. It can, also, be clearly shown that man, without any Intention or thought of improving the breed, by preserving in each generation the individuals which he prizes most, and by destroying the worthless individuals, slowly, though surely, Indnces great changes. As the will of man thus I comes into play, we can understand how it is that domesticated breeds show adaptation to his wants and pleas-ares. We can further understand how it is that domestic races of animals and cultivated races of plants often exhibit an abnormal character, as compared with natural species; for they have been modified not for their own benefit, but for that of man." There are two ways in which the skill of the breeders can be exercised. First, in the formation of new breeds; and, second, in the improvement of existing varieties. Both these are very desirable objects. The first because some of the most useful varieties of domestic fowls we possess have been what we term manufactured breeds, that is, they have been composed of two or more dis- tinct varieties. Without these our stocks of poultry would have been manifestly inferior to what they are at the present day. Crossing properly conducted is always a means of adding to the stamina of fowls and animals, and these new or manufactured varieties are usually much hardier than are older ones, for there has not been time for fine breeding to weaken the strain. This work, however, of producing new varieties is not open to many breeders, as it takes a considerable amount of time, and often the expenditure of much money. We were not long ago in the yard of a very noted and skilful breeder, who showed us the result of sonic of his experiments in the production of one new variety. He had been en- gaged on it nine years, and yet he had not fully suc- ceeded. Therefore the work of most breeders is limited to the improvement of existing varieties. And this second way permits of enough work to satisfy .the majority of people. Some breeds, it is true, appear to be as near perfect as it is possible to get, but these are few and far between,' and in the others there need be no lack of work. Whatever may be the object of the poultry breeder it is necessary, if he is to succeed, to have some ideal towards which he can strive, for without this he is almost certain to be erratic in his efforts. Those who object to the present number of varieties forget that each of them has some quality to conserve, and even if there be mistaken ideas as to the connection of colour and economic qualities, less harm is done than if we had not these clear lines ef demarcation. If it were not for the strict adherence to types and standards we should soon see a very marked decadence in our poultry. The law of reversion would come into play, and it would be impossible to gauge the merits of almost any stock, for breeding would then be a lottery and nothing more. Now we can say that certain breeds are most noted as layers, and others as table fowls, and there is no doubt on this matter, for years of experience and breeding have shown that this is so. It is true, as has already been acknowledged, that the attentions of fanciers in some breeds have been injurious, but in the majority of cases the reverse is the fact. In seeking for profitable poultry we are quite sure that it is the better plan to run upon regular lines, and as far as possible utilise ex- isting breeds, which, with due consideration for economic qualities, may be made first class in these points. It does not make the Shorthorn any worse as a useful breed because conformity to the adopted standard is insisted upon, nor does it detract from the mutton pro- duced because there is a defined standard for the South- down sheep. The reverse is the case. The connection between economic qualities and ex- ternal characteristics is full of very great difficulties, but there are certain characteristics which go side by side with specific qualities. For instance, the size of the comb is a pretty sure indication of laying or table quali- ties, and feathering on the legs seems to be co-relative with the buff tint on the shell. Nearly all the large combed fowls are the best layers, whilst the small combed fowls are those that excel in table qualities; and, further, the breeds that are feathered on the legs lay the smallest eggs in proportion to the size of the hen, and the eggs are tinted in colour. In all these instances probably the cause that rules the quality influences the characteristic. But we are confessedly most Ignorant on this point, for it has not yet, so far as we are aware, been taken up as a field of inquiry, fertile though it would be. There are, however, many characteristics which are not influenced in this way, and are not co-relative to any characteristic. Colour is a case in pciint. The plumage of the black-red Game fowl and of the brown Leghorn are alike, but these two breeds are entirely opposed in their special qualities. The Game is specially noted as a table fowl, whereas the Leghorn is strongest in its laying. Plumage and crests may be regarded as not affecting the economic qualities of poultry, and may therefore be lef out of this consideration.

Emerick Bell, of Mansfield, Rickland Co., Ontario, says an exchange, has a Durham cow that has given birth to seven cows in 700 days, and eleven calves at five births. Most of these births were triplets. The weight of the herd—cow and seven calves—is now over five tons. The cow has produced over four tons of beef and veal in three years, and will come in again in -November. HINT TO FARMERS.—A farmer in the neighbourhood of Sittingbourne has been supplying fine legs of mutton at Thd. per lb., and less prime parts at a lower rate. He says he realises 12s. more on a sheep than he can get from a :,butcher, and also retains e‘ the fifth quarter," which 30 years ago was considered a fair margin of pro— fit for the butcher. The agricultural prosperity of Holland, it is stated, is due to the quantity of live stock kept by farmers, hence foreign competition of cereals is not felt. Of the total arable land in that kingdom, 26 per cent. is under culti- vation, and 34 in grass. There are 41,000 holdings between two and 12 acres, and 51 between 375 acres and above. There are 1.1. millions of cattle, and of a million of sheep, while the goats number 156,000. In 1877 there were only 96 agricultural machines worked by steam; at present there are 150. "A TRUCE IN GOD'S NAME."—Under the above head- ing, and referring to the imprisoned crofters, the Oboe Times says :—" Shylock was no more exacting than the Highland landlords are in their present mood. Try to disguise it as we may, the fact stands forth that eight men are undergoing a term of imprisonment because the Duke of Argyll willed it. If the Duke had treated the people of Tiree with justice, there would have been no appropriation of Greenhill, no summonses to serve, no marine expedition, no arrests, and no cruel punish- ments." WORMS IN PIGS.—To destoy worms in pigs a strong purgative with two to four flt6:l drachms of turpentine should be administered. Considerable care must be taken in the administration of drenches to pigs, as the fluid must be allowed to trickle slowly down the cheek. If it be poured in rapidly, as the pig is certain to scream, there is a great danger that it will pass into the wind- pipe and suffocate the animal. "A practice which has been found to succeed admirably," remarks Professor Gamgee, " consists in taking an old shoe, cutting off the toe part of the upper leather, and allowing the pig to suck the toe part of the sole whilst the fluid is poured into the shoe. In this way the pig absolutely sucks the mixture, and there need be no apprehension of untoward consequences."—A. S. SUCCESSES OF TUB HEREFOrms.—At the New York State fair, held at the end of September, the bull "Cheva- lier," exported to Mr. Bissell by Mr. Tudge, took the first prize in his class, and was adjudged to be the best animal of all breeds in the show yard, where 700 beasts were exhibited. "Chevalier" was by "Auctioneer," out of "Cinderella," and was bred by Mr. Tudge, At the same show a On Of "Chetaliet" won the first prize in the Hereford heifer-calf Class.-Mr, Thomas Fenn, of Downton, has heard from Mr. Sandford Flemming, of Ottawa, Canada, that at ay.!, Ottawa annual show held in August, a bull-calf by "Ldtd Wilton" exported by Mr. Fenn last year, took the first prize for bulls of all breeds, and the champion prize against all classes and all breeds. DIARRITCRA IN CALVES.—ThiS is a frequent and fatal disease, attacking calves from a month to two or three months old, and in the majority of cases is the conse- quence of neglect and irregularity in feeding. Early ex- posure to cold and wet brings it on. Full and hearty meals occasionally given to half-starved calves often derange the whole alimentary canal, and cause violent purging. Young animals should never be stinted in the quantity or quality of their food, and changes from one kind of food to another must be carried out with care and judgment. When continual purging sets in in calves of the above age, give 4oz. of raw linseed oil, to act as a gentle purge, and a diarrhcea powder in six or twelve hours, as the case requires. Repeat the powder each day until favourable symptoms set in. With older calves the dose of linseed oil must be increased to 6oz. or Boz. The animals must be fed on sweet hay and plenty of gruel made from wheat flour. For young calves, arrowroot should take the place of milk in feeding. PIG SUCKLED BY Cows.—Within the last few months the rather unusual relation of several cows allowing a pig of seven months old to suck them has occurred on our farm. My notice was first drawn to the fact by the man who milks the cows finding someone had forestalled him in a very efficient manner, and then it was noticed, when the cows were driven from the meadows to the courtyard to be milked, a certain black pig was always waiting for them, and immediately sat up on his hind legs and commenced sucking. Out of about ten cows, five or six were very agreeable to this, but the remainder did not recognise the young porker as their legitimate offspring, and would not allow this irregular proceeding. Just at the time of the cows being milked, the pig would leave those he was with the other part of the day, and be in waiting for the cows to be in the farmyard for his extra meal, and during the fortnight it went on the pig gained in flesh considerably. As this was an expensive way of feeding a seven months old pig, and a bad example to his brethren, he was put in the sty and fed.—doma S. WROTE (Coomb), Bigbury, Devon). PROFESSOR GLEASON ON HORSES.—Mr. Jas. Long writes in the Manchester Guardian :—Professor Gleason, who has recently been giving some good advice to the American public about horses, declares that those animals having long ears with long straight hairs inside, and which have narrow foreheads and round sunken orbits, are invari- ably obstinate and stupid, and especially if the nostrils are small and thick. On the other hand, he believes that horses are generally intelligent and good and faithful servants when they have thort ears which are furnished with short curly air inside, and which have straight faces, broad heads, and large thin nostrils. This is worth remembering as indicative of character, for in an animal with which man is so much connected a knowledge ot character is essential. Speaking of training a colt, he places great stress on the word of order which is given to the animal, and which he is supposed to learn. There is a great deal in this remark; for example, the word " Whoa " really orders the animal to stop, but this is given at all sorts of times when the terms " Easy " or " Steady " should be used. If the colt is taught to stop when the word" Whoa" is given, it is evident that it should not be used when he is required to slacken pace or be careful. A colt should be treated firmly yet with kindness, and firmness is best indicated by seeing that an order when given is carried out, and by show- ing no fear of the animal either in his stall or when at work. I remember the case of a vicious stallion which no one dared touch except his attendant. A friend of mine was told this, and he said that he would go up to the beast and take hold of his tail. This he did without any fear, marching up boldly and seizing his tail as if he were going to harness the animal. It was the horse and not the man who was afraid in this case. Pro- fessor Gleason deals with the fear of a horse in somewhat novel terms. Most people who are used to horses are aware that they sometimes shy at a white object, at a bicycle, or at an umbrella. The professor says that to horses the white object may appear a yawning chasm, and a bicycle a wingless monster, and so on. Therefore the proper plan is to let the animal touch and smell these objects and see them on both sides, the off and near. He should be farnilarised with every object he fears, and he will soon cease to regard them with anything but con- tempt. To thrash a horse which has exhibited fear on this account is unwise, especially after he has passed the object of his terror; he should rather be spoken to kindly and encouraged continually. I once rode by the side of a splendid whip who drove me 40 miles behind a New Forest stallion of high mettle. Several times the animal refused to pass a bough of a tree lying in the road • on each occasion he was forced to do so, but not by thrashing, and subsequently he was turned round and made to face the object he had feared. Treatment of this kind is not lost upon horses, who speedily respect as well as fear the master who has given them the lesson.

t'L.A.NTING VRtr/T TWEEB.--aNQ time should be lost in planting all kinds of fruit trees, 2nd the fine open weather we are having is greatly in favour of such work, except perhaps in localities where the amount of rain has rendered the soil temporarily unworkable. Before laying out much money on trees, and sacrificing time and labour, it would be as well to ascertain first if the land is water-logged or not, by digging a hole or a num- ber of them down to the subsoil and allowing them to re- main until there has been a heavy rain or two, and if then water does not remain more than a few hours in the hole the ground may be regarded as fairly well drained. On soils with a sandy or gravelly bottom it would pass away as fast as it descended. When plant- ing is conducted in wet weather do not throw ay of the soil that has been trampled into the holes made for the trees, as its exclusion from the elements will cause it to remain adhesive, but after the roots are covered with good friable soil there is no objection to six inches of it being placed uppermost if it is otherwise good. As to holes for young fruit trees it is not advisable to go more than six inches deep, and we would as soon plant them on the surface when only a few odd trees are dealt with, and cover the roots over to a depth of eight inches with the neighbouring soil, so that by the time we had done our tree would be on a mound reaching to a distance of three or four feet from the stem and not terminating abruptly. Nothing can be more conducive to fertility in young trees than this method of planting, and the heavier the soil the more apparent will be the result. If every two or three years the points of the roots are raised until they reach the boundary of the mound, they may afterwards be confined to that area for years and dig- ging or trenching can be annually conducted to that dis- tance from the tree, providing it is performed about this time of the year, or not too late in spring. In the summer or during prolonged drought, the newly planted trees would be benefited with three or four inches of mulching with good manure, and, indeed, all mound- planted trees at that season, especially if carrying heavy crops, would derive equal profit and amply repay for the I labour incurred. Each tree should be staked, and for the 1 matter of that, the stake may be driven into the ground • where the tree is to be and after running a piece of rag two or three times round the stem at the point where the tie is to be, pass the string over this pad and round the stake and secure the tree to it before attempting to cover the roots; in this way it dispenses with a second person to hold the trees, and all risk of driving the stakes against some of the best roots is avoided. The following varie- ties of Kitchen apples do well in most gardens in Lan- cashire and the North :—Nelson's Glory, New Hawthorn- due, Colville Blanche, Yorkshire Greening, Scotch Brid- get, Lord Suffield, Livesey, and Wellington. Here is also a list of dessert apples :—Orange Pippin, Cox's Pippin, Golden Reinette, Cornish Gillyflower, Golden Pippin, Cox's Pomona, Kinn. Pippin and Blenheim Orange. Pears may be represented by the following :—Beurre d'Amau- lis, William's Bon Chretien, Louise, Bonne of Jersey, Hessle, Red Doynne, Comte do Lamy, Jargonnelle, Eye- wood and Yat. Of plums, Victoria and Prince of Wales are the most certain croppers. Greengage, Golden Drop and Magnum Bonum, producing a few at intervals of 4 or 6 years. Cherries will not pay for room, except such as may be planted against walls, and in this way they seldom fail a crop, the Morello doing well on a north aspect. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Rose Cuttings : These will be abundant on shoots that have been pegged down, and in all instances in which these can be spared, it would be as well to cut them close to the base, and then pro- ceed to slip the cuttings, and beyond shortening some of the longest, they require no further manipulating, and are ready to go In the ground. These trimmings are usually thrown away at pruning time in the spring, as it would be useless to put cuttings in then, but if inserted now the greater part will form roots. As they require to be put in firm it is a good plan to cut out a narrow channel eight inches deep, and against the solid side fix the cuttings' and cover their base with an inch of sand, or, perhaps, better still, spread that depth of sand on the trench bottom before fixing the cuttings. Fill in the soil and press it by walking in the direction of the row with one foot in the channel. Then dig more soil and press it in a similar way until about a foot distant from the row; then make a perpendicular cut, as before, about nine inches from the row, and proceed to lay in the second row of cuttings.

THE GREEINHOUSH.—A succession of dull, wet days will cause some of the occupants of the greenhouse to damp, and the first to show this most probably will be the flowers of Primulas, and, maybe, portions of the growth. It will, therefore, be advisable to light a fire in the morn- ing, and open the ventilators, so as to allow the moisture to escape and keep down the temperature, which will be unavoidably raised by the heating of the apparatus. Overheating must be guarded against, and it is sufficient for the pipes or the flue to be simply warmed, and the flue should be allowed to burn out some time before closing up. Watering the plants should take place early in the morning of fine days, or at such times as when a fire is going. Beep a sharp look out for green fly, which first makes its appearance on Pelargoniums, Calceolarios, and Cinerarios, and fumigate lightly for two or three nights, choosing a still one for the operation.

A love-smitten gentleman, after conversing a while ' with a lady on the interesting topic of matrimony, con- cluded at last with the emphatic question, "Will you ' have me?" "I am very sorry to disappoint you," re- plied the lady, "and hope my refusal will not give you ' pain; but I must answer 'No." "Well, well, that will do," said her philosophical lover; "and now suppose we . change the subject." . A PRIZE FIGHT. The fight between two light-weight pugilists, Kendrick and Cheese, which was prevented from taking place on Monday, at Barnstead, Surrey, Came off on Tuesday morning, near the Welsh Harp, at Hendon. After fighting twenty-four rounds, in one hour and twenty-five minutes, Kenirick was declared the winner, Cheese's second throwing up the sponge. There were few persons present. The police beard of the affair and overtook the parties. Four men were arrested including Cheese. Ma. STANSFELD ON THE IRISH QUESTION.—Mr. Stans- feld, speaking at the Bristol Operatives' Liberal Associa- tion meeting on Monday night, said that the future of the Liberal party, whether of union or disintegration, depended upon the relation of that party to the Irish question. There was no use in disguising opinions or pretending to union where it did not exist. It would not be found possible to drag- the hulk of the Liberal party from the principles laid down at the recent Leeds Conference. The desire of nationality had taken firm hold upon the Irish mind. The policy of delay enunciated by Lord Salisbury and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach was enormous folly which would dan- gerously stimulate the violent passions of the Irish people. The present quiet in Ireland, while largely due to pressure brought by the Conservative Government to bear on :he Conservative Irish landlords not to exact their high rents, was mostly due to the 'lrish people finding themselves in alliance with the great British Liberal party and feeling themselves bound not to damage that alliance by violence. IMr. Goschen has declined to become a candidate for the representation of Brighton. THE cERIOCS CHARGB AGAINST AN ARMY OFFICER. A Chatham correspondent states that a charge of a startling and painful character against an army officer holding a high position has created great excitement. The specific charge is that of fraudulently appropriating a large sum of money, the property of the War Office. On being arrested he indignantly repudiated the accusation, mad averred that the whole matter was a misapprehension on the part of the War Office authorities. At a private sitting of magistrates he was admitted to bail in £2,000. It was reported that the total sum alleged to have been misappropriated exceeds £4,000. The case will form the subject of a magisterial examination at the middle of next week, when it is expected that some revelationsof an extraordinary kind respecting the method of controlling and periodically inspecting the cleri- cal departments of the army will be made. HEARTLESS CASE OF BIGAMY AT HULL.--At the York Assizes. on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, a clerk named Thomas Mathieson, 45, was indicted for bigamy at Levenshul me, near Manchester, and he pleaded guilty. The prisoner lived at Hull with his wife and family, and under the guise of religion made the acquaintance of a Miss Baker in 1882. He paid her attentions, and represented that he was a widower. Questioned on several occasions as to whether he was married, he firmly denied that he ' was, and even went so far as to produce funeral cards purporting to relate to the death of his first wife. By this means he induced Miss Baker to marry him in August last year, after a long courtship, and since then a child had been been. After the marriage prisoner took his second wife to Hull, and actually kept both wives, though in different houses. His lordship said this was about as abominable and creel a case of bigamy as he had met with for many a day. The punishment must be exemplary. THIS SEBRIGHT NULLITY CASE: JUDGMENT.—In the , Divorce Court on Tuesday Mr. Justice Batt gave judgment in the Sebright nullity case, in which the wife petitioned for the nullity of her marriage, on the ground that her con- sent was improperly obtained. The e-eatest interest was evinced in the case. Long before the court was opened the doors were beseiged by people anxious to gain admission; and when the proceedings commenced the body of the court and gallery were crowded ; whilst many were unable to ob- ' tam n entrance. Miss Scott, the petitioner, her mother, and the younger sister were present : but Mr. Sebright was not in court, although represented by counsel. Justice Butt took his seat at 11-45, and at once proceeded to deliver judgment. He said the petitioner sought a declaration of . nullity of marriage, alleged to have been improperly solemn- ised on the 30th January, 1886, on the ground of fraud and duress. She also alleged that the marriage was never con- summated. The responeent denied the charges, and sought a decree of conjugal rights. On the evidence he had heard he had come to the clear conclusion that long before the ceremony was gone through Miss Ecott's feelings towards Sebright were such that of free and unconstrained will she would never have married him. She bad been reduced to such a mental and bodily state by coercion and threats. He should not consider it consistent with justice to hold this marriage binding, and declared the ceremony null. He pro- nounced in favour of the prayer of the petitioner and dis- missed the counter claim, and ordered the respondent to pay the costs of this suit. The petitioner, on hearing the judges's decision, showed no signs of emotion, but immediately they emerged from the Court the mother and daughter kissed each other passionately, amid signs of sympathy from the crowd assembled in the corridor. The petitioner, with her friends were heartily congratulated by those surrounding them on the result, and were followed through the corridors by a large crowd. Miss Scott then held a kind of informal levee, and on emerging from the chief entrance she was loudly cheered by a large number of persons who bad assembled, and the cheering was renewed as her carriage drove away. The greatest public interest had been aroused in the case.

To Boland brave in state, and Wyersdale, which as well As any sylvan nymphs their beautious scites may boast, Whose Ecchos sent the same all round about the coast, That there was not a Nymph to jollity inclined, Or of the woody brood, or of the watry kind, But at their fingers' ends they Ribbels Song could say, And perfectly the Note upon the Rag-pipe play.*
River Lune. Wyre leaps against the tides, and cries to cry-stall Lun The Flood that names the Towne from whence the Shire

begun, Her title, first to take, and loudly tells the Flood, That if a little while she thus but trifling stood, These prettie brooks would be before her still prefer'd, Whilst the long-wandering Lun, with good advisement heard, As shee comes ambling on from Westmoreland, where first Arising from her head, amongst the mountains nurst, By many a pretty spring that howerly- getting strength, Arriving in her course in Lancashire at length; And Wenning on the way presents her copious spring, And next she Henbourne hath, and Robourne, which do bring Their bounties in one banke, their Mistress to preferre, That shee with greater state may come to Lancaster, To give to this her Towne, what rightly doth belong; Of this most famous Shire, our Lune thus frames her song : "First, that most precious thing, and pleasing most to man, Who from him (made of earth) immediately began, His shee selfe, woman, which the goodliest of this Isle This country [county] hath brought forth, that much doth grace my style; Why should those Ancients else, which so much knowing were, When they the blazons gave to every several shire, Fayre women as mine owne, have titled due to me? Besides, in all this Isle, there no such Cattell be, For largene,sse, home, and haire, as these of Lancashire; So that from every part of England farre and neere, Men haunt her Marts for store, as from her Race to breed. And for the third, wherein she doth all Shires exceed, Be those great race of Hounds, the deepest-mouthed of all, The other of this kind, which we our Hunters call, Besides, her Natives have been anciently esteemed For Bow-men neere our best, and ever have been deem'd So loyall, that the Guard of our preceding Kings Of them did most consist; but yet 'mongst all these things, Even almost ever since the English Crowne was set Upon the lawfull head of our Plantaginet, In Honor, next the first, our Dukedome was alloyed, And alwayes with the great'st revenues was endow'd ; , And after, when it hapt, France-conquering Edward's blood Divided in itselfe, here for the garland stood; The right Lancastrian line it from York's issue bare; The Red Rose, our brave Badge, that in their helmets ware, In many a bloody field, at many a doubtful fight, Against the House of Yorke, which have for theirs the White. "So blyth and bonny now the Lads and Lasses are, That ever as anon the Bag-pipe up doth blow, Cast in a gallant Round about the Hearth they gee, And at each pause they kisse, was never seen such rule In any place but heere, at Boon-fire, or at Yeule And every- village smokes at Wakes with lusty cheere, ; Then Hey, they cry, for Lune, and Hey for Lancashire; That one high Hill was heard to tell it to his brother, That instantly again to tell it to some other, From Hill againe to Vale, from Vale to Hill it went, The High-Dinds they againe it to the lower sent, The mud-exhausted Mores, and Mosses deepe arnonge, With the report thereof each Road and Harbour rung; The Sea-Nymphs with their Song so great a coy-le doe keepe, They cease not to resound it over all the Deepe.

TERRIBLE BOILER EXPLOSION NEAR BRlSTOL.—Farring- t.n Gurney Colliery was the scene of a boiler explosion on Monday morning, when a large boiler supplying steam for Pumping exploded, killing and injuring a number of work- men. The boiler, by the force of the explosion was carried 70 yards, and then rolled thirty yards. Many bricks and Stones were blown 200 yards. All the buildings within that distance were extensively damaged, windows being blown out and tiles from roofs. A man named John Small was on the spot. Another is in a precarious state, having lost a leg. Many others were taken to the hospitals. LORD SALISBURY AND THE SOCIALIST DEIEOI4BE-RATION. —The Central news states that Lord Salisbury will de- cline to receive any deputation of Socialists on Sunday next. Even were his lordship inclined to recognise the Social demonstrations as in any way representing the working classes, he holds that a personal discussion between himself and the unemployed could yield no practical or useful result at the present time. Moreover, official retires in the possession of the Government prove that distress' as tested by the applications for relief. is considerably below the average, and there is not the slightest reason for suppos ing that the Poor Law authorities will not be able to deal effectively with any exceptional distress which may arise during the winter now commenced. It is not expected that the police authorities will interfere with the meeting pro- posed to be held in Trafalgar-square on Sunday; but no mob will be permitted to invade Arlington-street, as threatened.

AN OLD POET'S DESCRIPTION OF LANCASHISE PEOPILE AND RIVERS. The lines in which that quaint Jacobean poet- topographer, Michael Drayton, in his:wonderful poem entitled Polyolbion, describes the Rivers of Lancashire, and, incidentally, marks the characteristics of the people of this county—the handsome women in par- ticular—may he known to a few, but probably only a few readers of this journal ; for the Polyolbion is a scarce book, and one which only lovers of the older literature are likely to inquire for. The portion of Drayton's book in which they occur was published in the year 1622, and in the reign of James the First, who had travelled through Lancashire five years before. We extract only the lines relating to the Ribble and its tributaries, prefixed by two or three lines ending the description of the Irwell, and a portion of the story of the River Lune. Ye lustie Lasses then, in Lancashire that'dwell, For Beautie that are said to bear away the Bell, Your Countries Horn-pipe, y,ee so minsingly that tread, As yes the Eg-pye love, and Apple cherry-red; [He that will fish for a Lancashire manot any time or tide Must bait his hooka with a good Eg-pie, or an Apple with a red side] )grifttl In all your mirthful songs, and merry meetings tell That Erwell every way doth Ribbell fare excel. * * "But Ribbell that this while for her advantage wrought, Of what she() had to say, doth well herself advise, And to bravo Erwell's speech thus boldly shee replies. With that whereby the most thou thinkst me to disgrace, That I an Alien am (not rightly of this place) My greatest glory is, and Lancashire therefore To Nature for my birth beholden is the more; That Yorkshire, which all Shires for largeness doth exceed, A Kingdom to be cald that well deserves indeed, And not a fountain hath that forth from her doth flow, Within her spacious self, but that she can bestow, To Lancaster yet lends me, Ribbell, from her store, Which adds to my renoune, and makes her bountie move. From Penigent's proud foot as from my source I slide, That Mountains my proud Syre, in height of all his pride, Takes pleasure in my course, as in his first-borne flood; And Ingleborrow Hill, of that Olympian brood, With Pendle, of the North the highest Hills that be, Doe wistly we behold, and are beheld of me. These Mountaines make me proud, to gaze on me that stand, So Long-ridge, once arrived on the Lancastrian land, Salutes me, and with smiles me to his soyle invites, So have I many a flood, that forward me excites; As Hodder, that from home attends me from my Spring; Then Calder, coming downs from Blackstone Edge, doth bring Me easily on my way, to Preston the great'st Towne Wherewith my 13a,a$ are blest; whereat my going downe, Cicero Darwen on along me to the Sea cloth drive, And on my spacious fall no sooner I arrive, But Savock to the North from Long-ridge making way, To this my greatness adds, when in my ample Bay, Swart Dulas comming in, from Wiggin with her ayds, Short Taud, and Dartow small, two little Country Mayds, (In these low watery lands, and moory Mosses bred) Doe pN nvyo fely layd in mighty Neptune's bed; And (butting, in my (talrse, even through the very heart Of this renowned Shire, so equally it part, As Nature should have said, Loe, this I meant to doe; This Flood divides this Shire thus equally in two. Yee Mayds, the Horne-pipe then so mincingly that tread, As yee the Eg-pie love, and Apple eherry-red; In all your mirthful songs, and merry meetings tell That Ribbell every way your Erwell doth excel. "Here ended thee againe, when Marten's Mosse, and Mere, With Ribbels sole reply so much revived were, That all the Shores resound the River's good successe, And wondrous joy there was all over Andernesse, Which straight conveyed the newes into the upper land, Where Pendle, Penigent, and Ingleborow stand; Like gyants, and the rest doe proudly overlooke ; Or, Atlas-like, as though they onely undertooke To under-prop high Heaven or the wide Welkin dar'd, Who in their Ribbles praise (be sure) no speeches spar'd ; That the loud sounds from them downs to the Forrests fell,

div.head: PRESENTATION TO SCHOOL INSPECTORS.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO SCHOOL INSPECTORS.

On Saturday, a largely-attended meeting of the teachers of elementary sebools in the Southport and Warrington Educational District was held at the Albert Hall, Southport, for the purpose of present- ing to Mr. W. Scott Coward, late district inspector, and Mr. T, Glover, late assistant inspector, addresses of congratulations and goodwill upon their promo- tion to be inspector and sub-inspector respectively of the district of Manchester. The testimonial, sub- scribed to by all the teachers in the district, had been carried out by a committee consisting of , Messrs. C. Twice, J. Dewhurst, J. C. Crawford, R. J. Gosson, and T. Walbank, the latter gentleman act- ing as hon. secretary. On Saturday, Mr. C. Twiss presided, supported on the platform by the other members of the committee, Mr. Coward, Mr. Glover, the Rev. Canon Herbert Jones (Southport). the Rev. C. S. Hope, Dr. Mackie (Mayor of Warrington), Mr. G. R. Rowlandson (Bootle), Mr. C. T. Harrison (suc- ceeding inspector of the Southport and Warringtox district), Mr. G. Syder (assistant inspector), Mr. C. Bailey (Warrington), Mr. D. Finney, and other gen- tlemen. It may be stated that the address to Mr. Coward was enclosed in a handsome case, having folded doors of silvered glass, embellished with paintings of passion flowers, the whole mounted on an elegant easel. That to Mr. Glover was in book form, enclosed in a tastefully designed case of mor- occo, having in front an effective painting of sea- scape, and inside a border of conventual roses. The Chairman said it waa leis privilege in the name of the teachers to offer to Mr. Coward and Mr. Glover the warmest congratulations on their promotion, so well earned, wishing them a long, useful, and happy future, and hoping that tiler in their new district might earn as many friends as were then gathered round them (Applause.) Mr. Walbank then read the address to Mr. Coward as fol- lows :—Dear sir,—While congratulating you upon your well-earned promotion to the Senior Inspectorate, we regret that with this change ends your more immediate and perso- nal connection with us, a connection which, throughout the whole of the fifteen years you have held the office, has been ' marked by the most genial courtesy and kindly recoanition of all honest efforts on the part of those placed under your supervision. Your honourable devotion to the interests of the Education Department evidenced by your exactitude to the minutest details of the work, linked with your intelli- gent conception of the code, has not only raised the educe- , tional tone throughout your district, but has done much to, broaden the basis of national education and to make it a living power in the State. Possessing and importing bete the work, as you have done, the innate genius ef teachinef an intense sympathy with children, and rare natural refine- ment, combined with a keen estimate of character, a quick recognition of moral worth and great tact, you have placed the profession on a very high standpoint, and by dint of association and example have so striven to purify the aim and fire the zeal of tho teachers as to make the tvork to them, als it unquestionably is to you, a work of love, Wq that you may have a happy and useful future, and that while retaining our heartiest good wishes, yen may gain from the teachers in your extended district a repetition of all the good feeling which has prompted this expression.— We remain, dear sir, on behalf of the teachers, yours faith- fully, A. Kay (Chairman), T. Walbank (Secretary), John Dewleurst (Treasurer). The Rev. C. S. Hope having expressed the regret felt by echeol managers in Southport At tbc departure of Mr. Cow- ard and Mr. Glover, The Mayor of Warrington (Dr. Mackie) was called upon, and said for himself, as one who believed in volestary schools, it was gratifying that they had been able in Wars rington—not to try Board schools and then give them up— but to do without them from the first—(bear, hear)—and that they had been able to show that their voluntary schools were ample and equal to the requirements of a population by no means over rich, neither for education nor in any other respect. A number of years since they associated te- gether in Warrington to a man to aive rewards every Christ- mas to those able to show ability in reading and writ- ing, and to those who could show remarkable ability in those subjects. The movement was organised in fact for the purpose of producing readers with a view of sup- porting the lot of newspapers they had there—(laughter)— and there was no doubt about it but that the great expan- sion of educational machinery since that period bad en- abled much to be done, not only in spreading literature, but in its being actually devoured. The consequence was that - they heel at Warrington a splendid Museum and Free Library, and they were about to go at it hammer and tongs in favour of a Free Lending Library in the course of a few. day!. He congratulated them on (heir gathering that day,. and expressed a hope that they might see the growth of such gatherings between the inspectors and themselves, and they evinced a feeling without which educational work. would never be pleasant, and, he ventured to say, never profitable. Education and the cause of the people be noore especially represented that day. (Applause.) Mr. Rowlandson, of Bootle, having followed, Mr. Finney said Mr. Coward came into the district when the code was entering in the second stage of its develop- ment. He succeeded a gentleman of very high attainments, a gentleman, moreover, in every sense of the word, and for whorls even at that distant period he (the speaker) enter- tained a very lively regard. Doubtless Mr. Coward's , standard had been high—(hear, hear, and laughter)—but for himself be was not one of those who thought it too high; and Mr. Coward, it seemed to him, had every reason to be satisfied with the great strides which education in that district had made. He joined with others in speaking of Mr. Coward's unvarying courtesy, and in wishing him in the future even greater success than in the past. (Ape plause.) Mr. Dewhurst, of the Warrington Parish Schools' in mak- ing the presentation, said Mr. Coward had been long con- nected with the Warrington district, and during that time many new schools had been built, old ones enlarged, and a better supply obtained of apparatus, with a much larger adult teaching staff. All these things had coma about through Mr. Coward's suggestions, and as a consequence, the whole tone and character of education in the district had been improved. (Applause.) Mr. Coward, who was heartily received, in reply said that when he became school inspector of the district fifteen years ago, a desire for popularity was the last feeling in his heart, but be came among them with the feeling that all hearts were tender, and ought to be considered. He Came to his work convinced that there was a code to be adminis- tered, and that that code could be thrown into a letter, but that that letter, barely fulfilled, would be the most miser- able performance possible. It would mean condensing and devitalising the grand work and purpose of education. There was a spirit as well as a letter, and if they were to have elucation worthy the name, for which the people who were to pay would pay most willingly, it had need to be a real progress and developement of the powers of the mind. That had be.en his cardinal principle—making the mind a true brilliant with all its facets set to catch light from every, side. The true object of all education was that. Develop- ment might be too fast ; that was over pressure. It might be too harsh; that was imprudent and unwise inspee- tion, but it could be developed according to the analogy of nature with a' sweet unconscious growth, in which hardly the transition was marked from leaflets to stem, from stem to foliage, and from foliage to fl ,wer and fruit. Hoeshoped to see education of this kind In our schools, and not onlr to leave the desire of knowledge burning in the mind of the scholar, but to give him the instruments of thoughtful and observant men—men who could use a book intelligently and express their thoughts in words. Instruments such as these the population of the country could use to make their lives sweeter and better. Then there was again the great moral question of implanting in the mind a sense that they were not educating people merely to despise the kind of labour in which they were engaged, and to look forward to something a little higher but infinitely superior. To do that would be t• create discontent and misery. Education was to teach people that their present lives could be dignified and higher, to increase their sense of self-respect. That was the hind of moral training he hoped to see fulfilled in the schoole of the coentry. As to Board Schools he needed to say a word, because his name had been brought into connec- tion with them. He was no enemy of Board Schools. Board Schools were necessary and inevitable, and they were increasing, and would increase. Let them make the best of it. Let them not carry on with them an internecine feud. Board Schools would not be more friendly on that account. They sere, he believed, the growing means by which the country teas to be educated. The voluntary system had no means of coping with the great masses in the towns, who were really nameless as to religion, and those • responsible for them was clearly organised eociety in the shape of School Boards. In certain parts of England he regretted that thee() existed towards Board Schools a spirit querulous and unfriendly. (Applause.) A similar address was afterwards presented to Mr. Glover by Mr. Dewhurst.—A tea and concert of miscellaneous vocal music followed. During the concert items were contributed by Miss Fry, Mise Slater, 5E83 Podmore, Mr. Dewhurst, Mr. Price, Mr. Groyson, and Mr. Derry. Mr. T. Halsall acted with efficiency as accompanist.

_ FOREIGN NEWS- , THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. AUSTRIA'S ATTITUDE.—THE REFUSAL OF THE • THRONE. Pasts, SATURDAY.—An impoitant statement regarding Bulgaria was made to-day by Count Kalnoky at the sitting; of the Foreign Affairs Committee of the Hungarian Delega- tion. The Minister stated that the mission of General Eatilbars was merely a phase of the question, and one the Importance of which had been greatly over-estimated. The mission was only of a passing character, and would hardly leave lasting traces behind. It was, he said, to Austria- Hungary's interest that no step of an injurious character and at variance with existing Treaties should be taken, and that the independence ol the country as guaranteed by Europe should remain unassailed. Count Andrassy rose, and de- clared that it was the general opinion of the Home, that no sensible man in Hungary desited war, but rather peace, as long as it could be maintained without prejudice to the na- tional bonour.—The debate on Count Kalnoky's statement is fixed for the 16th instant. TIRNOVA, SATTIRDAY.—The King of Denmark has replied to the Bulgarian Regents by declining, on behalf of his eon, Prince Waldemar, the crown of Bulgaria. His MajestY states that in present circumstances he cannot authorise his on to accept the proffered hononr.—At to-day's sitting of the Sobranje, Prince Waldemar's answer to the telegram an- nouncing his election as Prince of Bulgaria was read, as well as the subsequent telegram to the King of Denmark, and the latter's reply. A deputation was appointed, composed of 01. Stoitoff, Minister of Justice. M. Grekoff, the Bulgarian de- legate, now in Constantinople, and M. Kalcheff, a member of the Chamber, to proceed to the European Courts and ex- plain the situation of affairs in the country. RUSSIA'S CANDIDATE ACCEPTED BY THE POWERS. ROME, TDESDAT.—The Powers having invited Russia to eiesignate a candidate for Bulgaria, that Power has named the Prince of Mingrelia, whom the Powers have accepted. Russia has now been invited to propose a satisfactory solution of her conflict with the Bulgarian As- feeMb y.

ENGLAND AND TURKEY. CONSTANSINOPLR, SATURDAY.—Tbe Porte has intimated to the various Embassies that it has decided not to take any initiative in reference to Egypt, but will await the proposals to be made by England. It is believed that Sir William White is expecting instructions to submit definitive pro- positions in reference principally to the organisation of the Egyptian army and the duration of the occupation. The first of these is of the greatest interest to the Turks, since Sir H. D. Woltrs proposition will probably recommend the appointment of English and other European officers, while the Porte is anxious that the army should be brought more completely under Turkish control than it has been since the time of Mehemet Ali. Mukhtar Pasha has been instructed to send a full report on the question, in order that the Porte maybe prepared to deal with the English proposals without delay. CAIRO, MONDAY WWl:U.—Official information received here states that a body of rebels about 500 strong suddenly appeared on a ridge twelve miles above Wady Haifa, and commenced demolishing the line and other works there. On the alarm being given by the scouts an ironclad train was sent in pursuit of the rebels, and after some sharp firing they retired, leaving many dead. Two sheikhs who were captured declared that the advance was solely due to scarcity of provisions, but added that a large and well-armed force was collecting further up the Nile. INDIA.—THE CAMPAIGN IN BURMAH.

RANGOON, SATURDAY.—The insurgents in the upper pro. Vince are showing considerable activity. In the course of a skirmish at Tontacin, a village to the north of Montehobs, Lieutenant Balfour, of the Princess of Wales's Own (York- Aire Regiment), was killed and several men wounded while ;tacking a stockade. Our convoys in the Tsagain district are a:WC h harassed by the rebels. 1 esterday the large vil- lage M ngoen, on the eastern hank of the Irrawaddy, op- lae o i posits nb a was attacked by dacoits, and more than 100 houses were burnt. The villagers, although badly armed, defended thetnselves. Mr. 'fucker, commissioner for the Blingyan diviSioi. reports that Brigadier-General Lockhart Yesterday attacked the Kym. andine Prince's forces, posted one march to the west of Mrtogyan, and defeated them, cap- turing some elephants. While leading the attack Lieuten- ant Eckersley. of the Prince Albert's (Somersetshire Light Infantry) was killed. The Kymandine Prince escaped. 'the Opinion is expressed in military circles at Mandalay that civil law will be found inadequate for restoring order in•Burnaah, and that severe measures will be necessary to effect the pacification of the country. The dicoits continue inflicting Cruel tortures on the natives whom they suspect of loyalty to the British. FRANCE.—THE LATE M. PAUL BERT AND THE GOVERNMENT- The French Chamber of Deputies on Saturday passed the credit of 500,000 francs demanded by the Minister of the Interior for the relief of the sufferers from the inundations of the south. M. de Frevcinet asked for a credit of 10,000 francs to defray the funeral ePx ceases of M. Paul Bert, the Mgr. late Governor of Tonquin. FroPPelt Bishop of Angers, opposed the demand on tbe around that the deceased was an inveterate enemy of religion, a remark which evoked strong protest from the Left. The credit was ultimately approved by 379 votes agsinst 45. The Chamber subse- quently agreed to the grant of a pension of 12.000 francs to the widow of M. Paul Bert.
