ALLEGED SHOCKING BRUTALITY AT SEA.—William Glen, cantaits , and Gorton, mate, of the barque Ivy, of Quebec, have been arrested at Halifax, Novo Scotia, on a charge of causing the death of a seaman named James Pierce, a native of Dublin, while on the high seas, off the coast of Java, about a year ago. Pierce was a prisoner, in irons, and was fed only on bread and water for 75 days, (luring which he is alleged to have been brutally beaten by the captain with belaying pins and loaded whips, this ill-treattnent resulting in his death. Halifax was the first British port at which the Ivy touched since the occurrence. "THE LYTHAM MURDERS. - James Moller, the Lytham blacksmith who recently killed his wife and her sister at Lytham, by beating in their heads with a coal hammer, was on Tuesday tried for murder at the Liverpool Assiz.s. The evidence showed that the man had delusions, and that he imagined he was being illuSed by his wife in order that she might secrete money. On the day of the tragedy some , words passed between them which he could not forget, and I having killed his wife he called the other woman and killed her also. Dr. Wallace, of the County Asylum at VVithing- ton, gave it as his opinion that the prisoner knew he had done wrong, but that he had no idea of the serious position in which he was placed. Further evidence was given as to the man'aiwinsanity by his son, who had at times been sum- moned borne by telegraph becauae of the condition of his father. The jury found the prisoner guilty but irrespon- sible, and he was ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasute.

LONDON, THURSDAY. I hear that the Cabinet are already at work on the bills which they propose to introduce. Lord Randolph is to be responsible for the new rules of procedure. In these he is falling into somewhat of a slower method than was expected of him. Not- withstanding all the trumpet blowing, the Tory word of command will probably, after all, be but their familiar "as you were." The two-third chi- tare will be the solution of the difficulty, and the Speaker will be given greater power in dealing with —which means in silencing—individual members. Local Government is still in thB dim future. It is just the kind of subject about which a good deal may be promised, and, when things are indefinite, promises are easy. In land reform Lord Halsbury is an enthusiast. Every possible grievance will, of course, be redressed—but then the bill has not yet been drawn. When it does take form it will be introduced in the Lords. The land question, in another form of it, will occupy the attention of the Prime Minister, and a bill for the sale of glebe lauds will also be initiated in the Upper House. On the subject of Ireland a sort of discreet silence is main- tained. In that distressful country—if we may be- lieve the Conservative orators of the past week— there has been something very like a revolution in rose water. The landlords are all liberal and the tenants are all punctual. No additional powers are to be asked from Parliament, because none are re- quired. If need should atise, the Government won't hesitate to do its duty, and Parliament won't hesi- tate to do its. In other words, it is "as you were" all along the line—masterly inactivity, opportunism,l and a policy of mild and hopeful expectancy. All this will do very well in fair weather. In the meantime Bulgaria looms full of trouble and per- plexity on the horizon. Mr. Justice Kekewick took his seat this week on the bench. The appointment has not been a popu- lar one. There were many men at the Equity bar who did larger business and had higher claims, but Mr. Kekewick was a Conservative of an unbending type. Year after year Lord Chancellors are getting more and more inclined, in choosing occupants for the Bench, to disregard politics and look merely to • merit. It is well to learn the good rule laid down, even though there are exceptions to it. Lord Hals- bury has made two exceptions, for Mr. Justice Grantham is not the kind of lawyer who may be expected to make a good judge. One great advan- tage of the new system will be that we shall not have so many lawyers in Parliament. A barrister who wants to change his bar wig for the full bot- tomed peruke of a Judge, seeks a seat in the House, and whether he gets in or not, "has a claim on the party." It is clear that the best lawyers should be the judges, and this is what things are coming 1 to. The Attorney-General and the Solicitor-General (must always be politicians, and they should have Ithe refusal of the big prizes that fall vacant, but the 1 judgeships should gO to the best lawyers without re- gard to political claims. Mr. Justice Kekewick is an exception to a rule which all honest politicians Iwould like to see inflexibly enforced. 1 Next month we 0411 see the great hall built, near the Addison-road Station, opened with fitting cere- mony and eclat. In the meantime the arrange- meats for the expected traffic are proceeding. The omnibus Company and the Road Car Company are both starting new lines, which shall take their cus- tomers to the door of Olympia. It is wonderful how that West Kensington district has been de- veloped of late. Wily a few years ago the railway bridge at Addison-read raight have been looked upon as the boundary of London. West of that landmark stretched Hammersmith, and when you passed Hammersmith you were in the country. Poor Mr. Burns Jones in his house in the Grange Ibelieved he was in the country till they called his district West Kensington, and then he knew he was in London. The Road Car Company did good ser- vice to the new suburb by making it the terminus of a new line, and then the Om- nibus Company of course followed suit. The attrac- tion of Olympia which will be permanent will cause the quarter to be even more accessible. The New Hall opens with a novelty. The famous IParis Hippodrome is to come over, and it is hoped thus to make horsemanship not only popular but fashionable. In Paris a pretty and dashing circus girl ranks as high as a popular actress. But Lon- doners have always held themselves rather aloof, treating horsemanship as a kind of pantomime to Ibe patronized during the Christmas holidays. The IFrench importation is a bold venture, but hi public amusements it is the bold ventures that pay. There has been great heart-burning about the con- tracts for the American mails. Southampton i4not likely to supersede Liverpool, but one reason is that Liverpool has acted with promptness and 1 courage. Without the subsidy from the Post Office the companies could scarcely carry on. They have been stimulated to build finer and finer ships, gaining additional speed at immense cost. The Umbria and Etruria were contracted for at the price of £310,000 each. They are Cunards. The White Star people will probably soon build new boats. If the mail contracts were to be mere monthly arrangements the companies would have no such security as would enable them to launch out into such costly ventures, and the mail service would itself suffer from the Postmaster's small shrewdness. The Cunard and White Star liner would sail direct from Liverpool to New York. Queens- town would be omitted and ruined, and from four to six lours would be gained in the length (If the passage. There is, too, another view of the question. The Conservatives ar the advocates of protection. It is rather an extreme measure for them to propose to take an important Government contract out of the hands of English companies and hand it over to Germans. The torpedo experiment on the old " Resistance " has been a failure, but Lord Charles Beresford does not despair. Ile says the trial had not been a fair one. Torpedoes are meant to be launched at vessels under steam or with weigh on them. It was no test directing this marine projectile at a motionless hull. The torpedo should be driven against a vessel under steam. But then who are to man her. All sorts of wild stories are told of the Beresford family, and the latest is that Lord Charles has himself offered to take command and to do his best to col- lect a crew. The Service Clubs are commenting upon the report very freely. Our junior naval Lord has never been deficient in pluck, and when there is a leader for a dangerous enterprise there are sure to be plenty of volunteers. Lord Charles is a very good teller of stories, and very good stories are told of him, and this may be one of them. The quarrel between Mr. Collins and Mr. Gosse is "a very pretty quarrel." I think part of its signifi- cance is due to the fact that Parliament is not sit- ting, and so the dispute is an item of news, and then both sides have their friends. I hear Mr. Howell is to take up the cudgels for Mr. Gosse in the "Atlantic Monthly," and of course Mr. Pollock is his friend in the "Saturday Review," and Air. Wates stands stoutly by him in the "Atheneum." Mr. Collins is in his way a very distinguished man. At Baliol he had the nickname of "Memory Collins." He could recite whole pages of Macaulay without a slip. The poor Empire Theatre that had tried so many ventures, is going to make one more experiment. Of course with that splendid stage a spectacular effect will be relied on. But the experiment will atl least have the attraction of novelty. The least- knows of all Shakespeare's plays is to be lyricisod. Herman Merivale is to write the lyrics, and Hamil- ton Clarke is to set them to music. "Pericles is the play. and Mr. John Coleman is to adapt it. The scenery is to be gorgeous. There must be a great deal of adapting done before even the Lord Cham- berlain of the 19th century will accept Pericles, and in the form in which Shakespeare lett it it is essen- tially an undramatic play. Still the piece is sure to have a certain success.

and H. B. D. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF 8DP13,--A public meeting in

connection witti this Bud of Hope was held in the Ebenezer School-room, on Tuesday evening. The chair was taken by the Rev. J. Johnston, who gave an address upon IP "The drink traffic of to-day," Every intelligent English- man, he said, admitted that the drinking customs of the country were more disastrous than commercial de- pression, explosi ns,, storms, earthquakes, pestilence, or war. The consequences were everywhere visible in pauperism, crime, demoralisation and insanity. The destructive agency had been carritd to the colonies, until the nati.qis were forced to petition Govern- • it__ ment to restrict, if not entirely to prohibibit its sale. In face of these indictments it was some relief to learn that the number of prisoners in the gaols at home was steadily de- clining. Whether temperance, education, or religion had been the principal instrument in effecting this diminution, there could be no denial that tbe drink traffic was the most gigantic, evil of the age. He referred to the rapidity with which the sharPs of Guinness and Company had been taken up as evidencing that the traffic in drink, unlike other trades, had not suffered much from depressirm. No one disputed that this was a drinking age, but was that any proof that the .;onsumption would not be reduced and the passion allayed if the temptation were removed. It was in- fatuation to think England could maintain ber position as the leader of the civilised world if the drink curse was per- mitted, encouraged, and sanctioned by law. An address was also delivered by the Rev. W. Powell.

PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the Prescot Sceool Board was held on Monday evening, when there were present Mr. W. L. Evans (chairman). Mr. T. P. Hewitt, M. J. B. Sanders, Mr. d. Fogg, Mr. W. Goldsworth, and Messrs. H. Cross (clerk), and Cowherd (assistant clerk). TnE VACANCIES ON THE BOARD.—Before the Commence- ment of the ordinary business of the Board, a special meetinge was held to fill up the vacancies caused by the non- attendance of Mr. C. Spenceley and Mr. J. T. Hall at the Board meetings during a period of six months.—The Chair- man said that although those gentlemen had not attended a meeting of the Board for six months, they had attended com- mittee meetings, and their clerk held they were really still entitled to the office.—The Clerk then read a letter from Mr Spenceley, who wrote that he thought his attendance at committees was sufficient to maintain his membership. A letter was also read from Mr. J. T. Hall, who stated that he had not intendei his appointment as member to lapse, but during a portion of the time he had been unwell, and his business bad interfered with his attendance. If re-elected he was quite willing to serve again.—Mr. T. P. Hewitt moved that Mr. C. Spenceley and Mr. J. T. Hall be re- elected members of the Bear.—Mr. W. Goldsworth secon- ded the motion, which was passed unanimously. PAYMENT OF Smoot, FSES.—The question of arre ire in school fees was considered, and Mr. Sanders afterwards moved that when a scholar was is in arrears the teacher should instruct the school attendance officer to that effect, end the attendance officer should apply to the parents for payment. If he failed to obtain the naoney the parents ehould be summoned to appear before the committee.— Mr. T. P. Hewitt seconded the motion, which was adopted. THE VACANT FCIIOOI. ATT,NDANCE OFFICEIRSHIP.—The Chairman stated that the next business was to consider the resignation of Mr. Baylis, who had been appointed school attendance officer at St. Helens. He explained that in order to fulfil his new appointment Mr. Baylis Was allowed to go a fortnight ago, and his work had since been carried eut by Mr. Lloyd, who had come forward and said he would do the dnty until a successor was appointed. The Board then for- mally accepted Mr. Baylis's resignation, and the Chairman said the next business was the appointment of a successor. The Clerk said applications had been received from the fallowing : John Brotherton, 38 years of age, residing at 109, Park-road, St. Helens; William Arkell, ;.'.2 years of age, Shaw's- lane, Prescot ; Nathan Abbott, 49 years of age, St. Helens- road, Prescot ; JameaJackson, 53 years, 26, Market-place, Present; John Bixter, 46 years, 10, Chapel-walks. Prescot ; Thomas Willis, 48 years, Derbyesquare, Prescct ; John Jackson, 40 years, 7, Derby-street, Prescet ; William Lloyd, 35, Warrington-roed, Prescot; James Bullock, 46 years of ace 48, High street; Prescot ; and James Sefton, 43 years, 34;Argyle-etreet, St. Helens. During a discussion as to the duties of the School Attendance Officer, Mr. Fogg said the officer was responsible for the attendance of all children at the various schools apart from the Board school.—The qualifications of each of the applicents for the post were censidered, and ultimately Mr. William Lloyd was nnanie- monsly elected, at a salary of £4O per year. This was the only business.

- --- FRANCE AND THE VATICAN. ROME, WEDNESDAY.—The Vatican will confer with the French Bishops on the coarse to be followed by the Catho- lic clergy in France should the Chambers vote in favoie o° the separation of Church and State. From neKotiatioes which have already been entered into between France and the Holy See, it is, however, believed at the Vatican that the proposal for annulling the Concordat will be opposed by M. de Freycinet. REJECTION OF THE FRENCH BUDGET. PARIS, TRURSDAY.—The Chamber of Depeties tceday resumed the debate upon the clauses of the Budget, which came to an abrupt conclusion last Tuesday owing to the confusion prevailing in tie House. On the motion of M. Mail!efeu, the Chamber decided, by 342 to 164 votes, to re- fer the Budget proposals to a committee, with instructions to devise means for establishing at equilibrium without having recourse to a new loan or to fresh taxation. The sitting was then suspended for an hour in order to enable the Budget Committee to confer with the Government. DISASTROUS FLOODS IN ITALY. BORE, MONDAY NIGHT.—Serious news continues to ar- rive from Northern Italy relative to the floods at Albenga, in the Western Riviera. The water has entered the town, and swamped the first floor of shops and houses. The dis- aster arose from the overflowing of the neighbouring tor- rent Center, which bad already flooded several villages. causing great distress among the peasantry. From Come comes iatelligence that the principal square is under water, the Laete being swollen. SWITZERLAND. GENEVA, TUESDAY.—The final results in the elections to the Grand Council show that 51 Radicals and 41 Democrats have been returned. THE STATE OF ZULULAND. PIETERMARITZBURG, TUESDAY.--Mr. Stanhope, the Secre- tary for the Colonies, has promised to covsider the Council's representations concerning Zululand when full information arrives in England. It is reported that the Umzilas people have retired from Inhambane, after suffering severe losses. Zulu chiefs have been ordered to meet a joint commission at 11 lhowe on the 2nd DecenTher. They deny prior knowledge of the settlement and express their indignation. The Coun- cil has reduced the Governor's salary to £3,000 until Natal and Zululand are under one government. PROBABILITY OF AN " INTERNATIONAL SETTLEMENT." BERLIN, WEDNESDAY.--Tne reports current here of the impending departure of General Kaulbarg from 'Bulgaria are interpreted by the semi-official" Post" rie indicating that an international settlement of the Bulgarian question will now take the place of the attempts to solve toe diffi- culty on the spot. BURMALL—SUBMISSION OF REBEL LEADERS. BAGAING, WEDINTESDAY.—A powerful rebel leader, with many follewers, has submitted to Mr. Colquhoun, bringing in a number of rifles and cannon. Several of the smaller chiefs have also submitted. Military operations are being commenced in the Chindwin Valley. MANDALAY, WEDNESDAY, 6-20 P.M.—General Roberts has arrived here. He will go back as far as Ave and Sagaing to inspect the forts at those places, and on his return here he will make a formal entry into the palace with a cavalry es- cort. DEATH OF EX-PRESIDENT ARTHUR. Mr. Chester A. Arthur, formerly President of the United States, died on Thursday. He had been in ill-health since his retirement from office, but his death was unexpected, as it was lately understood that he was improving. On Thurs- day night last he bad a stroke of cerebral apoplexy,followed by paralysis of the right side, and lingered in an uncon- scious state until five o'clock on Tnursday morning. The President, in a proclamation announcing the death of Gene- ral Arthur. orders all public buildings to be draped in mourning and business to be suspendfd on the day of the funeral.

RUGBY RULES. SANKEY RANGERS V. HOWLEY ROVERS. -- Played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter. Score : bankey, 1 try, 3 minors; ROVQIS, 1 try, 2 miners. WYCLIFFE RANGERS V. LATCHFORD EXCELSIORS —This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the for- mer, and after a well-contested game, resulted in a draw, each team obtaining five minors. COCKHEDGE MISSION STAR OF ROPE V. WARRINGTON Tana BLUES.—This return match was played on the ground' of the Blues on Saturday. The Stars finally won by 2 tries and 3 minor points to 1 minor (or, new rules) 2 points to nil. ST. HELENS RECREATION (2ND TEAM) V. ST. HELENS Teton BLUES.—These teams played their first match to- gether on the ground of the former on Saturday, a one-sided game resulting in a victory for the Reeveation by two tries and seven minors to one try. BIINCORN FREE WANDERERS V. WEST BAITIC WATEELILIES (2nd Team).—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. After a pleasant and well-fought game the Wanderers won by two goals, four tries, and nine minor points, to one try and two minor points. WARRINGTON ST. PAUL'S V. LATCHFORD 2ND TEAM.— This match was played at Warrington on Saturday last, and resulted in a draw. Latchford claimed a try which was got after the call of time, so it was not allowed. Score : St Paul's, 9 minors; Latchford, 1 minor. RUNCORN V. BIRCIL—These club contented OR the Irwell- lane ground, HAMM, on Saturday. The home club con- tributed six players to the county team engaged against Lancashire, and were consequently weak, but were good enough to win by one goal and three tries to a goal and three minors. WARRINGTON RECREATION V. WELLINGTON JOCKEYS, WtherEs.—"llis match was played at Widnes on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by 1 try and 7 minors to 1 minor. The try for the Recs. was got by Char- Dock which, however, Forster failed to improve. For the Recs. Charnock and Tully at back played a good game, while Hackett, Forster, and Lawless were the best of the forwards. SANKEY V. WIGAN WANDER ERs.—The above match was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter, which, ow- ing to the recent heavy rains, was in a wretched condition. Owina to the late arrival of the visitors, a short game of only twenty minutes duration could be played. The first half was very even, no point being scored, but in the second half Sankey had slightly the best of the play, scoring two minors to their opponents nil. Sankey also pot a free kick, in front of the posts, which, however, was not allowed. RUNCORN RECREATION V. SWINTON HORNETS.—The Re- creation journeyed to Swinton on Saturday to play off their fixture with the above team, which, after 60 minutes' play, resulted in a draw. Score—Hornetsl one goal two minors; Recreation one goal one minor. The try for the Recreation was got by Burton after a grand run in. S. Booth kicking a neat goal. Teams: Recreation—S Booth, back; 1) Burton, Carr, S Abrams, and E Howard, three-quarter baeks; G Pen- dlebury and H Pendlebury, half backs; J Acton, S Wor- rell, D relaesey, H Grounds, W Johnson, J Price, R Lowe, and G H Jones, forwards. WARRINGTON ST. FAULS V. LATCHFORD (let Teams).— This match was played at Latchford on Saturday last and resulted in a victory for the visitors. Newton kicked off for St. Paula against the wind, and some good play took place. Emson, by a good dribble, took the ball into the home 25, but Barber relieved. Some give and take play then occurred, and at half time Latchford had scored one minor, St. Paula nil. After' change of ends St. Paula made some determined lefforts to score a brilliant rush of the forwards resulting in a try (Eyre). 'Of the St. Pauls, Eyre, Aimer, Barlow, and Binks played a grand game, while Lally at back did some good work, es did Barber and Holbrook for Litchford. Score—St. Paula: one try and one minor; Latchford : two minors. RUNCORN WANDERERS V. HALTON.--Thio match Was played at Halton on Saturday. The Runcorn forwards followed up well, and Kirkham gained a try, T Cook kick- ing a neat goal. Shortly afterwards P Jones for Halton gained a try, Crompton kicking a goal. At half time the score stood Halton one goal three minors; the Wanderers one goal one minor. By a good run Kniveton scored a try near the touch line, no goal resulting. Play was now of a very rough character. T Cook, however, got hold of the ball, and succeded in getting a try, the kick at goal failing. The Halton forwards now worked hard, but by a good kick by the Wanderers' full back, followed well by all, T Cook succeeded in getting a second try, the kick at goal again failing. No side was now called, the game ending in a win for the Wanderers by one goal, three tries, five minors, to Halton one goal and three minors. For the Wanderers in the foryrards Kniveton. Peck, Ford, and Kirkham played a good game, while behind Shaw, Cook, and Handley were the best. For Halton Crompton at three-quarter played a splendid game. The best forwards were Foster. Ellame, Inglesfield, and P Jones. ST. HELENS V. MANCHEsTER GYIINASIIIII.—PIayed at Manchester on Saturday. when the St. Helens added another easy victory to their long list of successes this season. The home team, winning the toss, elected to play with the wind. Varley kicked off, and the ball being well returned, play for some little time was in the visitors' 25. This was only for a short duration, as the St. Helens forwards soon showed their strength in the pack, and on the loose the ball was taken in the Gymnasium territory, where, from a scrim. ' mage, Anders cleverly obtained a try, which was not im- proved upon. Immediately after this the visitors obtained four minor points to the borne team one minor. In the second half, with the wind, the St. Helens team went off with a rush and completely nonplussed their opponents who strove gamely to equalise, but without success. Anders getting another try soon after, Foreman put in a splendid run, but on being collared passed to Halton, who then passed to Haeledon, who dropped a fine goal. This was soon fol- lowed up by Halton and Finney getting a try each, which were converted into goals by Hasledon. The f erwards worked well, and special mention must be made of the fine play of Tickle at full back, who played with his usual dash and safety. St Helens won by three goals, two tries, and seven minors, to two minors. Teams :—St. Helens: A Tickle, back; E Foreman, J. Helton. and W Hasledon, three-quarter backs; A Borth wick and C Anders, halfbacks; H Varley, T Finney R Ellison, D M‘Loughlin, L Ker- shaw, J liarnpson, "13asnett. J Thompson, and T Penning- ton, forwards. Manchester Gymnasium: Gregory, beck; Blinkhern, Broadhurst, and Poole, three-quarter backs: M'Cracken and Poole, half backs; Fnion, Gadd, Green, Daniels, Radford, Froggart, Wall, Stevenson, and Graye, forwards. WIDNES V. Eccuss.—This match was played at Widnes I on Saturday, on a very heavy ground. Neither team was fully represented. Widnes being minus Hardman, Plnrnpton. Parkinson, Ridyard, and Morris. With the wind in their favour. Eccles had a decided ativantage the first half. About a quarter of an hour from the commencement Worthington ran splendidly from the Widnes quarter to the line, where be was collared and passed to Moxon, who secured a try, which Worthington failed to improve. The visitors continued to have the upper hand during the remainder of that period, but no sooner was a change of ends effected, and with it a change of tactics on the part of the Widnes forwards, who up to then had been heeling out to their backs disastrously, than the home team at once showed a marked superiority. The Eccles line was attacked, and Farrell, dashing splendidly through the midst of his opponents, secured a try near the posts, from which he landed a beautiful goal. He also suc- ceeded in getting another try soon after, as the result of a smart run, but failed at the place. Smith's dribbles were the best features of the match. He was several times near scoring. The Widnes forwards completely eclipsed their opponents, Smith. Hughes. and J Bingham being worthy of spacial mention. Farrell, Howard, Harding, and Pennington played well behind. Widnes won by one goal, one try, and two miners, to one trY and one minor. Pervin, Fogg, Hughes, J Binghem, Spencer, 8 Wilkinson, and Meagher, forwards. Shrewsbury, Rhubottom, and Pickup, forwards. WARRINGTON "A " v. WIDNES RECREATION IST. The above teams met at Widnes on Saturday. Warring- ton had a very weak,tearn (Appleton, Antrobus Boardman, Walsh, Littlewood. and E. Dillon being absent), and arrived at Widnes with only 13 men, consequently had to play two substitutes. The visiting captain won the toss, and elected to play with the wind, and Grandy kicked off, Whittle fail- ing to return. From the scrimmage Unsworth got the ball and made a good kick, Jones by a neat dribble relieving still further. On a scrimmage being formed in the centre the home forwards rushed the ball to the visitors' 25, where Randles panted into touch. From the line out Adamson made a good run, but was brought down by Broome. Whit- tle here made a good dribble, but Bradshaw responded by putting the ball to centre, the ball eventually going into touch. Warrington now rushed the ball to the home 25. Barber saving nicely, but the Widnes front rank took the ball to the centre again. Jones, Craghan, Molyneaux, and Telford now came through and dribbled to the borne 25, where Rimmer picked up and passed to Jones, who gained a try, Ashurst kicking a neat goal. From the kick off Ash- nrst received the ball and punted to Barber, who failed to hold the leather, and Aigby and Eye following well up, the latter player gained a splendid try near touch, Ashurst fail- ing at the place. Grundy dropped out. and Randles' return, was charged down, thus causing a scrimmage to be formed in the visitors' quarters. The Widnes forwards came through, and Jolley picking up put in a tremendous punt, the ball goine into touch near the home quarter flag. Tel- ford, Jones. Molyneaux, and Craghan worked the bah to the Recreation line. where Whittle picked up and transferred to Randles, who dropped at goal, a dead ball resulting. Grundy dropped out, the ball going in touch at half flag. Rigby received the ball from the line out, and dribbled into Widnes quarters, bat Barber saved. Whittle now gave Unsworth chance, this player sending the oval in touch near the home line. After the throw out some rough scrimmaging took plice, and on the ball becoming loose some good passing between Whittle, Unsworth, and Bandies resulted in the latter getting over the line, but the try was not allow: d. Broome relieved the pressure by a good kick, and Nevins receiving same claimed a free kick, but the referee was against him. The Widnes forwards now worked the ball up the field and col- lared Jolley with the ball in his possession. Eyes, As- burst, and Craghan broke away, but Broome saved by kick-

A CONSERVATIVE CLUB FOR ASHTON. On Saturday afternoon Lord Gerard opened a new Conservative Club at Ashton-in-Makerfield. The premises are situate in Bblton-road, and consist of reading-room and bar on the ground floor, with care- taker's • premises in rear. Upstairs is a neat billiard room, committee room' caret room, &c. The furnishing has cost about £250, and the whole expense of the club, with the exception of a small balance still due to the treasurer, has been raised by public subscription. Subsequently a public meeting was held. Mr. W. Valiant presided. He proposed that the members of the Ashton-in- Makerfield Conservative Club and their friends hereby thank Lord Gerard for his presence here to-day, and beg to convey tohim their heartfelt thanks for his untiring and unceasing efforts in aiding the Conser- vative cause."—Mr. Clark seconded and Mr. Brown- Westhead supported the resolution, which was car- ried with loud cheers.—Lord Gerard, in reply, said be had given his services during the whole of his life- time to the Conservative cause from a strong sense of duty, and also from a religious feeling. It was not his intention to dilate upon political topics, but he should like to say one word about Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone had no doubt been a very clever man throughout his day, but he feared his days were numbered, and so long as they had such men as Lord Hartington, Sir Henry James, Mr. Goschen, and Mr. John Bright resolved to maintain the honour of the Queen and the unity of the British Isles, then be was sure they need not fear Sir William Harcourt and , men of that kind. (Oheers.)—Mr. R. Pierpoint (War- rington) moved a resolution congratulating Mr. Legh on his succem at the last election, thanking him for the assiduous attention he had paid to his Parliamen- tary duties during a most arduous seQsion •, approving of the demestic and. foreign policy of Lord Salisbury, and expressing confidence in the conduct of the nation's affairs by the present Conservative Go- uernment.—Mr. Bidden seconded the resolution.— Colonel Blundell, M.P.' in supporting the resolution. heartily approved of the foreign policy enunciated by Lord Salisbury at the Guildhall banquet. With regard to the domestic policy of the Government, he was sure that the measures enunciated by Lord Randolph Churchill at Dartford ought to be sufficient for any- body. Lord Randolph was no doubt a man of 'great ability, but he thought the Conservative party should guide that ability. (Laughter.) As they well knew some steam engines required a regulator. (Renewed laughter.) Much of what his lordship said at Dartford was very good, but he thought on some points he had gone too far, or was too far reported. (Laughter.)— The resolution was carried.—Mr. Legh, MP., who was received with applause, said the fact that amongst the Liberal Unionists were such men as Mr. Peter Rylande and Mr. Chamberlain accounted to some ex ent for the Liberal part of the policy of the Ccnservative leaders. The programme OI the Con- servative party had been plainly put before them at Dartford, Bradfood, and the Mansion House; and they also had the Liberal programme issued by the National Liberal Federation at Leeds. The latter be should characterise as one of 'Wait till the clouds roll by r—(laughter)—because it amounted to this that they hoped for better luck next time—(renewed laughter)—secondly, that they had the most implicit and blind confidence in Mr. Gladstone ; and thirdly, that they preferred, rather than otherwise, being in opposition. (Laughter.) As to the Liberal party saving better luck next time, that must be left to the Conservative ontlook—(hear, bear) es to the Liberal confidence in Mr. Gladstone, they were welcome it. (Laughter.) Mr. Gladstone was liable to error ; he was now en- vious of the Liberal policy of the Conservative party; and on the third point—namely, preference of being in opposition, it would be very much better for the country if they continued in that estimable frame of mind. (Cheers and laughter.)—Mr. Legla then pro- posed a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was seconded by the Rev. W. J. Melville, and heartily ac- corded, after which the meeting concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.

GOVERNMENT einem, toas IN IRELAND.—"United Ireland" publishes a confidential Government circular, dated Novem- ber 6, to the police stations throughout Ireland, asking for reports as to the attitude of landlords and tenants on the rent question One of the points on which information is asked is" interference of the National League with payment of rent." The sime paper also reproduces a circular cal- ling upon the police to furnish precise information as to the movements of leading Nationalists and "influential Fenians." This latter paper is dated 9th November. " United Ire- land" save the conception of such documents are tit work for the wooden-headed and stony-hearted Chief SecretarY, a man whose political mission it seems to be to do Lord Randolph Churchill's dirty work, and to take snubs for pay- ment. Public Analysts have submitted CADDITEv'S 0000 k to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nottrlshing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

Grundy returning to Randles, who made the ' finest run of the day, running from his own 25 to near the Recreation line. and Gregory (substitute). WARRINGTON V. CASTLEFORD. The general anticipation in football circles that the visit of the well-known Caslleford team to Warrington would re- mit in a fine match proved to be correct on Saturday. When these two teams met previously at Castleford the Warrington men were defeated, though not very decisive- ly, and there were certain circumstances in connection with the match that made it not a very trustworthy criterion of the respective merits of the two lots. In the first place, through some misanderstanding as to trains. the Warrington players had a railway journey of about a hours duration, which was certainly not calculated to im- prove their form, and then, owing to this protracted jour- ney, ths game had to be cut short and was altogether of a somewhat makeshift character. It was therefore felt that the real merits of the two teams had yet te be decided, and the great interest felt in the match was evidenced by the gatheting on a very unpleasant afternoon of something like 4,000 sivctators on the ground off Wilderapool Cause- way. The Castleford men arrived in Warrington early in the afternoon, and the ball being put in motion about three o'clock, a game of two thirty-fives was played. Dickinson kicked off, but Fair Turner only made a poor return. Gilbert soon made himself conspicuous by a good dribble and kick, being followed by a rush by Fair Turner, who was well collared by Hartley. The visitors' forwards very early on took the ball to the home 25, seri from a loose scrimmage Massey kicked the ball dead. The kick cut was far from being a good one, but the Warrington forwards, prominent amongst whom eters Rigby, Dillon, and Fovea?, took the sphere to halfway. LI Ashton next showed up with one of his famous dribbles, and then Barnes put in a good kick to Castleford quarters. J Dickinson, Asquith, and Cockcroft next broke away, but Massey saved in grand style, and also got in a nice little run and kick. The Cas- tleford forwards again showed up prominently, and by the aid of Wilkinson, who kicked to touch, play for some time settled down in neutral quarters. Fair Turner again essayed a rush at goal, but was cleverly stopped by Hammond. The visitors' forwards again broke away, but Speakman had his weather eye open, and saved in a praiseworthy manner. Speakman again collared the ball, and panted high, the ball falling into the hands of Wilkinsen, who made his mark ; but Gilbert obtaining possession made his mark and gained greund. Hartley from the loose !picked up and put in a tremendous kick. Jolley obtained hold, and gained a lot of ground. The same player shortly afterwards made a good run and dribble, and a try seemed inevitable had he 11 crossed the ball to the centre. The forwards then took the oval to the line, its stay there being of short duration, as the Castleford men soon removed to neutral quarters. Barnes, however, propelled the oval to the 25, bet Morton put in a long kick to the Warrington quarters, where the forwards, by good loose play, forced Buxton to call into requisitlon the caving clause. After a couple of good dribbles, one by Dale and one by Jolley, half time was called, with the score standing—Castleford two minors, Warrington nothing, On resuming, Frank Turner kicked off, and Brookes failing to return, Jolley obtained posses- sion and got to the visitors' 25. After a short time in this position Gilbert led off with agood rush. Barnes in the end kicking the ball dead, this being the first score for War- rington. From now until the end of the game nothing else was scored, the game being very fast and exciting.

The game from be"illning t() end was hotly contested, the teams being so toady matched that neither side could afford any loose play. In the first bait the visitors lead the best of It. for although the ball occasionally travelled into their quarters Ashton's followers were generally on the defensive. in the second half, however, the reverse of this wi the case, the acknowledged staying qualities of the home team standing them in good stead, and they pressed their oppo- nents very severely. The home team were several times within an ace of scoring a try, but the Yorksbiremen defen- ded their line so desperately that this point was never scored. What was notable in the Castleford play was the readiness with which they saved by dropping on the ball, and their weakness for what seemed to spectators to be a straining of the off-side rule. More than once their half backs Came round the scrimmages before there was any sign of the ball coming out, and several timeswhen the leather was passed to Barnes by Speakman or Gilbert, Hartley, the op- posite centre three-quarter, was up to him before it had reached his hands. The home captain, seeing this towards the end of the game, put Fair Tuner on-as an additional three-quarter. Taking everything into aceount, how- ever, the game was one of the best played on the Warrington ground, and was very pleasantly contestedl Buxton was tried again at back and bad very little to do, but this little was done well. Barnes although so well looked after by his opponent, nevertheless got in some nice runs and kicks. Jolley tackled strongly, and this week got in some nice dribbles, whilst Massey played It grand defen- sive game. The two half-backs had a tremendous lot of work, which they performed in a creditable manner. The forwards one and all worked with great vigour, none being more prominent that Fair. Turner, Ashton, Dillon, Davies, and Povey. Of the visitors Hanson, the tremendous kicker. only handled the ball about three times, and was then brought down by the home team before he could reply. Wil- kinson at times got in some fine kicks and occasionally a run or two, Hammond did not do much, and Hartley at centre played a good game, although rather off-side. The two half-backs played well, and the forwards played a good, sound game, evidently being deterinined to win if they could, Brookes, Dickinson. Cockcroft, and Asquith being the pick. Teams :—Warrington : Back, Buxton; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey; half backs, Gilbert and Fpeakman ; forwards, Fair Turner. F Turner, Hough, W Dillon, Rigby, Littlewood, Davies, Povey, and Ashton. Castleford : Back. Hanson; three-quarter backs, Wilkinson, Hartley, and Hammond; half backs, Clarkson and Morten; forwards, Philip., Jones, Cockcroft, Dale, Dickinson, As- quith, Osborne, Dickinson, and Brookes. The referee was Mr. Naylor, of Wigan, whose decisions gave every satis- faction.

BROMBOROI7OII POOL.—Tkese teams met at Earlestovrn on Saturday, when the home team again showed their superiority throughout the game despite the wind. Bromborough kicked off with all in their favour, and both goals were in turn assailed. Then Ogden headed one through from J. Shaw. This was the only score during the first half. On changing ends, Earlestown played a faster game, and when Fazackerley put in a splendid screw, and Siddley breasted the ball through. Simms was the next to score, followed quickly by Ogden. Towards the and the home full backs drew closer in, and Clough shot the fifth goal. Williams (goal) for the visitors was well applauded for his grand defence, and certainly played the best game on his side. The final result was: Etrlestown five goals to Bromborough nothing.

As we predicted, the game between Warrington and Castleford was an exciting aff air. and although it is wished that the result had been more favourable to the home team than a draw, the match was a very satisfac- tory one and goes to prove that Warrington may be re- lied on to come creditably out of a contest with the best Rugby teams that can be put in the field. Judging merely by the two minors to one, it might be thought that Castle- ford had slightly held the upper hand, but this would be a mistake, for Warrington showed a decided superiority in that part 4f the game when the merits of the players are apt to be the most keenly tested, namely, the latter part. It is said that the Warrington Committee have decided upon erecting a new and improved grand stand capable of helding 500 people. If this be so it will be welcome news to the increasing number of grand stand spectators who turn out to witness a " big match." Raised footboards, it is added, are also to be laid for the accomodation of specta-

tors. It is rumoured that none of the Warrington players will take part in the match between the W.L.8.1.R.U. against Westmoreland County at Kendal. on Saturday week, as the Rochdale Hornets are coming down and the home team wish to pat a strong team on the field. Aspnll are coming down to-day and the Warrington men will have a tough struggle to beat them as, we believe, two of their best players will be absent. The "Yorkshire Post" characterises the match between Warrington and Castleford as a "magnificent one," and says the forwards were "as fine a set of fellows as those of almost any club in the two counties they represented." div.head: ALLEGED -MANSLAUGHTER
div.p: THE ALLEGED -MANSLAUGHTER
AT EA.RLESTOWN.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Friday, William Campbell (20, collier, was indicted for haying, on the loth or iith of September, feloniously killed Hannah Smith, at Earlestown.—Mr. Swift prosecuted, and in his opening statement said that it appeared the woman Smith lived with the father of the prisoner as his wife. They had lived in the same house at Earles- town with the prisoner, a man named Finch, and another son. On the night of the loth September, the prisoner's father, the woman, and the man Finch were out in the town drinking together. They met the prisoner in two or three public•houses, but there did ! not seem to have been any dispute. When they re- ! turned the prisoner came home, and an altercation arose between the Prisoner and his father, the result of which was that the two went out to fight. They fought for some time, and Finch then separated them. They got together again, however, and when the prisoner appeared to be gaining an advantage over his father Smith came out of the house and hit him. He immediately left the father, went round the corner of the house, and returned, throwing some- thing at Smith, witnesses would say was a brick. He stooped and picked another brick up, and again threw it. It hit the deceased on the side, and she fell down.. She was carried to the house, and after lingering for • five days she died. The prisoner had admitted that he threw the brick at his father, but did not intend hitting the woman at all.—Evidence was called which went to prove that when the prisoner came home he said he had a bottle, and invited his father and de- ceased to drink. They all refused, and then the row commenced. When they got outside the house Smith struck prisoner four or five times on the back. Medi- cal evidence showed that death was caused by inflam- mation of the intestines, which might have been brought on by such a blow as a brick, thrown as it was suggested this was, would give.—Prisoner, in defence, stated that his father ordered him out of the house in the first instance, and when he left the house his father ran after him, caught him, and commenced thrashing him. The quarrel then went on, and he threw the brick at him, and not at the deceased.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and strongly recovn- I mended him to mercy.—His Lordship sentenced pri- soner to one month's hard labour.

SHOOTING A .MOTHER'S PAR COUR- At Liverpool Assizes on Saturday Henry Lionel Stringer (19), shipwrights apprentice, who is a native of Warrington, pleaded guilty to having wounded William King at Liverpool, on the 30th October, with intent to do grievous bodily harm. Mr. WConnell appeared for the defence and Mr. Shee for the prosecution. Mr. M'Connell explained that the prisoner's mother was living with King, although she was not married to him. He had been greatly excited by King's conduct, and he must, as he said, have been mad when he did as he did. It was true he purchased a pistol, but he was in a state of great excitement and irritation when he fired at the man. Mr. Shee, on behalf of the prosecution, said he wished to endeavour to obtain an acquittal for the poor :lad. He was a most de- • serving laoy, and a petitioffe had been signed by all his fellow-workmen on his behalf. He had been ikeeping his mother with his hard-earned wages, and this man King imposed upon him and upon his mother. Ile had suffered a long-standing system of persecution from King, culminating in this boy being beside himself when this act was done. lie did not think there was any intention on the part of the poor boy, for in a fit of passion he asked his mother for money, rushed out of the house,. pur- , a cgaSe,the pistol and cartridges, and rushed back, I only again to be insulted, and shot at King. He was so sorry directly the shot had been fired that before the police could be informed he went and gave himself up. He (Mr. Shee) earnestly asked that his lordship would let the prisoner off, as the provocation was very great, and the case one of the most unfortunate it was possible to conceive. His Lordship deferred judgment. On Tuesday his Lordship, in giving judgment, said the prisqner was singularly fortunate in two respects. Counsel for the Crown (Mr. Shee) had most generously recommended him to mercy • and the prisoner was advised by counsel (Mr. Ikon- nell), who made a most eloquent appeal on his be- half. It would not, however, be seeming for him to pass any light sentence upon the prisoner, but , he would take another course, and that was to post- pone sentence. His lordship ordered the prisoner's I discharge on his entering into recognisances to be of I good behaviour and come up for judgment when I called upon.;

THE STRIKR AT COLLINS GREEN. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, James Anders, a collier, formerly in the employ of the Collins Green Colliery Company, was summoned for using language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, and for intimidating Thomas Bate and Edward Pollitt, colliers iu the employ of the company named. Mr. P. Davies (Warrington) appeared far the prosecution, and Mr. H. L. ftiley (St. Helens) for the defence. In opening the case, Mr. Davies said that about seven weeks ago there was a strike at the Collins Green Colliery, and some four hundred men went out, they having the belief that a reduction of threepence per ton all round was going to be made. Bate and Pollitt went nut with the others, but in a month's time resumed work. On the morning of the 2nd November they were going to work when they saw defendant Anders opposite the Pear Tree Inn. He said to them, "You are nice men, going in in the face of all the men."—Bate said, "There's plenty of room for you, why don't you come to your work ? " Anders then "You are a pair of knobsticks,' and you deserve your heads cutting off," further saying "I'd do it myself if there were three or four here. If you don't stop work at once a gang will meet you, and they will throw you down the pit, both of you." Defendant shouted after them in a very excitable way. In consevence of this threat one of the men left work the next day, but 14oth men had since gone to work again, much to the disgust of those oat on strike. Evidence as to the threat was then given by Thos. Bate and Edward Pollitt, and the latter, in reply to ques- tions, said that the colliers had been under police pro- tection, but he had not personally been protected. On this point Mr. Henry Fairclough, a director of the Company, said that the men were promised protection when they resumed work ; the company bad to have policemen to see that the men were not met on the road and stopped from going to work. Speaking for the defence, Mr. Riley referred to the reason why the men struck work at the outset. Defendant at all events had written notice to leave, and he believed that similar notices were scattered broadcast. The men well understood that that was the first step towards making a new contract ; and possibly it filtered out through subordinate officials what the alteration would be. He then spoke in defence of his clients, remarking that the best iceurse to ensure a continu- ance of proper relations between the firm and the men was not to show the latter how powerful the law was, and to try and awe them into subjection. The magistrates found the case proved, and inflicted a fine of 203 and costs.—Another collier on strike, named Andrew Cotterill, was fined lOs and costs, and ordered to be bound over to keep the peace. on charge of assaulting Thomas Bate and intimidating hirn.

div.head: ASK YOUR GROCER FOR
div.p: ASK YOUR GROCER FOR
FLETT'S

Mr. James Russell Lowell is engaged to be mar- ried to the Dowager Lady Lyttleton. The marriage will lie siagular in this respect that both parties were twice. praviously married. Lady Lyttleton is a fine looking woman, some forty years old. She was the wi.low of Mr. Mildmay, M.P. When she married Lord Lyttleton. this Mr. Mildmay's fl cousin married a daughter of Mottle', the historian -31 - of the _Netherlands, who hi'auself had been American '") Minister at our Court before Mr. Lowell. There will be all sorts of Lingular complications arising out of the marriage. Lord Lyttletons first wife was a sist.ir of Mrs. Gladstone. Now Lady Caven- dish was second daughter of Lord Lyttleton, and(l niece of Mrs. Gladstone. Mr. Lowell will thus be- - come a sort of stepfatherto Lord Frederick's widow. No American who ever visited this country left it with so many friends, and his return will be a dis- tinct gain to London society. The Sebright-Scott case carries with it one very obvious moral. Our marriage laws need some re- consideration. Marriage by register is even yet rather rare amongst the wealthy classes, and when the woman is young and the surroundings are sus- picious some discretion should be allowed to the of- ficiating registrar. The office is open to all; the fees are extremely modest; the services of the neces- sary two witnesses very easily secured. In other countries, where the civil marriage is more usual, and in some where it is obligatory, there are checks and safeguards and delays. The facilities which our own system affords amount almost to an eneoUr- agement to fraud. Paris and New York hold opposite opinions on an important sartorial question. The question is one of tailcoats. John Bull is not a dressy man. He leaves fashion for the most part to his wife, who is ably assisted in the discussion of it by her daugh- ters. But in one department he is more exclusive than his neighbours. At our Italian opera dress is tie rigeur. It Is not so in other capitals We have probably the shabbiest opera house at this side of the Alps, but no gentleman can sit in its stalls ex- cept in evening dress. Elsewhere on the Continent there is no strict rule. The foreigners are generally married in evening dress, and go to the theatre in morning costume. And now in Paris it is sought to introduce the same restriction,and to make the swallow tail a eine qud non. Meanwhile, across the Atlantic they are trying to abolish what in Paristhey are trying to enforce. There is a reaction against the swallow tail. It is sought to make tail-less coats all the vogue, and to induce gentlemen to appear at evening parties in the jackets of Eton scholboys. ; But—as happens in the case of all truly important revolutions—this momentous question is compli- cated by side issues. It is not to be fought out on the lines of tail or no tail. Yet another innovation is announced. The evening vest is threatened. It is sought to dispense with it. The article of dress which Highlanders ignore, in the new fashion, 7,`,. ; comes up a little higher on the figure than the swallow tail coat, and has one button in front. Per- 7 i haps the Parisian authorities should hesitate to I issue their expected edict as to evening dress till the question of what evening dress is has beet: finally settled. In the meantime at home in London we can retain our accustomed costume.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 20, 1886.

- - IT seems to be regarded as a matter of course that at Warrington, as at other places, something must be done to commemorate the Jubilee of QUEEN VICTORIA'S accession to the throne. Already various suggestions have been made—some likely, and some un- likely; and, as one or other in due time will • in all probability be acted upon, there can be no harm in discussing their merits and de- , merits. The RECTOR, preaching to the MAYOR and members of the Corporation on Sunday, made known his particular proposal; i and it s due to his high position that it should be considered. In the course of his sermon he said :

-- Let them honour the occasion at home by erecting a Jubilee House, where useful work might be done for the rising generation after they have left school, and for those of a larger growth, where their habits and learning might be further improved, and tech- nical work of all kinds instructed. Where, it might be asked, can it be built? He said "Close here, ad- joining the church-yard. lie would petition the body corporate, to grant the removal and license of the present public-house to some more distant part of the parish, where on a largely extended scale its usefulness might be required', and become most beneficial to the wayfarer and visitors to the mar- ket and tpwn." On a site of 156 ft. by 117 ft. a fine structure might be built, where night schools for adults, libraries, reading rooms, lectures, music might be given; and above all he should recommend a large entrance hall, where the Mayor and Corpora- tion, as in other towns, with their town servants and police, might on each Sunday assemble, and go to church, and occupy those seats which were placed and retained here for their occupation and use. It is a good idea, to begin with, to get rid of a public-house near a chinch ; or, for that matter, anywhere else—there are so many of them—but is it not a little comical to talk about transferring it to where it can be useful "on a largely extended scale ? " If the RECTOR hadn't been preaching, it might have been thought he was indulging in a jocular gibe at the " usefulness " of the pub- lic-house. But passing this by, it must be remarked as to the proposed site of the pro- posed educational structure, that if it is too out-of-the-way for a public-house, it is cer- tainly not sufficiently central for a public institution. A school where "technical work of all kinds" could be taueht—not "in- structed," as the RECTOR has it—would be a boon to the inhabitants; but from the nature and variety of the trades in Warrington, it would need to be on a large scale ;it would

div.p: be a great and costly undertaking-, and would require above all things to .be centrally situated. As to providing " night schools for adults," that can be done in any part of the town where there happen to be day schools —that is if school managers care to make the experiment. "Libraries, reading rooms, lec lures, and music" are altogether unobjection- able, but, to be of use to the public they must be easily accessible to the public ;„ if they are to be successful, it is surely obvious they must not be placed or held at one end of the town. In the Wednesday's issue of our neutral contemporary, the hope is expressed that a Free School is "not beyond being secured in the Jubilee year." The editor says :—" One free school of this kind we believe to be necessary in every large town, and it should be kept entirely for a class of children sent on a well-established claim of poverty. Of course, such schools, so far as religious educa'ion is concerned, would retain all the rights and immunities of the ordinary day schools, but nothing more." The proposal is plausible and generous on the face of it, but we hold that, in the form in which it would require to be car- ried out in Warrington, it is neither desir- able nor practicable. As tee free scholars who attended such a school would be free because their fees were paid by the local authorities, they would be under a stigma ; they would be regarded as little better than pauper children—as one degree, and one degree only, removed from the Workhouse scholars. At present the school children of parents too poor to pay the school fee are, happily, in this respect lost sight of, ab- sorbed as they are .by twos and threes in every school in the town. Then in the conduct of such a school the religious spectre would instantly arise—especially in a town like Warrington, which has had no experience of Board -Schools. It would have to be "Church," of course, to suit the pre- vailing type of our pastors and masters; but in that case, would not the poor amongst the Dissenters and Roman Catholics feel that they had a grievance in being com- pelled, because of their poverty, to send their children to such a school? Perhaps we shall hear it said that it might be " un- sectarian," but that would most probably pro- voke a parsonic protest all round; for would it not be urged that "godless education" was being given, and that we might just as well convert the school into a Board School? No, a Free School 'kept entirely for a class of children sent on a well-established claim of poverty will not do. If it were tried, it would fail; it would result in recrimination rather than jubilation. We respect our con- temporary for having declared, as it has done, in favour of "free education : " and we shall get "free education" before many years .are .over—not in part, but as a whole, and in a less objectionable way. 'We must confess that we like the educa- tional turn which many of the suggestions take as to celebrating the Jubilee; but we have seen inone yet comparable to the proposal to,distinguish the year by making the War- rington ;Lending Library absolutely free to the -ratepayers. Carlyle's best teaching is summed up in the phease—" Do the duty which lies nearest thee " ; and what duty can be nearer to the authorities of the town than that of placing the treasures of the Pub- lic Library where it was intended they should be—in the hands of the people. A Jubilee memorial to be worthy of the name should be unsectarian, and it should be of a kind, if possible. that shall make itself felt in the home of every inhabitant of the town. " Free " Library meets these conditions it is an institution which is capable of convey- ing instruction, and solace, and delight to the khome of the lowliest as well as the high- est, 'which is demanded by the ,necessi- ties of the time, by what is due to those who have been paying a library rate for so many years, and which is, moreover, easy of attain- ment as the duty which lies nearest to the townat the.present hour.

THERE were high .jinks at Ashton on Satur- day afternoon on the opening of a Conserva- tive club. Lord GERARD performed the ceremony, • and sundry speeches followed which went to show that the Conservatives, though they are in office, are not in an en- tirely happy .frame of mind. Lord GERARD 'took occasion to observe that he had "one word to say about Mr. Gladstone," and that one word was that he had "no doubt been a very clever man throughout, his day, but he feared his,days .were numbered." ." Feared" —is that wh it he really meant ? Was there not a wish that was father to the thought? It would be interesting to know how Lord GERARD would take it if he were told that the Liberals of the Newton Division regarded him as a stumbling block, in their path, and that they had been publicly remarking as something to be thankful for that they "feared his days were numbered." He would probably regard it as an evidence of bad taste, and as a piece of impertinence. He would be right in taking that view, and, this being the case, we do not hesitate to say that it is equally in bad taste, and not less impertinent of his lordship to speak of Mr. ,Gladstone's days as being numbered. But his lordship tells us Conservatives need not fear so long as they have men like Lord Hartington, Sir Henry James, Mr. Gosehen, and Mr. John Bright reseilved to maintain the honour of the Queen and the unity of the British Isles. It is de- lightful to see the Tories thus clinging to the leadirz Dissentient Liberals—paricularly when it is remembered th .t it is not long since these same Liberals, as members of a Libecal Administration, were denounced by such men as Lord GERARD as cowards who were responsible for the murder of Lord -FREDERI CAVENDISH, and as traitors who CK ihad sacrificed thousands of lives in the Soudan, and on whom rested tile s' indelible disgrace" of leaving GORDON to perish at Khartoum. 'Was it all "cake believe" when the Tone shot rubbisk of this kind? Or are we to infer that it is all " make believe " now when they profess to be en- ainGuredi of men who, if what they have previously said f o them is true, should he held up to the execration of mankind? The fact is the Tories have a miserable misgiving in the knowledge that the Government de- pend for their existence upon "union with the Unionists." They speak fair words when they would, if they thought themselves strong enough, ease the ship by throwing the jonahs overboard. Colonel 13LuNDzI,L, M.P. for Ince Division, didn't exactly let the cat out of the bag as to this matter, hut he displayed an inch or two of its tail. He is a slow-going Tory, and he doesn't care to be told that he must now go "Quick march" to keep time to the music of the Liberal Unionist band. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL knocks him out of breath; his lordship was "no doubt," the Colonel says, "a man of but he thought the Conservatigreat ability, ve party should guide that ability. As they well knew, sothe:steatri

engines required a regulator." Just so, but Lord RANDOLPH is not to be compared to anything so useful or regular as a steam engine; he is more like a weathercock that will turn any way with the wind. He is more, too, in touch with Liberal Unionist 3 than Colonel BLUNDELL ; he is less scrupulous about breaking a score or so of Tory oaths ; and has made 11p his mind to dance to any tune that the Liberal Unionists may pipe, for he knows that upon this depends his retention of office. Perhaps when Colonel BLUNDELL and other stiff-necked and stiff-legged suppor- ters realise the situation, they also will be wit- ling to try to trip it, politically. on thelight fan- tastic toe. Mr. LEGH. M.P., like " Barkas," seems to be " wiltin " ; he is younger than Col. BLuNDELL, and perhaps we should say naturally more flexible. "The fact," he urges, "that amongst the Liberal Unionists were such men as Ar. PETER RYLANDS and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN accounted to some extent for the Liberal part of the policy of the Con- servative leaders." To be sure—that does to some extent account for it. Seeing that the Tory, leaders have no programme of their own, why shouldn't they accept any prin- gramme that any allies may lay before them? It is very convenient when you have no pro- ciples ; yiou can turn any way. For instance, Mr. PETER RYLANDS has had a motion before the House of Commons declarinc, that the Bishops ought to be removed from the House of Lords; and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN goes far- ther—he is ready for breakine, the bond be- tween Church and State. ''Now when the new allies of the Tories press these i'ssues—as it is to be hoped they will—Lord RANDOLPH and Co. will be bound to giv their support; they have simply to treat the matter as "the Liberal part of the policy of the Conservative leaders." Liberals won't mind it; not a bit. They are of course interested in the working of the new patent for mixing oil and water; they may have their doubts as to the experi- ment, but if it should result in the carrying out of first-class reforms, they will thank their stars that it has proved successful.

The Royal College of Surgeons is in luck. The late Sir Erasmus Wilson has left a legacy of £3130,000 which reverts to 'the college on the death of his widow. That is something like a windfall.

Councillcr Roberts, in a letter which will be found in another column, makes a strong appeal for the extension of Warrington Public Baths. If the work could be done in ilia Jubilee year, without seriously increasing the rates, it would undoubtedly be regarded by the public as a great boon.

The "Era," in bidcling adieu to the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Harrison), on his retirement from office, is not unmindful of the way in which Mr. Edward Terry and his com- pany were entertained A taste of breakfast makes us wondrous kind.

But what about dinner? Are potatoes not cheap enough that we hear nothing of the borough member catering to the inner ntan of the Corporation ? it was not thus, they say, when Mr. McMinnies was M.P. And what of the ex Mayor? is he to be left to fatten on compliments? If he cannot have a bust, he might be given a " buster " by the incqrbers of the Corporation. He ought not to be treated shabbily.

Four persons, it is stated, are under treat- ment at Alcester for poisoning, caus-A by drinking home made wines which had been brewed in glazed earthenware pots. The glaze contained oxide of lead. In some coun- tries the manufacturer would, we believe, be punished for using poisonnus materials. Why should it not be the case in this country?

Justice seems to cltnand something more than the nullity of the marriage (so-called) .between Mr. Sebright and Miss Scott. The ,conduct of Arthur Sebright is so bad that one His tempted to exclaim with " Emilia " :- 0 heaven, that -such companions thou'dst, unfold, And put in ie very honest hand a whin To lash the rascal naked through the wvrld.

Mr. John Crosfield made a stirring speech at a Liberal meeting at Lymm, on Saturday evening. In dealing with the Irish question,. he detailed some of his own experiences in Ireland in a way which brought the matter right home to the audience. Speeches of this kind are much needed; the country re- quires to be educated as to how the people live in the sister isle.

The Liberals of St. Helens are astir, and feeling the need of a new club, they are about to establish one on the limited liability prin- ciple. Colosel Gamble, the new Mayor Wag precent Lt a meeting which was held on Mon- day evening. He,cannot, whilst Mayor, de- vote himself to political matters, but he has promised his help; and there is every pros- pect of the new undertaking proving success- ful.

The yoting collier, at Earlestown, who kille his father'sd paramour 'with a brick has been sentenced to one month's hard labour only. It is not denied that when father and son were fighting, the victim, whose name was Smith, struck the son several times. But tke son alleges that the brick was intended for his father-3 little evidence of filial piety. There was a doubt in the case; and the prisoner certainly got the benefit of the doubt.

The " Aberdeen journal" does not think that the best Way to commemorate the Queen's Jubilee is to add an olive branch and call it Victr or Victoria. Over i,OOO children are born each day .in the United Kingdom. Fancy 200,000 Victors, and zoo,coo Victorias by the end of 1887 I Chan this, let us rather have a few lectures on Malthus; the struggle for existence, especially where there is a large family, is already hard enough.

The new Vicar of Runcorn is making what many will regard as a bad beginning. He has, it is stated, made it known that he will bring, his present curates with him. This may be of some convenience to him person- ally, but what of the parishioners Who will have three new clerics groping their way amongst them? And what of the present curates? It is not very considerate to turn them out of a field of labour with which they are familiar; and it is certainly ques- tionable as a matter of policy.

A pertinent protest was made by the sit- ting magistrates (gessrs. Holmes and Bur- gess) at the the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, against the manner in which rail- way companies make themselves a party to drunken people travelling by rail. The of- fender in this case was not only drunk and disorderly, but had travelled without ticket. It would be a good thing if the clerks at booking offices were instructed to "refuse to serve" people likely to become
