TEE REV. D. J. LLEWELLYN, formerly curate of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, has been offered the chaplaincy of Berst Chapel by Mr. E. 0. V. Lloyd, of Berst and Regatti. The chaplaincy is worth £2OO a year, house, and some glebe. Mr. Llewellyn has not yet given a de- cision. LACROSSE: WIDNES V. ST. HELENS.—PIayed on the ground of the latter on Saturday, resulting in a victory for Widnes (who were one short) by two goals to nothing. Widnes. who had not their best team up, were best repress*, ted by Longton, Wylde, and Wilson. Watts played best for St. Helens. WIDNES C.E T.S.—The monthly meeting of this society was held on Tnursday evening, at the National Schools, when Mr. H. N. Wharton delivered an interesting lecture on America. The American melodies, To the West," and " Tbe Star Spangled Banner," were sung during the evening. The Rev. J. R. Jones. BA., presided. Sr. JOHN'S BAND OF HOPE. RUNCORN.—An entertainment was given be the members of this society on Wednesday eveniog, in St. John's School-room. There was a capital attendance, and the Rev. E. Williams occupied the chair. Mr. J. Morgan, of Wigan, delivered an address, and a pro- gramme of songs, recitations, was gone through. 'IRE LATE CANON BARCLAY.—Many of the parishioners having manifested a desire to pe. petuate the life and work of the late Canon amongst them by a suitable memorial, a meeting will be held in the National School on Monday evening, for the purpose of deciding upon what form the memorial should take. A committee will be appointed to receive subscriptions. WIDNES SCHOOL ROALD AT WORE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not sending their children regularly to school :—Elizibeth Walton, John Smith, John McCann. Joseph Shone' Gordon McKaye. James McCana, Robert Hoey, William Percival. and Robsrt Birch. The usual penalty was imposed in each case. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—An accident, which might have been attended with serious consequences, oc- curred at Widnes, on Friday evening, to a man named Nor- bury, who resides at Chatham-street. He was employed at the Dennis Copper Works, and while at work on the date above-mentioned, was caught between the buffers of two wagons, receiving severe injuries to his chest and back. Be was attended by Dr. McCarnhridge, and is now progressing favourably. A PROMISED REFORMATION AT WIDNES.—Rose Kelly, an old offender, was Charged with having on the previous day been drunk and disorderly in Grove-street—P.C. Moores proved the case.—Mr. Gossage: We have bad you here so often, that if you will promise to leave drink alone we will let you off this time.—Defendant: Faith and sure, I will. You will not see me here again. God bless ye. De- fendant then left the court invoking blessings of all kinds en the heads of the magistrates. CURIOUS ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—On Sunday morning the raof of the shop of Messrs. Steed and Simpson. Bridge- street, Runcorn. suffered serious damage by the fall of the coping stone and a portion of the chimney stack. The accident occurred at about ten o'clock, and the noise occa- sioned by the failing debris caused much alarm in the neigh- bourhood. Stone portion of the falling material passed through the rad, and a portion into the street, where a child had a narrow escape from death. WEs-rox CHURCH Scnoons.—On Wednesday a concect was held at the Weston schools te provide funds for the annual Christmas priz.s of the children. Mr. F. Joule, of Leinster Gardens, Runcorn, took the chair. Sonars were given by lilies Clarke, Miss Hampsen, Miss Siinkin, and Miss Howard; Messrs. R. Morris, F. Joule, and J. Tudor. The Parish Church Ckoral Society contributed to the plea• sure of the evening by rendering several glees. The enter- tainment was arranged by Mr. Morris, schoolmaster, SUSIRCIOUS CHARACTERS AT RENceast.--William Henry Percival, s. young man, was brought up at Runcorn Court ohs Wednesday charged on suspicion with steeling a quan- tity of wheat from a boat. He was met carrying a beg of wheat upon his back, and as he could give no proper account of it he was apprehended, and was now remanded. He gave information which resulted in the apprehension of George Nichols and John Arrowemith on a like charge. They were brought before Mr. Headley on Thursday, and also remanded. DVANGELISTIC SERVICES it RUNCORN.—During the past week Mr. W. Tharme, evangelist, of Liverpool, has conduc- ted a series of successful evangelietic -services in the Primi- tive Methodist Chapel, Greenway-road, Runcorn. Three services have been held each day, and over-40 converts were merle. many of whom will join the denomination. Mr. W. Erignall, the secretary to the mission, conducteel the Ser- vices held on Tuesday night, and ids address made a deep impression. Mr. Toarme has accepted an engagement to labour in the Preston Brook circuit until the end of the Tear. Tien NEW VICAR OF RUlnGati.—The Rev. Alfred Mait- land Wood. M.A., Vicar of St Mary's, Liscard, who has been appointed by the Deaa and Chapter of Christ Church, Ox- 'ford, to the living of All Saints' Church, Runcorn. will be 'formally inducted into his new pastorate on the first Sunday, In the new year. The rev, gentleman has intimated that he intends to appoint as his curates the Rev. Frederick James. Wiseman. Mai, end the Rev. J. Park, 8.A., who have: laboured with him in his present parish for some time. The , Revs. T. M. Amnon and R. Edwarde, who have been in 1' Runcorn for several years, will have, therefore, to find other curacies. ACCIDENT AT Wments.—George Halms, a married man, who lived at Ditton Junction, and worked at the works of Messrs. Vickers and Co, was received into the Widnes Acci-,, dent Hospital yesterday, suffering 'from several fractured, ribs and serious internal injuries. After coupling some, waggons on the company's sidinge, he attempted to make, his way through a narrow space between the wall and the' waggons. Whilst so doing the engine started and the iron- work of one of toe trucks jammed him against the wall, ,causing the results mentioned. He was attended by Mr. Richards. assiatant to Dr. McDonnell, but is in a very criti-,' cal condition. CAMDEN IMPROVEMENT CLASS, 'RUNCORN.—Tbe usual t; weekly meeting in connection with the above was held on a Friday evening, when there was a large attendance. Mr., Henry Randle presided. Mr. S. C. Beckett (vice-president) was also present. lecture was delivered by the Rev. R. F. Hornabrook, the subject being " Reminiscences of life in.l Smith Africa." The lecturer has spent several years in ' missionary effort in the country of which he spoke. He dealt with his subject in a very' pleasing manner, describing many incidents and objecte of interest to be seen on thej voyage out to Canetown, also describing many things to be seen in various towns and villages in South Africa, the nes live customs and habits and modes of travelling. The lec- ture was interspersed with racy anecdotes, and t ie audience from beginning to close were kept in continual good humour by the felicitious manner with which the lecturer handled his subject. At the conclusion a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Hornabrook, on the motion of Mr. J. T. Nickson, and :seconded by Mr. J. Higgins. RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRAEZ COMMITTEE.—The monthly meeting was held on We.inesday night. Present— Messrs. F. A. Lake (chairman). W. Handley, T. Riley, .E. Marwood, J. R. Firth. and J. D. Jones (librarian). The Librarian reported that during the month of October 1,812 books were issued, of which 1,503 were pose fiction. He also reported that on Thursday, the 11th inst., certain boys bad maliciously hacked the table in the reading room with a Knife. With a view to preventing a recurrence of such practices, the Librarian was instructedto get notices printed calling attention to the wilful damage done, and a citation from the Malicious Injuries to Property Act, which applied to the case. The law was very stringent to such a matter, the punishment for such offences being six months' im- prisonment, and if a male under 16 years of age he might be whipped. in consequence of the continued accession of new books to tbe Library, and the deficiency of shelf room, the Librarian was instructed to request permiseion from the Runcorn improvement Commissioners to use the room over the reading room for the purpose of storing some of the reference books, thus providing accommodation until the premises are enlarged. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—Great preparations are being made to commemorate the jubilee of the opening of this chapel by the members of the congre- gation on the 6th December. On that day and two fol- lowing days a "Nationalities Bazaar, or the World's Fair," will be held on a scale of considerable magnifi- cence and originality. America will be represented by. a correct representation of the old log cabin, in which President Garfield first saw the light; whilst "Old Eng- land will be typified by a model of the dwelling-place of „Edward Underhill, who attempted to assassinate queen Mary. Egypt, China, and Switzerland will also be repre- sented by appropriate buildings, and the whole will be utilised as stalls, which the ladies hope to beautifully stock by the aid of kind friends. Besides this display there will be numerous other attractions. The money that may be obtained from the "fair" will be devoted partly to the ex- tinction of the debt on the minister's house, and for the execution of necessary repairs in the chapel. The Manse was erected some four years ago, at a cost, including free- hold, of over £7OO, of wkich sum £4OO has already been paid, leaving £3OO still to he raised to free it entirely from debt. The proceedings will be commenced on the first day by Mr. Robert Verdin, M.P., and on the second day, Mr. P. Speakman, the chairman of the Commissioners, will officiate.

Mr. W. Scott coward, in responding after the presentation. to him at Southport, on Saturday. gave the! Mayor of Warrington a Roland for his Oliver in reference to Board Schools. He said :—•‘ A:s to Board S chools he needed to say a word, because his name had been brought into connection with them. He was no enemy of Board Schools. Board Schools were necessary and inevitable, and they were increasing, and would increase. Let them make the best of it. Let them not carry on with them an internecine feud. Board Schools would not be more friendly on that account. They were, he believed, the growing means by which the country was to be educated."

PROPOSED NEW THEATRE .A.T WIDNHS.—A proposal for the erection of a new theatre at Widnes has been much dis- cussed in various circles during the past few weeks. No formal steps have as yet been taken, but it is probable that in a few days a tneering will be held for the purpose of float- ing a company. Although the present structure, known as the Theatre likyal, is far from an attractive and comfort- able building, the audiences are all that could be desired, and there is a widespread desire, that a more pretentious structure should be erected in the main thoroughfare. WORD COMPETITION.—We have pleasure in direct- ing the attention of our readers to the offer by Messrs. Crosfield and Sons of 45 guineas to be given in prizes for the largest number of words formed out of "Perfection Soap." Particulars as to the conditions will be found in our advertising columns. The substantial character of the prizes will attract a large number of competitors;p and we look to see a long list of words as the result of the compe- tition. _ _ _

"THE MANX LINE."—The Isle of Man, Liverpool, and Manchester Steamship Company, Limited, bet- ter known as the "Manx Line," expect to begin their daily service between Douglas and Liverpool on Saturday, the 28th of May, 1887, when one of their steamers will leave Liverpool at ten o'clock in the morning, after which a regular service of ex- press boats will be continued throughout the entire summer season. Two magnificent steamers' are now being built for the " Manx Line" by Messrs. John Elder and Co., the world-renowned builders of the Clyde. A SUCCESSFUL WIDNES PEDESTRIAN.—On Satur- day afternoon, at the Moorfield Grounds, Failsworth, J. Carney, of Widnes, was successful in winning the champion £llO quarter-mile handicap, promoted by Mr. A. Fletcher, who added £5O to an acceptance fee of £5 each. There were twelve entries, and the • opening heats were run on the 6th inst., when the following were . successful :—J. Martin, Halbeath, 12 yards start; J. Carney, Widnes' 21; 11. Gent, Darlington, 16; and D. WWilliams, llulme, 19. For the final heat on Saturday Gent was made a warm favourite, 6 to 4 being laid on him, but in the race he could never overtake the Widnes representative, who won easily by three yards. The prizes were divided as follows :-1, £BO, J. Carney; 2, £2O, H. Gent; 3, £5, D. MlVilliams ; 4, £s,_ J. Martin. THE ADVANTAGES OF WATER TRANSPORT. A pamphlet on " Inland transport and the Manches- ter Ship Canal "has been reprinted from the "Scot- tish Review " for October, and is very well worth reading, not merely for what it puts forward about the advantages of water transport, but for the light it throws on the position of our railways as heavy goods and minerals carriers. Those of them which conduct a mixed traffic at different rates of speed are bound, the writer thinks, to go from bad to worse as dividend-earning lines. The remedy is to throw the slow heavy traffic back upon the water- ways of the country. Without question there is truth in that view. But the most striking points in the essay relate to the heavy ehargesrA the railways of England, and their enormous capital outlay, as compared with those of other countries. By reason of the cost of carriage alone the manufacturing trades of this country tend to migrate to the sea- side. If they stay inland 'hey have to struggle for existence or die.—Standard.

Mn. W. CROSPIELD AND TIM LIVERPOOL SELECT VESTRY.—" The Liverpool Daily Post" says :—By fifteen votes to six, the Select Vestry on Tuesday declined to adopt a motion by Mr. Cropper, sup- ported by Mr. W. Crosfield and Mr. W. Rathbone, in favour of appointing ladies on the Vestry. The probability is that more will be heard of this pro- position. It was argued by its supporters that there are many questions affecting workhouse ad- ministration with which ladies are necessarily much more familar than men, and that the assist- ance of one or two lady members would.conse- quently be of great value. On the other side, it was firgued that women were best at home, and Mr. Boote ungallantly suggested that the result of their introduction to the Vestry would be increased chatter. Mr. Woodcock contended that there were already a matron and lady superintendent of nurses, and that they managed as well as lady members of the Vestry could, but he might just as well have argued that as there are a master and other male officers gentlemen are not needed on the Vestry. IMPROVEMENTS IN LAMP Burmuts.—The firm of Thomas Rowatt and Sons, of Edinburgh, has for many years been identified with improvements in mineral oil lamps, and it is therefore not surprising to find they have been able to devise a method which, in its results, places the domestic table lamp on a level with the better kind of gas burners. By the introduction of the "Lorne" burner Messrs. Rowatt do all tins and more. By the use of two wicks two independent flames are produced, and by their con- verge-nee at the point of ignition perfect cornbas- tion is obtained; there is no smell, and a brilliant steady flame results. Added to these manifold advantages is another—that while the greatest amount of illuminating power is obtained by the more perfect combusion of the oil, the two wicks barn no more oil than the one; indeed, it is asserted that they burn less. By a previous invention—the "Anueapnie"—a double dome was substituted for the old-fashioned brittle lamp chimney, and this principle being applied to the "borne," combines to mike the latter as perfect an oil lamp as it is possi- ble to secure.

WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIDRA.ItY.—A. meeting of the Widnes Free Library Committee was held on Wednesday evening, under the presidency'd Mr. 11. Wade Deacon. There were present Messrs. S. Sad- ler, F. lleyes, E. Carey, R. Lewis, J. Morrison, and T. Allen (clerk). About 154 applications had been received for the Situation of Librarian at a :-salary of £65 per annum. The number was reduced to 16, and included four librarians, who resided out Hof the town and 12 -townsmen and townswomen. It was decided that these applicants should be in- terviewed by the committee on ThursdaT next. A 'letter was read from Mr. T. E. Ellis, MX.. private secretary to Mr. J. T. Brunner, of \N-mnington, en- closing the promised.,cheque for £lOO to be utilized by the committee for the purposes of the library. 'The writer expressed the hope that the money would be spent in such a form that the gift would be commemorated. It was decided that the library should be lighted by five "sunlight" chandeliers, and that a lamp should be placed at the entrance, with an inscription of the name ,c,if the insti- tution.

RIVAL BILL POSTERS. He said he would put it thta ugn his mother for not having Isis dinner ready in time for hon. She (witness) went to bed about ten minutes to eleven o'clock, and at that time her husband went to the back door. Immediately afterwards she heard him cry " Murder ! lam stabbed with a knife." She got out of bed and ran to his assistance, when she saw prisoner and his mother, and her husband kneeling on the ground between them. Prisoner, with the knife produced in his hand, was making a blow at her husband, when she got between them. and received the blow on her right hand. Prisoner also struck her on the breast. The knife pierced her chemise, but it did not draw any blood. Blood was coming from her husband's head very profusely. She gave information to the police, and on the arrival of a constable her husband went to the doctor's.—ln answer to the prisoner, witness said the knife produced was the one she saw in his hands during the afternoon.—P.C. Porter said that at a quarter past ten on Sunday morning he went in search of the knife, and found the one 'produced io a yard at the back of Mr. Stead's chemist shop. at the corner of Lugsdale and Widnes roads. That is about fifty • yards from Where prisoner lived. The knife was closd, and on it were marks of blood.— Dr. O'Keeffe said between eleven and twelve o'clock en Saturday night the first witness (John Toohey) went to his surgery. He examined his head, and found upon it, a little to the right, a punctured and incised wound, and a punc- tured wound at the hack of the bead. Both penetrated to the bone. He did not think his had lost much blood, and only the one at the back of the head was dangerous. The knife produced would be likely to cause such wounds. , Great force must have been used to make the knife pene- trate to the bone. He bad also examined Ellen Toohey, and had found a wouud an inch and an half in length on the back of the right arm, and a slight wound on the breast. —P.C. Almond said he apprehended prisoner at 11-15 p.m., on Saturday night in Widnes-road. He took him to 9, Moon-street, and there John Toohey said to prisoner, " You have stablsed me twice on the head." Connolly replied, "You struck me on the bead with a poker." He (the con- stable then took prisoner to the police station, and there I charged him with he offence, to whien-he replied, " I sup- I pose he (meaning Toohey) can say what he likes. He does not say anything about fetching the poker out to me."— On prisoner row being charged, he pleaded not guilty of stabbing Toohey wilfully—lie was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

div.head: STABBING AFFRAY AT WIDNES.
div.p: STABBING AFFRAY AT WIDNES.

At Widnec Police Court, on Morriav, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, John Connolly, a rough-looking yoniig fel iG,V, was charged with having on Saturday night unlawfuliv and maliciously wounded his uncle, John Toohey, by stabbing him with a pocket knife.—John Tochey said he was labourer, and resided at 9, Moon-street, Widnes. Prisoaer, who is his nephew, resided with him. On Saturday night, about eleven o'clock, he was closing hEs back -..srd gate, when he saw prisoner and his mother there. He said, "Hello, John, is that you?" when prisoner, without utter- ing a word, struck him on the head with a knife. He shouted " Murder! I am stabbed," and his wife went to his assist- ance. He was bleeding from two wounds on the top of the head, and had lost a great amount of blood. He was sober, but he did not know whether prisoner; who afterwards ran away, was. He went to Dr. O'Keeffe's and had his wounds dressed.—Prisoner: Didn't I go to the door of the back yard at eleven o'clock, and it was locked. and I said " Let's in, Johnny," and you said "No" ?—Witoess (excitedly) : Never.—Mr. Gossage (to witness) : Behave yourself.—Pri- soner: Did you not come out with a poker ?—Witness (again excitedly) What did I want a poker for? div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.-THE
div.p: THE WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.-THE
COSTS.

The morthly meeting was held on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. T. .S. Timmis. and there were present the Rev. Father Finegan. Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Hever, Wareing, and Danby (clerk). Tue Finance Committee recommended that the costs of the recent election, amounting to £l6O, should be paid to Mr. S. H. Hartley, the returning officer. —Dr.O'Keeffe moved the passing of the minute.—Mr.Ware- ing said he had seen Mr. Hartley, And endeavoured to induce him to reduce the expenses in some way. He pint-rd out to Mr. Hartley that the Board thought ten polling stations excessive, and he replied that there should be a polling sta- tion for every 1,000 voters. Although there were only 4,525 voters in Widnes, the Education Department had given him power to increase the number allowed. Mr. lirrtley further pointed out that he could'have charged 70 guineas for these polling stations, but that he had actually charged only £4. With regard to the item £6 13s 61 for hire ot cabs, that charge was not allowed by Act of Parliament, but it was allowed by custom, and Mr. Hartley was prepared to stand by it. Mr. Hartley's personal remuneration was about £ss.—The Chairman said Mr. Hartley ought to have con- sulted the Board as to the number of polling stations that were to be fixed, and with respect to the hire of cabs, the Board, in his opinion, should not pay it. He did not think the auditor would pass it.—Several other members coincided, but ultimately the account was passed.

div.head: RUNCORN CRICKEI CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN CRICKEI CLUB.

The Annual meeting was held last night in the comnier- cial room of the Wilson's aotel. Mr. J. B. Frith, the pre- sident, oceupied the chair.. The Secretary (Mr. H. Wright) read a report, which stated that the reallt of the last sea- son'e cricket had not been encouraging. Out of 17 engage- ments played, the club had won 7, lost 7, and drawn 3, Their opponents had scored 14017 reins far the loss of 185 wick4e, whilst their club had scored 937 runs for the loss of 163 wickete, giving tke club an average of 5 76, against tneir opponents 549. The highest score made in a match by tue club wae 90, and their opponents 138. Their least score was 13, and their opponents 21. The number of extras conceded by us was 83, whilst they had allowed 94, this Proving indisputably that they were in advance of their opponents in the fielding department. It was cer- tainly in the batting department the club was weak, although they had emerged from the conflict slightly better than their opponents, and if the members could only be induced to practice more they might have better results. They had at the present time the best wicket that ever existed in the town, and, as they would hear from the treasurer, the club was not in debt, so that the proepects for the cowling season were of the brightest. Mr. J. M. Flrth headed the list for batting with an average

of 9.05 for twelve completed innings. Mr. J. Gatley was the highest.scorer in any one match, scoring 35 against Crewe It N.-W.) at Runcorn. The highest score made against the club was 47 bv Mr. L. Voisey, of the Warring- ton second teatn, on their ground. Three scores of over 100 had been made against the club by Prescot, Wallasey Village, and Warrington second respectively. The Club it- self had been unable to raise a three figure innings, although in their match 'vita Warrington Garrison they were within an ace of accomplishing this feat, time robbing them of shat appeared a certainty, the score standing at 95 for five wickets, and against Crewe they got within one of the number. They had had to rely on their old bowlers, Wood and Gatley, pretty much this season, the former concluding the season with an average of 460 for 53 wickets, whilst Gttley was just behind him with an aver- age of 650 for 55 wickets. Mr. C. E. Norman had an average of 5*14, he having bowled in three matches for the , first eleven, and when it was remembered that he accom- plished this in both ma,ch4s against Prescot and Warring- ton Garrison, there was great credit due to him. Mr Wright then gave an elaborate and interesting acconat of etch match, concluding with complete batting and bowling averages, which pressure for space prevents us publishing. I —Mr. J. M. Frith, the treasurer, gave a statement of accounts, which showed a balance in favour of the club of £3 23101 The reports were adopted, and votes of thanks were ac- corded to the various officials.—Tne Chairman, in a brief ' sJeech, said there were some voati4 players amongst them who had developed great talent, and with a better ground next year they would no doubt distinguish themselves next season.—Toe Chairman declined to again accept the office of president in the face of a unanimous wish, and proposed I that Mr. E. A. Chorlton have the lionour.—M.r. Haddock seconded the motion, which was carried unaninsonsly.—The vice-presidents were re-elected,on the motion of Mr P Smith. Mr, R. Cookson was re-elected captain, and Mr. H. Wright cab-captain; other officers were also appointed.

div.head: VISIT OF THE MARQUIS OF
div.p: THE VISIT OF THE MARQUIS OF
RIPON TO RUNCORN.

The date of the projected visit of the Marquis of Ripon to Runcorn has been altered from Tuesday, the 7th, to Monday, the Gth December, because it was discovered that the former date did not suit the engagements of his lordship. The local com- mittee have met this week in order to make the necessary arrangements. It was decided that a conference should be held in the afternoon, under the presidency of Mr, E. H. Moss, of Middlewich, and Mr. Schnadhorst has already consented to be present. Matters of great importance will be discussed, and the following associations have been invited to send delegates :—Eddisbury, Crewe, Altrincham, Wirrall, Knutsford, Hyde, Mac- clesfield, Birkenhead, Chester, Stalybridge, Stock- port, Widnes, Newton, Liverpool, St. Helens, and Warrington. At the evening meeting Mr. It. Shaw ; will preside, and besides the Marquis several mem- bers of Parliament are expected to speak. Admis- sion to the meeting will be by ticket, of which 400 , will be reserved at. a cost of 1$ ettch,

div.head: FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT IN
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT IN
WARRINGTON.

Last evening a deputation waited upon the Mayor, and presented the following requisition, which was supported by over 400 signatures:—" To his:Worship the M a,yor of Warrington, Councillor , Dr. Mackie. The undersigned ratepayers and in- habitants of the Borough of Warrington, respect- ' fully request your worship to convene a public ' meeting of the burgesses and ratepayers, to take into consideration the advisability of making the Warrington Library a Free Lending Library, and to pass resolutions thereon." The Mayor said that after receiving such a numerously signed requisition, he should most willingly call a Town's Mer:ting, and should be glad to aid the requisitionists in the ob- ject they had in view. lie would in a day or two decide as to the time and place of the meeting. The deputation, after some conversation, thanked the Mayor for his courtesy, and withdrew.: The following letter to a contemporary from the chairman of the committee for freeing the Warring- ton Library will be read with interest:— Sir,—Please accept my thanks for your short leader in Saturday last's impression. 1 give way with all due respect to your definition of the manner we were treated who waited upon the Library and Museum Committee. Together with a host for a town like ours behind me, we intend to do as you suggest—" continue to labour at proving our case to be good "—converting all we can to our way of thinking, by telling them, amongst other things, that pupil teachers and others are compelled Ito take their dinners to school with them, so that j they can, so soon as school hours are over, run off to the library to eat and drink, read and think at the same time.. Cramming by the „teacher is not a tithe on this form of stuffing the stomach and the brain at the same time—a system which is condemned by all physiologists—that some parents who can afford to pay the 5s per year so that their boy can have the privilege of taking the book home to avoid this health-destroying medium. That some parerts have boys and. girls getting up their lessons, or to orthodox essay at one and the same time, andfe,annot afford the needful lOs or 15s, and in this casc. the children must go and consult with pencil and paper in hand, in all weathers and at all hours of orming, the boeks they desire to read. Often enough the book has to be closed to get home before tl,e information has been obtained.. That so ranch e this sort of reading is being done now, and especi- ally just previous to examinations, that these young m#eople take up all the sittings in the commodious proom, and the -man who has been 6i-ling all thy, kand is longing-for a rest and .a read, has to go out j again. Where;? Yes: 0! where? Sir, this is no imagination; indeed, it is such a truism that some of my committee are so impressed by it that earnestness for our aim to be -consummated grows upon them as hunger and thirst grow upon them. In a paragraph' (same iwpression) Tou tell us Mr. Beamont arras again elected chairman of the Museum and Library Committee, and "delivered a short but 'effective address?' I have scanned the paper all aver, and fail to find what he said. I ad- mire that grand old gentleman. arid we agree in ninety-nine views in every hundred, and this fact makes Mc feel sorry that we differ on this free reading question, running as it does in parallel lines with his every day's actions in the cause of education of the young. How he can turn away from thew at the "leaving school station," where there are .so many junctions, I cannot.conceiive. This leaving school period of a lad's life is a most critical one to him, and a very anxious one for the parent. If the lad inclines to reading, and the parent has no library, because perhaps he himself never learned to read, the youth's inclination dies for want of the food for his mind, and whilst this spirit is kTing, he is floundering until he fiads rest,. maybe among that company in which there is no safety nor security. Stopping the augmentative, we don't want to shift Mr. Beamont from his post of chainuan, nor a single member of his committee; we don't v:ant to move Mr. Madeley, nor any of his staff. We don't want to increase the rates, neither will we try to do so. All we desire is to increase the usefelness of the institution. _ -

Surely this is not too mach to ask for a working manufactiring population, whose productions are so various, and the improvements thereon are so numerons and come so rapidly from so. many quar- ters. that cur skilful men are smarting under the competition. The "knowledge is power" maxim is knocked on the head as with a blow from a steam hammer by the learned men who are op- posing us. A few days ago you were elected chief magistrate of this important, though not very large, manufac- turing town. Over its moral interests you should watch with a jealous care, and I have faith that you will do so. Allow me to introduce to you the very good idea of Mr. Thomas Greenwood, author of "Free Public Libraries." It is "that there scarcely.. be abetter way of celebrating her Majesty's Jubilee Libraries Act, and establishing for the use .e of its inhabitants a free library and art Liusemn.-

lean hardly stay my pen, but I must, and in con- clusion I ask you to prepare yourself for that immorable day in June next, when, with all the reasonable pomp and flourishing of trumpets, you will announce to the people of Warrington that from that day the 'newly titled " Victoria Free Lend- ing Library " is open .to all and every one of proper age in this borough, as our Art Museum is now. Whilst you are thus preparing, I and my fellow workers in this cause will be exerting ourselves to find the needful means whereby the scheme may be carried out without the least friction, those against us in this month of November joining with us next June round the festive board in the evening, after a well-spent day, joining in a unanimous chant of heart and voice in praise of our beloved Queen, under your chairmanship.—Yours faithfully, November Isth, 188 G. THOMAS MORRIS.

SEQUEL TO A 'WARRINGTON
ELOPEMENT.

The Borough Court at Warrington was crowded yesterday morning during the hearing of a ease that has excited considerable comment in the neighbour- hood. James William Woodcock (42), styled as a general labourer, and Annie Goodier, wife of a shoe— maker living at Latchford, were together brought up on remand from Monday, and were charged with stealing several articles of wearing apparel and other things, of the value of £3, the property of the husband of the female prisoner,Thonaas Goodier. Woodcock was algo charged that he, on the 2nd of November, at Latchford, being the bailee of cer. tam n moneys, to wit .EOO, belonging to Ann Wood— cock, did fraudulently take and convert the same to his own use, and thereby did steal the same. Annie Goodier was also charged with being an accessory before the fact. Ann ‘tioodzock (Ti). who is a widow, is the mother of the male prisoner.and a native of Duke-street, Manchester. She lived there up to two or three years ago, when she came to live at Berry-street, Warringtoa. Sub- sequently isos went to lodge wire Thomas Goodier, a mar- ried man, a shoemaker in the employ of Mr. Sudlow, Horse- market-street, who lives at 78, Green's-row, Latchford. Mrs Woodcock's son, James William, left his home in Manches- ter in 1865, when be was 21 years of age, and west to Queensland, where he remained a number of years. In 1883 he returned to Manchester. His mother at that time was ill, and was attended by a woman named Mary Perry, with whom the returned traveller soon became on good terms, and who he married in March, 1883. They had lived to- gether in Manchester until 1884, when they removed to Warrington. Some difference arose between tnero and they parted, Woodcock goingiback to Queensland and his wife to Manchester. This year Woodcock wrote for money to bring him home again, and his mother sent him £25, with which to pay his passage. He arrived in Warrington on • the 12th of September last, and lodged at the house of the Goodiers', where his mother was still living. It appears that his wife, bearing of his return, wished to live with him again, and afterwards got an order on him to pay 3s per week towards her main- tenance. Old Mrs. Woodcock endeavoured to effect a re- conciliation, saying that she should like her son, his wife, and herself, all to live together. and to go into some sort of business. The elder Mrs. Woodcock had £125 nod invested in Parr's bank, and the son suggested that the money should be put in his name, to which she assented. On the 29th Oct. the two went to the bank, where the transfer was effected. Afterwards the money was drawn out, and the son deposited £3O in the Post Office Sayings' Bank to the credit of his mother. He also gave her £3 just before the was going to Manchester to see some one. This left the son with over £9O of the money ha his possession. Early on the morning of the 2nd November, Goodier went to his work, and his dinner was sent for him as usual at noon. The Goodiers have three children, and the eldest (13) was told to get his dinner out. It seems that Woodcock and Mrs. Goodier then commenced to pack things up, and left the house. As they were crossing Warrington bridge, Mrs Goodier having the two children with her, she met her eldest son and told him that , she was going to the Exhibition, and should be back that night or the next morning. See added," Be a good boy to your father; when you get home at six o'clock look under the sofa and you will find a letter ta your father." The lad did so, and upon Mr. Goodier being informed, the police were made acquainted with the affair. Enquiries then in- stituted elicited that Woodcock and Mrs Goodier, with two of the latter's children, went from Bank Quay to Liverpool by the 2 40 p.m. train, and when there Woodcock wrote a letter for his mother to a Mrs Cody, which is given below. The same day the eloping party proceeded to London, and aext morning went to the offizes of Messrs Donald Currie and Co., in Fenchurch-street, and took passages to Cape Town under the names of Mr and Mrs Stery and their two children. For these £42 6s 63 was paici. They remained in London from the second to the tenth, on which day they embarked at the East India Docks on the Castle Packet liner, the Pembroke. Castle, bound for Cape Town. Meanwhile a warrant bad been issued, and information re- ceived at Warrington from Scotland-road to the effect that persons answering the description of the missing party had booked for Cape Town at the shipping office is Fenchurcha street. The Dartmouth police were telegraphed to, so that the elopers might be intercepted there before the boat pro- eteled on the voyage, and on the Thursday information reached Warrington that the arrest had been effected. Sergeant Bowen fetched them back, and £l6 in money was found in the possession of the male prisenee. They arrived at War- rington early On Sunday morning, and on the Monday were laroutihtbgore the magistrates on charges of theft, and were temanded until yesterday, an application for bail made by Mr. Goodier on behalf of his wife being refused, both on that day and the following one, when the application was made by Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, who intimated that Goodier believed his wife virtuous, and was willing to receive her . back. Yesterday the prosecution was conducted by Mr. Schofield, of Manchester, and prisoners were not defended. The charge of stealing wearing apparel, &c., was first gone into, and the following evidence was taken. Thomas Goodier, boot and shoe maker, 78. Green's-row, Latchford, said that he was the husband of the female I prisoner. She left a letter, saving that Ehe had gone. Wit- did not miss any articles belonging to him from the house. There were none of the articles produced his own property. Mr. Schofield: The case on that point breaks down en- tirely. • There is only the charge of larceny with respect to I the money, and that affects more particularly the male coi- -1 , Boner.

The letter referred to by witness was couched in the fol- lowing terms :—" Dear Tom,—l have taken a great thing upon myself. I have had the offer of my Passage paid at once, and the children, but not enough for all, but you shalt be with me in leas than six months, that is if yon will come, koping my dear husband, and that is more to me than anything on earth. I am taking James more because he can tell yea how his mother lives while you are away. am sce, ill that I think it will either kill me or cure. me. I went to a doctor yesterday, he said it' I could get to a warm place it might do me good. Do not think bad of me, if had asked you to let me go you would not, bet when you know everything you will bless me. log can tell ceople that gone away for my health, which is true-. I should eel all the things and go in lodgings, you and Alfred., and save as much as you can; so may God bless you. Tkrust me, and all will be well. I will write to you at your shop. Do not make a bother after me. I don't owe ' any money to anyone only Mrs. Green for rent, and that is ever since I was so ill. You can pay her at 2s GI a week: I did net know that I was going till just now. Forgive me, but we should never be able to save enough. for all of us. So you have to save as mochas you can. I will send your ;rassage as soon as get there. God bless you and Alfred. Be good to him. We shall soon meet on this earth or another. I have pat all the bills in the bottom drawer."" The letter, which was almost illegible, concluded with "Your Loving Annie." The aecond charge was then gone into, and Ann Wool- cock widow, now of es, Sidney-street, Halme, Manchester, the mother of the male prisoner, said that over £lOO of her money was transferred to the name of the nale prisoner; ' but wiatess did nut eve P• him. 'file transfer took piece on Seuteteber 18:h. Witness could not write well and did mot hue .irming cheques, se she transferred it to sin in. order that he might sign them. Ber son was married. but did not live with his wife, and witness suggested that all ' three should live together. Her son told her that he had ' drawn the money out of the bank. I should onely be giving myself away by my starting in annythank, so i have thought better of it i have been thanking that i should like to see Tom i have made up my mind at wonce to see him the ship sales from Leverpool 5 on Wednesday morning next. My Dear Mother the monney that i am taking i am only borowing it as i shall be dewing better than to stop hear as i shell start in America at somthing. One of the questions which seems to be forcing its way to the front, and which threfttt.l., ere long to become a burning one, is that .•f Vegetarianism. Prior to 1847 the disciples of Daniel and Pythagoras had no union save that which their principles made, but in that year they formed themselves into a society, and issued a periodical entitled the "Vege- tarian Messenger ;" but subsequently this title be- came altered to that of "Dietetic Reformer and Vegetarian Messenger." They did not create much publicity until within the last ten or twelve years when through the aid of literature and vegetarian ; dining rooms they have at last succeeded in awak- ing some portion of the British public to the fact ' that to " slay and eat" is not an absolute necessity to preserve health and strength. Whether the system contains the virtues ascribed to it by its advocates or not, is a question I will not discuss at present; certain it is that principles, which can enrol among their adherents such names as Milton, Newton, Franklin, Byron, Shelley, and Newman, are worthy of serious consideration. There is an old saying that an ounce of practice is worth a pound of precept, but for a long time. in fact ever since its commencement, the Vegetarian Society had been giving the people plenty of the r, latter, without mixing in any of the former. They had issued scores of publications, but had not opened a single dining-room where people could see the practical side of the system (it may have been from lack of means.) Here and there in large centres in- dividual enterprise had started some of these insti- tutions, but until 1884 the society had not woke up, or been able to adapt themselves to the fact that the ; way to a man's—and especially an Englishman's ; —heart is down his throat. In that year the first vegetarian restaurant belonging to the society (and the first ever introduced into an exhibition) was opened at the Health Exhibition, London, and our fellow townsman, Mr. W. 11. Chapman, who, it may be said, was the inaugurator of vegetarianism in Warrington, was given the honour of managing it. It was in this restaurant that the now celebrated , principle of providing three courses for six- pence, was adopted, and which no doubt largely contributed to its popularity and great success. Thousands of people who scarcely knew what Vegetarianism was, flocked into the dining-room to try a dinner, and were surprised to find that they did not want another dinner im- mediately after. During the six months the exhi- bition was open more than 160,000 persons were catered for, or an average of over 1,000 per day. They had also several notable persons who patron- ised them, among whom may be mentioned the Marquis of Northampton, the late Mr. Samuel Mor- ley, and Dr. Norman Kerr. The two following years. for some reason or 1 other they do not seem to have had a restaurant in in either of the London Exhibitions, but as most of your readers are probably aware, they succeeded in opening one in the Exhibition that has just come to a close in Liverpool, at which Mr. Chapman was also appointed manager. They fol- lowed the same rule as in London, that of providing; three courses for 6d. giving a choice of two soups, two savouries, and two sweets, and an a la earte, from which people selected as they chose ; bread was also given with the soup. The success which they scored in London has been repeated in Liver- pool, although not so great, the total number reach- ing over 140,000, which bears a greater proportion to the number of visitors to the Liverpool Exhibi- tion than to the one in London. The numbers served on any one day were also greater in Liver- pool, the occasion of the National Temperance Fete being the highest, on which day over 2,500 people were served, while the greatest number on any given day at the Health Exhibition was only 1,900. This shows that had the number of visitors to the Liverpool Exhibition been equal to the London Ex- hibition in 1884, the Vegetarian Society would have catered for over 200,000 persons. There is a possibility of their opening a restaurant at the exhibition to be held in Manchester in the coming year. If they do, I could wish them no better assurance of success than that Mr. Chapman should again undertake the management. It may be stated, with regard to the spread of vegetarianism, that since the Health Exlaibition in 1884 no less than twenty restaurants have been opened in different parts of the country, of which fourteen are in London alone, and the cry is, more are wanted. There is no doubt that, right or wrong, the vegetarian system of diet is making headway, and there is no better way of advancing it than by the opening of dining-rooms,which show the people that it is quite possible to have good, wholesome, and satisfying meals, at a far less cost, without the introduction of fish, flesh, or fowl.

TER COLLINt GRIIHN SlEll[ll.—A meeting of colliere was held at the George Inn, George-street, St. Helene, on Monday afternoon, when abovt 150 of the men at present on strike at Collins Green were present A ballot was taken as to whether the men would consent to return to work upon the master's terms. STOPPAGB OF GOLBOTINB COrMIC Maa.;l.—We regret to announce that the extensive cotton mills' and weaving sheds for many years worked by Messrs. T. Brewis and Co., at Gol*orne. Newton-le-Willows, are now entirely clooed for an, indefinite period. Notices, warning the bands that this might occur, were posted a few weeks ago, and ore Saturn'ly last all hands were paid off and the whole of the machinery brought to a standstill. Messrs. Brown and Wigan, who have purchased the premises, will work the concem at some future date, but as yet it is not known, when the place will re-start. CHURCH or FrTGLAND THMPRRANCIS SOCIRry.— On 1 Tuesday night the first meeting of the season of the Lymrn 1 branch of the Church of Erie land Temperance Society took 1 place in the Boys' School, Pepper-street. The chair wile, taken by Dr. Wilkineon, who argutd, from a medical point of view, that alcohol was not necessary to life, as many people erronecrasly supposed it to be. The Rev. E. G. Lomax said it was their intention this year to make the monthly meetings of the society more attractive than was the cAse last year, by combining the serious part of the business with entert,inmeram of a varied character. Mr. Naylor, of 1 helwall, delivered an amusing and highly en- tertaining address on the temperance question, which was fully appreciated by the large company present. On the conclusion of the address, &logs were sung by Messrs. John Dixon, W. Teynson. El. Clara, W. Ardern, and W. Bradburn, the entertainment concluding with a laughable farce en- titled, " Who would be a bachelor ?" the characters of which were admirably sustained by Messrs J E Blackmere, H Clare, W Joynsonrand Misses Gosling and Moston.

ALLEORD ASSAITLT.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Wiles- pie,.Martha Ellison, an elderly female, was summoned for assaulting Kate Saul, who resides in Derby-street, Earles- town, on. the 14th ult. Defendant pleaded not guilty. The complainant stated that the defendant came to her house and cursed her little boy, saying she would take hi s• life. She (complaisant) spoke to the defendant about her conduct and the defendant used abusive language to her, afterwards breaking open the house door,—The defendant denied hav- ing assaulted the complainant and the Bench dismissed the case.

GOOD T EXPLLIM. —Brother John Taylor, W:C.T., presided at the weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars, on Monday evening. There was a good attendance. Three candidates were initiated, and ar- rangements were made for paying a friendly visit to the , Lo ton Primitive Methadist Band of Hope, and the Ashton I Congregational Band of Hope. The evening's programme was "Visit of the Ashton Excelsior Lodge," nearly 2O' members of the Ashton Lodge attended, and occupied the I various offices,. Brother E Chesworth, P.W.C.T., presiding. An enjeyable entertainment of songs, reAdings, and recita- tions followed, and at the close the visitors were warmly thanked, on the motion of Brother debit Warburton, secon- ded by Brother Min Taylor. 1 ROBBING- A- POMATO CABT.—At the Newton Pettyy Sessions. on Saturday, John Walsh and his mother, Bridget , Ann Walsh, were charged with stealing 120Ibs. of potatoes 1 from a cart on the farm of John Prescott, Burtonerood, on the night of the 2nd inst. On the morning of the 3rd inst.' it was found,that the potatoes had been tah.en from the I cart, and footsteps were traced to the row of houses, in one of which the prisoners lived. The potatoes were found in the back kitchen of the prisoners' heuee. The female prisoner was apprehended, and in reply to the charge she - said she knew nothing about the potatoes. The male prisoner was afterwards apprehended at Ormskirk, and in reply to the charge-he said his mother was not guilty, as. she knew nothing about them. The prosecutor said he did not desire to press the ease. The magistrates discharged' the female prisoner, and fined the other prisoner lOs andtl costs, or 14.days' imprisonment. EABLEBTOWN. CO OPER/MYR SOCIETY.—The rov,h I quarterly meeting of the members of this society wae held, in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening.. There was a good number of members present. Mr. .1: Letham presided, The report and statement of accounts, for the quarter showed that there had been an increase-in the Bele!, over the previous quarter of £133 Os 1141, the total sales lying for grocery £2,996 93 31. boots, drapery,. drc, £426, 12s 6d;. and the expenses £297 18s 6JI •, the disposable profit being £415 lOs 3p, which enabled the I payment of a dividend of 2s 7d in the .£ to members, and is 3d in the £ to non-members, carrying a balance of £776s 31d to the contingent fund. Messrs. Cordingley and Sed- don were re-elected to serve on the Committee of Manage- ment. It was decided to give a donation of £5, to the Science and Art Classes of the Viaduct Institute, to be com- peted for by members of the Co.operatiVe Society or their children.

Superintendent Weir rose to state the facts of the case, and said : John Prescott is a farmer, and the potatoes wert secured in a cart on the evening of the 211.1 inst.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Buckton) : Mr. Weir ? —Superintendent Weir (continuing) : On the following mornieg it was 17eind they were inissing.—The Magistrates' Clerk (louder) : Mr. Weir ?—Superintendent Weir (still continuing) : Communicition was made to the police-- The Clerk (interrupting) : Mr. Weir, will you listen ? div.head: MUSPRITT WILL CASE.
div.p: THE MUSPRITT WILL CASE.

In the Probate Division, Dandon, on Monday, Mr. Justice Butt had before him the case of Muspratt and Another v. Porwood and Others. It had refer- ence to the testamentary dispositions of the late Mr. James Muspratt, the well-known alkali manufac- turer, who died in Seaforth Hall, Seaforth, near Liverpool, on the 4th May, 1886, at the advanced age of 93, possessed of a considerable amount of property, amounting to about £150,000. The plain- tiffs. as executors, propounded a will dated the sth July, 1876, and two codicils, of 31st July, 1883, and. 29th August, 1885. Probate was opposed by the de- fendants, who allege undue execution, unsound mind, and non-approval of the contents. They sought to have established a will executed in 1874, under which they were benefitt.d. The Attorney-General (Sir R. Webster, Q.C.), and Mr. Middleton appeared for the petitioners; and the Solicitor-General (Sir E. Clarke, Q.C., M.P.), Mr. Inderwick, Q.C., and Mr. Bargrave Deane for the defendants.

In opening the case, the Attorney-General said that the testator was born in 1793, and in his early career he certainly led a most adventurous life.l He had served both in the army and the navy, and narrowly escaped with his life at the time of the Peninsular war. Originally he had something to do with chemistry, and after his adventurous spirit was cured he established what has become one of the most important industries in Lancashire, viz., the manufacture of alkali. He was a man of strong will and remarkable judgmenti being capable of understanding things as well as any man. During the last five or six years of his life he had suffered from rheumatism and other bodily ailments, making it difficult for him to get about. For the last four years of his life he practically resided in the upper part of his house, where he used to see his friends. He became acquainted with men of literature, and took a keen interest in all matters connected with chemical science. He was an intimate friend of Baron Liebig, and was brought in contact with men of culture. He always took great interest in his pecuniary affairs. He made a number of wills. Originally he had seven children—four sons and three daughters—his eldest son being Dr. James Sheridan Muspratt, who was a very distinguished chemist. The learned counsel then detailed the history of the will-making and the two codicils. By the will of 1874 it appeared that the two defen- dants and grand-children were benefited to the ex- tent of £15,000, but by the will of 1876 and the two subsequent codicils they were deprived of that altogether, this practically being the question at issue. _ _ _

Dr. Bickerstaffe, the medical attendant of the de- ceased, gave evidence to the effect that at the time the testamentary papers in question were executed the deceased was of sound disposing mind. There was no defect in his mental power. lle died at the age of 93. He was a man of remarkably strong will, and was very firm in judgment, being a per- son of culture. He was perfectly competent to , transact. business. In cross-examination the wit- ness said the testator had a delusion that he was ruined, and that people were coming to arrest , him.

Mr. Frank Dobson Lowndes, solicitor, of Liver- ,mpoionld aelfs ot hgea vdee eeevaisdeedn. c e Haes ut soe tdh to s oj ue kn ed a bd ei supt ops ei nl ig_ tics, and discuss matters that were going on. A number of other witnesses deposed as to the mental capacity of the deceased, while the manager of the firm of Muspratt and Sons spoke of the keen interest the deceased always had in connection with business matters, there benign° failure of memory or want of testamentary Capacity. Mr. Gorst, a broker, of Liverpool, said that the deceased was a wonderfully clear-headed man, and retained his faculties down to the last. • The deceased felt the death of his son Richard very keenly. Dr. George Harley, in practice in London, hus- band of one of the daughters of the deceased, said that in 1884 he was going to Canada with the British Association, and previous to embarking he saw his father-in-law, who was then perfectly of sound disposing mind. Upon the return of wit- ness from America he again saw the deceased, who conversed with him most intelligently about America. Mr. Edmund Knowles Muspratt, one of the sons of the deceased and an executor, a member of the firm of Muspratt and Sons, also gave evidence as to the testamentary capacity of his father. He was not present at the execution of either of the wills. The codicil was made, and his father said that the two defendants were well provided for. In the result the learned judge found for the last will and codicils, and condemned the defendants in costs.
A fire occurred on Wedneqdav at Downpatrick, by which damage to the amount of £lO,OOO was done te the premises of several tradesm-n.

At a large meeting of merchants and traders in the prin- cipal business centres of North-East Lancashire. held at Blackburn on Wednesday, it was decided to form a Cham- ber of Commerce for the district.

The Marquis of Sligo has offered to sell his land in the parish of Westport to the tenants thereof at 18 veers' pur- chase of the existing judicial rents' and it is said that many of the tenants have gladly accepted the offer. A Cabinet CPuncil was held on Wednesday afternoon at the Foreign Office. After the Council Lord Salisbury had a consultation with Lord Iddesleigh, and subsequently had an interview with Count Corti, the Italian Ambassador. THE COLERIDGE LIBEL CASE.—The hearing of the case of Adams v. Coleride•e commenced on Wednesday in the Queen's Bench Division, before Mr. Justice Denman and a special jury. The action is to recover damages for alleged libels arising out of certain legal matters pending between the plaintiff and the defendants, which by mutual consent had been referred to arbitration, and the lheels complained of consisted of letters charging the plaintiff with base con- duct in pursuiny Lord Coleridge's daughter for mercenary motives. The ulaintiff, who is Lord Colerid9,,e's and who is conducting his own case, claims £20,000 dam- ages. The pleadings in answer deny the publication, and also the rra.anings attributed to the words. Evidence was given on Wednesday by the Earl of Iddesleigb, the Earl of Selborne, the Bishop of Oxford. and Lord Herschel', and the bearing was adjourned. On Thursday the action was re- sumed. Evidence having been given by Mr. Stephen Coleridgs, the son of the Lord Chief Justice, and formerly his private secretary, several documents bearing upon the case, including the statement by Miss Coleridge which was submitted to the arbitrator, and the case Lord Coleridge submitted to the assessor in connection with previous litiga- tion, were read, and the hearing was again adjourned.

.Under the auspices of the Earlestown and District Liberal Association a miscellaneous concert was given in the Co- operative Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday craning. Though the artistes are all locally resident. their popularity. was suf- ficient to raise hopes that the gathering would be a success, and these anticipations were fully realised. The room was comfortably filled, and a keen interest in the proceedings was maintained to the end. The vocalists were Mrs. Hen- derson, Miss Thompson, Miss Fleming, Mr. Peter Hastie, Mr. S. Swann, Mr, J. Giboone, Mr. J. Harrison ~humoureas), and pianoforte selections were 2iven by Miss Jackson and Miss Edwards. The duties of accompanist were performed by Mr. E. Cor- lett. Before the commencement Mr. Thomas Morris,. the genial secretary of the Liberal Club, stated that Mr. J. Wil- liams, who had been announced to attend, was unable to be present miring to a death in the family. Mr. Joseph Harri- son, however, had kindly come forward and caasented to appear on Mr. Williams' behalf. (Applause.) Miss Jackson commenced the programme with a pleasant pianoforte ren- dering of 'Caller Herrin," and she was succeeded by Mr. P. Heade. whose effective interpretation of "The. man of war" secured him warm applause. Miss Thompson was heartily greeted, and she gave a pretty rendering of Green's song "The kingdon blest."' Mr. J. The appear- ance of Mrs Henderson was the signal for hearty applause, and her inimitable rendering of "Robin Adair" ensured a recall, and she responded with an equally popular selec- tion. "Trusty as steel " was vigorously sung by M. S. Swann, whose recall was demanded, and he gave "Heroes." div.p: SUPPOSED EXTF,NSM ROBBERIES
AY LY34111.

Yesterday, at the Lymm: Petty Sessions, Edward ! Rowles an elderly man, employed as a fustian cut- I ter at gtathain, near Lymmi was charged with hav- ing committed robberies on. a. very extensive scale. I He was first indicted for having stolen a quantity ! of Indian meal, bran, and wheat, the property of Mr. Joseph. Marsh, farmerrLymm, and in support of I this charge P.C. Dutton stated: that about half-past one o'clock on the morning of the 14th November, he was hidden in Mr. Marsh's shippon, .when a per- son came in and struck a match, by the light of , which the officer saw it was the prisoner. The offi- cer afterwards heard him handling the meal and corn bags, and then went up to, him, shone his lamp ' in his face and asked him, what he was doing there. Prisoner replied "What are you going to do with me," and Dutton said "I' am going to lock you up." The officer then took p,risoner towards the police station, but in coming across, the fields Rowles at- tempted to, escape in the direction of his own house, but the officer caught him and after a struggle put the handcuffs, on. Prisoner was then charged with having stolen a quantity of I wood and some tools, the property of William Ard- ern, builder,.Statham, in 1877. In support of this I charge it was stated.by P:C. Dutton that atter pri- soner's apprehension he searched his house, and I found a back bedroom full of articles of almost levery imaginable description. There were guns, I netting, telegraph wires, wire fencing, a variety of I artisans' tools, &c., amongst the rest being the ar- ticles referred. to, which Mr. .Ardern identified as part of a large number of tools, &c., that had been stolen from his workshomin 1877. Nearly a cart load of these articles were brought to the police station, and there were almost as many more left behind. It was stated by Sergeant llarrington that the police had not yet been able-to4race the owners of any other of thearticles than those recognised by Mr. Ardern. The prisoner had nothing to say in reply to the charges,.and he was, committed to the next QuarterSessions,to be held, at lin utsford..

Eccles gave an address on " Socialism " on Tues- day evening to the largest gathering of the season. He argued in favour of raising the masses, in preference to lowering the upper strata of society, by encouraging thrift and total abstinence principles. -During the evening solos were rendered by Miss Dearden, Miss Smith, Miss Saunders, and Mr. William Smite ;, a pianoforte duet by Misses C. Williams and Leach ;. a recitation by Mr. J. Stott; and a reading by the citairman. SHOCKING, DEATti,AT Wlitt3TON.—An inquest was held en Thursday mornine.,,at the Carrs Hotel, iabiStorl, by Mr. S. Brighouse, on the body of Simeon Whitehead, collier, in the employ of the Carr's Colliery Company, who met with his death by a fall of coal. about a ton in weight, on Monday merniug, soon after nine o'clock, death being instantaneous. Deceased lived at Prescott and was 25iears of age. Elia father gave evidence of identification, tyhe widow being too much overcome,.and the manager, Mr. George liarto/1, and reter Cunningham, deceased's mate, deposed to the facts, from which it appeared the fall took place without any warning whatever.. A verdict of accidental death was re- turned. Deceased leaves a widow and three children.

PI,T ACCIDENTS- AT WHlsTore.—This week has been pecu- liarly unfortunate at the pits in this neighbourhood, not a day passing without its record of disasters. Besides the fatality at Caree,.a serious mishap betel a young man tamed John Ashton, of the Factory, Huyton Quarry. He is em- ployed at the Wigan and Whiston Colliery, and whilst tipping coal on Wednesday he became entangled in the tip. pler, and was with great difficulty extricated, his head be- ing crushed in a dreadful manner. At the same time Ann Byrom, of Prescot, also received serious injuries to her head and one of her hands by the same accident. Thos. Peters and George Gee,the first named had his fingers and the latter his foot crushed, whilst at work in the Wigan and Whiston Col- liery. The whole of the cases are being attended by Dr. Brindle, of Prascot, and are progressing favourably. Wittsti. CHAPEL, HUYTON QUA3RY. A unique enter— tainment was given at the above place of worship on Satur- day evening. It consisted of the celebrated "Trial of John 'Barleycorn ''' in the Welsh language, and in character. He- was duly tried anti condemned under eight terrible indict- ments by a host of witnesses, the principal roles being sus- tained. as follows :—Judge, Mr. Isaac Williams, who was supported on the bench by Mr. Edward Ellis and Mr. T. Twiss ;- counsel for prosecution. Rev. John Roberts; counsel for defence, Mr. John. Williams; clerk, Mr. W. Jones;- Sir John (prisoner), Mr.. John Jones; police-con- stables, Messrs. Richard Williams and .D. Jones. The several parts were well sustained, and as the "judge " sig- nificantly remarked, the prisoner, as a Welshman, had the right and privilege of being tried in his own tangos on that occasion_ The building was well filled, and as a small charge had been made for admission, the Children's Cloth- ing Club was thus enabled to replivish its fund. LECTURE AT HUYTON.—On Thursday evening the Dam- house-lane schools were filled to their utmost capacity, the attraction being Mr. George St. Clair's popular exposition of recent discoveries in lands renowned in Biblical history, under the auspices of the Palestine Exploration Society. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn. The chairman briefly introduced the lecturer, by remarking that be had taken an interest in the work of the society since it started 21 years azo, having previously had the advantage of a tour through Palestine, and experienced great difficulty of recegnising places owing to the changed coefiguration of the ground, since made comparatively plain by the recent excavations. Mr. t-t. Clair then proceeded with his inter- esting lecture, whith wai illustrated by a number of coloured diagrams and maps. He opened by remarking that the value of the society's work was apparent in adding to the history of the world, besides substantiating by side lights the authenticity of the Bible. A collection was taken at the close in aid of the exploration fund.

At Bedford Assizes, on Wednesday, a labourer, named Alfred Hitch, was sentenced to death for the murder of Chas. Plumbridge, near Uxbridge, on August 25. PULPIT AMENITIES.—A Conference, held on Thursday at Dr. Parker's City Temple, London, discussed whether a State Church is compatible with true Christian unity. The Rev. J. Guinness Rogers presided, and Churchmen, Con- gregationalists, Presbyterians, and Baptists took part in the discussion, which turned chiefly upon the question of the interchange of pulpits. GORED. TO DEATH RV A BUM—A shocking occurrence was on Thursday reported from Tongwymalis, in Wales. As a young gentleman named Lewis, son of Mr. John Lewis, of the Laurels, was proceeding along the highway he was suddenly attacked by a bull which was being driven to the slaughter-house. The animal tossed the poor fellow over its head, and then gored him 80 ftiKirtfUlly that he died soon afterwards.

Flicns-linhem ON IRELAND.—Sir Michael Hicks- Beach, speaking on Saturday evening at. the Dolphin So- ciety dinner in aelebration of the Colston anniversary at Bristol, said tha primary duty of the Government inllreland was an administratioa of the law so as to teach people that the reign of the law meant the reign•of justice to the ricb and poor alike. There was an evident improvement in the state of Ireland'. Irish tenants had, found themselves de- ceived by persons anxious to destroy. the rights of property, and the people were beginning eadisplay irritation at the tyranny to which they had been. so long subjected. The law must be enfored by all the powers at the command of the Government, and if they were not found to be sufficient,. Parliament must be asked for more. The Qinservative Gov- ernment were not going to compete with. Mr. Gladstone in a Home Rule Bill for Ireland, yet they recognised that there was much in the law that might be amended with benefit to Ireland. In approaching the thiestion of local gov- ernment they must preserve complete responsibility to the Imperial Parliament, and infuse into local government the popular element which now dominated the political con- stitution' but before any impotaant legislation could be attempted, the House (re' Commons must his enabled to do its work by new rules of procedure. William Cross- Eccles, of Str, Helens, with Miss Edith Julia Cripps, second daughter of Mr. Richard Cripps, of Biistol, cook place in Christ Church,. Clifton, Bristol. Owing to a recent bereavement in the bride's family the wedding was of an unassuming character. The bride was given away by her father, and she was accom- panied by Miss Hirst, of Llanfairfechan, Miss Cole. of Bath, and Miss Trippe, of the Vlcarage, Winfotd.,an bridesmaids. Mr. j. Snap° Eccles, of St. nelens, officiated as. the best man. After the interesting ceremony the bridal party had lun- cheon at the residence of Mr. Eater Cripps, brother of the bride, and the happy pair subsequently left for Lonclon en route for the continent. The presents were•macY and vain- able, including some from the servants and tenants at Windle Grange. SBILIOUS ASSAULT, ON A COUNT- Z- Co OFFICIALva„?` At the St. Helens Town Hall on Tuesday, before Mr. Wm. Pilkington and Alderman Mcßry.de, John Fairclough, a middle-aged man, living at 4, Raven-street; was charged with assaulting Pollee Constable Carter, ami also with as- saulting John Jackson, a bailiff of' the County Court. Mrs. Fairclough, prisoner's wife, was also charged with assault- ing Police Constable Carter. Me,. Masse'', solicitor, said Jackson was a warrant officer, and for some time he hadhad in his possession a warrant to apprehend defendant, but had not been able to meet him. The previous night be heard that Fairclough was in the British Lien, and knowing that he was a rough character be asked Polic.b Con- stable Carter to assist hii . in the arrest. They went into the house, and Jackson, called Fairclough to him, told him what he wanted him for, and asked him to go quietly. Fairclough said he would not have any bother in the house, but on getting outside he struggled violently, kicked Jackson on the legs, and struck both him and Carter. Mrs Fairclough also came up, seized her husband, tried to drag him from the officers, and struck Carter many times. The assistance of several other persons bad to be obtained to get prisoner to the police office, and on arriving there he refused to be searched, and again struck Carter in the mouth. The offi- cer said prisoner knew him and said he would give him more than he gave him before. Superintendent Johnston said prisoner had been convicted PwiunslY of assaulting and resisting officers. The magistrates said prisoner knew perfectly well what it was to resist the authorities, and he would be fined £1 and costs, or one month's imprison- ment in each case. Mrs Fairclough bad to doubt been led away in acting for her hashand, and ehe would be Ai°. charged.

A rousing speech—" Get up ! breakfast's ready !" A Carson, Nev., newspaper says that in the Carson ' River, above Empire, the fishing is good, but below the town the fish will not bite, "having lost their teeth , from salivation by the mill chemicals." "Don't sprinkle your milk punch with nutmeg. It is poisonous," says a Philadelphia paper. If you also don't take milk punch with your nutmeg you will be all right." "That's a splendid structure," said an Englishman to a New Yorker, referring to the Brooklyn Bridge; "who built it ?" "Hanged if I know," said the New Yorker; "but Brody was the last man that jumped over it." BUYING A PIG IN A POKE.---rat, ruefully, to his old Sow with a litter of two, he having sold six pigs in advance: " Och, shure and ve've made a fool ay versa fur wans ! an me too !" Morrie was given tivo apples because she had behaved well. "Come," said her mother, "don't be greedy. Give one of them to your little brother." Florri, with very good grace, held out the fruit to her brother. "You may choose," said she, "but don't take the biggest one." HARD TO "WRESTLE" WITIL—Mr. Dana, of the Nevi York 81171, declares that the most difficult subject for a newspaper reporter to handle well is a big fire. By a curious coincidence, that is the most difficult subject for a fireman to handle, too—though the latter can wrestle with a fire without saying anything about the "lurid and seething flames with their forked tongues" licking up valuable property. A sentimental and sermonising father reproached his youthful cues at breakfast recently for their epicurean desires, saying that, when he was a poor Scotch lad and had little prospect of becoming the great millionaire he is at present, he was contented to live on porridge and dry bread. "Oh, papa," exclaimed his eldest maiden, "what a lucky thing it is for you that you are now living with us! You must indeed feel the change, and that you are having a good time of it. Aren't you grateful?" A NEW JOKE ON BORROWERS.—Brown, an impecu- nious bachelor, complained to Smith, married, of his deplorable lack of acquaintance among young ladies with eligible dowries. "But," interposed Smith, "I can introduce you to three pretty young ladies having at least $lOO,OOO each." "For heaven's sake, do," cried Brown, "and I will be your creditor for life." "Credi- tor? My dear fellow, you have the terms confounded; debtor you mean." "No, creditor. As soon as I get possession of that $lOO,OOO, you will strike me for a loan, which I cannot refuse, though I know you will never repay it." A DEFINITE ANSWER.—One hot afternoon in July a traveller stopped at a farmhouse and asked for a drink. A country girl barefooted and sun bonneted passed him out a dipper and said "There's the well!" He was evi- dently inclined to indulge in a little rural flirtation, and after making all the known varieties of "sheep's eyes" at her over the edge of the dipper, he xlade bold to in- quire: "What might your name be, Miss?" "Wall," she said, in a matter-of-fact tone, "Ef I can convince young Smiler that it's about time to come down to business, it might be Mrs. Mary Jane Smiler before next winter. At present it ain't nothin' but Mary Jane Simpkins." PARTNERS.—A Yankee and a Frenchman owned a pig. When killing-time came, they wished to divide the meat. The Yankee was anxious to share so as to get both hind- quarters, and persuaded the Frenchman that the way to divide it was to cut it across the back. The Frenchman agreed on condition that the Yankee would turn his back and t = alie the Qf pieces after it was cut in - • - - is es two. ..he Yankee turned his back accorclingl. French- man " \rich vill you have—ze piece vid ze tail on, or ze piece vidout ze tail on?" Yankee: "The piece with the tail on." Frenchman: " Den, by gar, you can take him, and I take ze ozer one!" Turning round, the Yankee found that the Frenchman had cut off the tail and stuck it in the pig's mouth.

LII3ERA.L MATING AT LIM% SPEECH BY ALDERMAN JOHN CROSFIELD. On Saturday evening a crowded meeting of Libe- rals, called to hear an address by Mr. Jos. Howes, on "The Present Political Situation," was held at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, under .the auspices of the local Liberal Association. Alderman John Crosfield, of Warrington, occupied the chair, and was suppor- ted by Mr. Brewtnall, Mr. Welford, Mr. Howes, and others. The CHAIRMAN, on rising to address the meeting, was heartily cheered. lie said: When Mr. Swan- wick came and asked me to take the chair here to- , night, I very willingly consented to do so, because , many of you will know that I lived in Lymm for ten years, and that I have always felt an interest in the place, and I have always hoped to live to see the day when there would be more Liberals than Tories in that little village of Lymm. (Hear, hear.) I was told in Warringtonby some of my Tory friends the other day that there were only three Liberals left in Lymm, so I advised them to come to the meeting to-night to help to increase the numbers. I said " I should like an opportunity of speaking to some of you Tories, because I can toll you some- thing that will do you good." But I am afraid they have not accepted the invitation. (Laugh- ter.) You know that I contested the borough of Warrington at the last general election, and that I was defeated. But it was not a Tory victory; I was defeated because a cer- tain number of our Liberal friends either abstained from voting, or else they voted for the Tories. They did this because they did not understand the Irish question. The fact was that the Irish question came upon the whole country too quickly. The people had not had time to ascertain the merits of the question. (Cheers.) But I have no fear what- ever, gentlemen, about the next election—(cheers) because, as I said in Warrington, I'll fight that borough until . I do win. (Cheers.) I am not anxious to become a member ot Parliament ; far from it, but I shall fight it because I believe it is my duty to fight for the Liberal party, and for our great and grand leader, William Ewart Gladstone. (Cheers.) I have been engaged in polities for more than five and thirty years, and I never felt so con- fident in my life before as I do now that Mr. Glad- stone's policy for the settlement of the Irish ques- tion is the right one and the only one. (Cheers.) I have been over to Ireland. I spent a month there. I went to Killarney for a week. I inquired of the people there their condition, and I met some of the most respectable workmen that I ever met in my life. I have employed 150 workmen for a good many years, good honest Lancashire workmen, for whom I have the greatest respect, but I never met a decenter set of men than those I met that day at Killarney.
