div.head: EXAMINEF, SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 20, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINEF, SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 20, 1886.

Gladstone proposed that a two-thirds majority should stop a debate, and here he says that a Tory majority is to do it. The fact is the man's got no consistency, (Laughter, and a voice: " He's a Tory.") I have said all along that he would "jump Jim Crow.' (Renewed laughter.) He makes no ex- cuses. He simply says,." Gentlemen, I have changed my mind." (Laughter) He is a nice statesman! (Laughter.) There are a number of these Tories who are anxious to go back to Protection. There are some of them so rash as to say that there should be a duty put upon corn. Do you think the people of England will stand having the price of food raised to put money into the landlords' pocket? Let them attempt to do that, and they will be hurled from office in a month. They dare not do it. (Cheers.) if they attempted to do that you would have another Peterloo at Manchester. There is a lot wants doing, gentlemen, in this country. I ven- ture to wonder sometimes if we shall ever come to our senses as a Christian people. Look at the ex- tent of our army and navy—perfectly disgraceful, squandering the taxes of the people in a monstrous manner. It is high time the nation arose and de- manded, insisted upon, half the army and half the navy being put down. We don't want them. We are safe enough in England. (Cheers.) Let any nation attempt to come here and, if they can get back, they will go back quicker than they came. The time has come when we must cease fighting other people's battles, and, as Cobden said, "mind our own business." (Cheers.) What are they doing now, do you think? They are building two more of those stupid ironclads which are to cost £BOO,OOO a piece. They put a hundred ton gun on board, and how much do you think that cost? It costs £llO,OOO. They fire those cannons off for practice. What does it cost every time they fire one cannon? £120! It is no wonder that we have got 8d in the pound income tax. That is the way your money is squandered. Let the people of this country come to their senses, and say, "'We'll have no more of this." lam for peace, but lam in- terested in a thing which I believe is going to do more to do away with war than anything that has ever been done yet—and that is the shell which fires dynamite. One shot will sink the biggest ironclad. -Well, if they find out that, that one shot will sink an ironclad, I think they will begin to think it is no use spending .£BOO,OOO on a big clumsy thing of that sort. It also can be put into a revolver or cannon, and a regiment armed with that would blow a regi- ment opposite into a thousand pieces. Then they will begin to think what is the advantage of fight- ing. They should have thought that long ago. John Bright said twenty year ago, "Pull down the ten commandments out of your churches, you have no business to have them up." When I argue with the Tories they tell me I am a fanatic, and I say, "You are not a Christian," First of all I ask them whether they believe in the New Testament. There's a good many hesitate whether they do or not. Then I ask them if they nave ever heard of the fifth chapter of Matthew. A good many of them never did. (Laugh- ter.) I say you had better read °Tile sermon on ti Mount ; " that will do you good. If 79u are a Christian follow the teaching Jesus Christ taught, and then you will stop this wicked, wasteful, cruel war. As I said just now, I long to see the day when the English nation will rise as a man and declare that they will live a life according to the teaching of the New Testa- ment. Let us live as Christians—(cheers)— and not try to see how many men we can destroy, and how much property we can seize, for we have seized pro- perty all over the globe. We are the biggest set of thieves, I believe, on the earth. (Laughter.) These are the sort of commonsense principles that the working class of England will have to come to. As' for Toryism—Toryism is dead—(cheers)—dead as a 1 door nail. There is not a consistent Tory left that I know of. (Renewed laughter.) The moment they get into power they have to abandon their old Tory principles, and steal Liberal measures. How- ever, it is all right. If they will adopt Liberal measures, we'll support them, So long as they will give us the measures we require, I do not care which Government is in office. Let us have the nation properly governed. (Cheers.) Let us have a re- duced expenditure, and do away with the building of these stupid ships, give peace in Ireland and take half the soldiers from it. We have an army there of 30,000 sOdiers. How much do you think they cost? Goodness knows how much they would cost. Soldiers are as bad as a flock of locusts. They eat up—they consume—but they never produce any- thing. (Cheers.) You had better grow cabbages than soldiers. (Laughter.) You can eat cabbages, but you cannot eat soldiers. But, gentlemen, lam taking up too much of your time. My duty to- night is a very pleasant one. lam delighted to be here amongst you and to introduce my friend Mr. Howes. (Cheers.) I have heard him lecture in Warrington several times, and I'll back him against any lecturer that there is in England. (Cheers.) Mr. Howßs then delivered his lecture. He re- marked that the present political situation was ter- ribly mixed. It was made up very much of the im- portant question to which the chairman had re- ferred—the state of Ireland—for at present it was impossible that any of the other great political questions could be taken in hand with any prospect of solution, or of the removal of difficulties. Ano- ther point the chairman touched upon, peace or war, was certainly one of the most important points that the people of this country could at any time, and especially at this time, consider, and he thought that, as a matter of practical reform, it should be in- sisted upon that no monarch should be able to de- clare war, without the consent of the representa- tives of the people being asked and given. likdi- calism, he continued, was making increased headway, because there was in power a Tory Gov- ernment that dared not be Tory. They knew Tory- ism was not respectable, and for the purpose of trying to make a decent appearance in public they talked Radicalism. It was amusing to hear Conser- vatives saying that the old Toryism was dead. The old Toryism was either good or bad. If it was good they should not rejoice at its death, and if it was i bad they should not have defended it when living. I Speaking of the political question of the day, he. maintained that the Irish had always been a con- quered nation, into whose souls had entered the iron of oppression, and that the Empire had never yet been what could be properly designated as a united one. (Cheers.) A vote of thanks was afterwards accorded the lecturer,_ on the motion of Mr. BREWTNA.LL, seconded by Mr. WBLFORD.

••• PERSECUTION AND RATIONAL CONVICTION AT
EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—Anti-vaocinarori—are sometimes told that "they may believe what they like," but that they most have their children vaccinated. The remark is as false as it is spiteful and insulting. No man is at liberty to " bAieve what he likes." Belief is the direct result of conviction, not of volition. Rational argument may make a man believe what he woale'. rather not b3lieve ; but pereecution cannot act thus on a man's belief. What persecution may do, is to compel a man by threats to act or speak in a manner incon- aistent with his cou7ictions, or to visit him, for not doing sop with punishments of such cruelty and severity as may be sanctioned by conventional morality for ths time being. The Vaccination Acts do this, and the Inquisition could do no more.

THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—This movement affords another proof thaL difficul- ties met are difficulties overcome. Many people like my- self were a short whilg ago quite of opinion that the diffi- culties in the way of makiog the Warrington Library a real free library could not be overcome, and that it was no use dreaming of enjoying the same privileges as the inhabitants

of neighbouring towns, but I think there is no excuse what- ever for taking so gloomy a view now. The old adage is still true that "where there's a will there's a way." What- ever else those who are carrying on the present movement have done, they have clearly shown that "there's a way" to free the library if " there's A will." The suggestion that 1 Councillor Dixon made at the meeting reported in last week's

paper, namely, that the library should be relieved of its gas bills, was a very useful one, and if carried out would almost of itself break down the only real obstacle that even the Library Committee can point to. Why the Library CORI.. mittee, which is a department of the Corporation, should

• pay a heavy gas bill every half-year to the 'Gas Committee, which is another department of the Corporation, is hard to understand. The only effect it can have is to complicate the books and give needless work to clerks and accountants. Certainly a private firm would aot conduct its business in this way. RA.TEPAYER.

div.head: EXCAVATIONS IN BRIDGE-STREET.
div.p: THE EXCAVATIONS IN BRIDGE-STREET.

Sir,—l have been much interested in reading your weekly notices of the excavations in Bridge-street, and the alai- quarians of the town must feel immensely proud of the wealth of old stones and rubhish that is being brought to light, not forgetting the skeleton, coffins, cic., and they must find no small difficulty in finding suitable places for their reception. Our museum will no doubt b 3 greatly enriched, and numbers will flock to see the grinning skeleton of by- gone days—if it finds its way to that institution. But to come to the really practical side of the question; who is paying for the work ? I have often made this inquiry, but as yet have not been successful in gaining an answer. Some people suppose that Mr. Beamont is paying for the work ; others aver that the rates will have to bear the expense. And so, sir, it is in the hope that you or some of your Teaders may be able to enlighten me that I trouble you with 'this letter.

I have several times made my way to the site to get a peep at the work, but have been unceremoniously repulsed by one of the guardians of the peace, who, by-the-by, has to he paid also, and who must be reckoned in the bill, but as yet, beyond a glimpse over the top of the fence, while the " bobby's " hack has been turned, I have been unsuc- cessful, except so far as viewing the before-mentioned stones and robbish. As a personal ratepayer I fancy I have a right to see and know what is being done with ratepayers' I property, awl how my money is being spent, and should like to pet a slight return, if enly in eight-seeing. It does not appear enough that this property should be standing idle and ruinous, but that money must be spent in digging and harrowing for what is really worthkzs. Truly our Council want looking after a bit at times, if only to let them see the ratepayers are not forgetful of the trust reposed in them. Hoping that you may be able to answer my question, I am, sir, yours, &o.,AN [I-HUMBUG. [We believe the sum of £2O has been voted by the Town Council for excavation purposes ; and it is suggested that the "finds" should be got together and placed where the ratepayers can see them without hindrance.— ED. Er.]

SPIRITUALISM CONJURING. Sir,—l was pleased to see a letter from our friend " Clif- ford Dix" on the above subject; also a few lines from Mr. Thomas Acton. I have read many letters in your paper from the fermer, on various subjects, and derive I much pleasure therefrom. I have also admired the manner in which he has dealt with some of our religious, social, politi- cal, and trade grievances; but I am sorry that neither he or Mr. Acton are able to record any personal experiences of the occurrence of phenomena, be it writing or otherwise, in their presence, or in the presence of any of. their friends, which cannot be accounted for by the conjuring theory, or any of the operations of nature with which we are already ac- quainted; and this is what I should like to see recorded in your columns. I tkink such can be given, as I believe there are families in whose homes such phenomena are being ob- tained without the aid of professional mediums. There is no doubt a difficulty in getting persons to do this, owing, I presume, to the great amount of prejudice that exists in the minds of many with respect to this matter; but I was hop- ing that the " nom de plume" under which correspondents are allowed to write would have inducd some one or more to give us the benefit of their experiences as investigators without fear of being ridiculed. With regard to Mr. Acton's suggestion as to getting a medium to come here, I cannot do better, I think, than gnat° from the journal 1 spoke of in my last for October 16th of this year, which says, under the heading of " Advice to Inquirers:" by (M. A.) Oxon :—" If you wish to see whether spiritualism is really jugglery awl imposture, try it by personal experiment;" and again, " In any case you must rely chiefly on experience in your own family circle, or amongst your own friends." I had pro- posed writing at greater length n answer to what has been said by your correspondents, but I will trespassne further on your beaee, and I would suggest that we all write briefly on this matter, avoiding controversy as much as possible, and I conclude with the hope, as your correspondent " Clif-
ford Dix" ays, that some one will step forth and bravely give us the benefit of his or her experiences.—Yonrs faith- fully, BETA.

ISir,—ln reading over your papers for the last few weeks, I I first saw the letter of "Beta," then those of "Thomas Acton" and " Clifiord Dix," and having had some experi- ence of spiritualism, I take upon myself the duty of re- i plying thereto. I must say that, judging from the tenor of I Mr. Acton's note, he seems to be full of belief, for he says he believes that" Beta" wrote his note with good intent. ; He also believes that the phenomenon of slate writing is all "humbug," and nothing but a trick, awl he still further be- lieves that the professor meant nothing but slate writing when he termed spiritualism all a "humbug." Now in passing here let me say that people used to believe that the sun revolved round the earth. But it was a fallacy. Thou- sands of other subjects could be named wherein people were at fault. Now, it is just possible that Mr. Acton may have made a mistake in this instance, and perhaps very rash, though he may be very clever in making the statement that he would prove slate writing nothing but " humbug " and a trick, and this before he has had any knowledge of the matter.

Before I bring my evidence with regard to slate writing, ' let me take up the proposition of Mr. Acton, by laying down another. I do not see why lor any other Spiritualist should bring a medium to Warrington simply to satisfy the whims of such men as Mr. Acton. Knowledgelnevor comes to a man without searching for. If Mr. Acton knows this thing to be all a "humbug," ant nothing but a trick, I maintain that it is his duty to expose the whole thing to the world. My proposition is, if he means to expose this thing, that he (Mr. Acton) shall arrange with Mr. Eglinton, of Loudon, to come down to Warrington, or he with his friend shall go to London, by arrangement with Mr. Eglin- ton,and if be will prove that the phenomena which occur in the presence of Mr. Eglinton are done by a trick, and that he will produce the same trick under similar conditione though a clever conjurer Mr. Acton may be, I will forfeit L 5 to any charitable purpose in Warrington ; and if he fails to perform the same tricks under the same conditions be (Mr. Acton) shall give £5 to the said purpose. Now what is this slate writing which there is so much objection to? It is a fact which occurs under certain con- ditions; a double slate locked and sealed, with a small piece of slate pencil inside, where it is utterly impossible for a human band to get inside. Intelligent messages are written therein.

I will now give to you the evidence of a number of well known gentlemen. I will first give the evidence of Harry Keller, the well known Indian and American conjurer : "In respect to the above manifestations I can only say that I do not expect my account of them to gain general cre- dence. Forty-eight hours before I should not have believed any one who described such manifestations under similar circumstances. I still remain a sceptic as regards spirit- ualism, but I repeat my inability to explain or account for what must have been an intelligent force, that produced the writing on the slate, which, if my senses are to be relied on, was in no way the result of trickery or sleight of hand. In conclusion, let me state that after most stringent trial and strict scrutiny of these wonderful experiences I can arrive at no other conclusion than that there was no trace of trickery in any form, nor was there in the room any mechanism or machinery by which could be produced the phenomena which bad taken place. The ordinary mode by which Maskelyne and other conjurers imitate levitation or the floating test could not possibly be done in the room In which we were assembled." Among others who have given their testimony are the following :—Professors Hare, Alfred Russell WallacP-, F.G.S., Professors Gregory. F.R.S.E , also De Morgan, Baron Carl Da Prel (Munich), Dr. Robert Chambers, and Lord Brougham. and one of the finest men who lives to-day, our late Premier, Mr. W. E. Gladstone. I could go on writing names which would fill all the columns of this paper, but for the present we will stop and ask the question—Have the evidences of such men whom I have named to be cast away because two men wir) hive bad no experience like Mr. Acton and "Clifford Dix" cry out it is all a " humbug " and a farce? lam quite willing to leave the verdict in the hands of your intelligent readers. A few words to "Clifford Dix." If be desires to discuss the question on its merits instead of ridiculing and catering to the lowest forms of bigotry and sarcasm, let him use argument, not playing with words. My object is to get at the truth, whether it be from a Christian, an atheistic, or a spiritualistic platform. If I come in contact with facts no amount of ridicule or sarcasm will change my course. Like "Clifford Dix," I hope I dare to think for myself, and I can say that spiritualism has developed this more than any other " ism " I_have yet come in contact with.

Now, Mr. Editor, I am afraid I shall be taking too much of your space, but I will say this, that I am prepared to take the subject point by poin`. We will, therefore, finish this point of slate-writing before we enter on another phase of the question, but in conclusion let me give the teachlngs of Spiritualism as I have found them. It has taught me by facts and philosophy that I am a being of progression, from a !ewer to a higher phase of life, and tat what- ever act of crime I commit I, and I only, will toe re- sponsible for the penalty of that crime, and if I am dis- honest and a hypocrite when I &part this life I shall b 3 the same character ; neither better nor worse than I was when on the earth plane. when I get to the other side of life. This Ido net "believe," but know, for I have seen those who are called dead, and talked with them, and be- cause they live I shall live also. This in the Cause Of truth.
JUSTICE.

A SUGGESTION. Sir,—Some one has said that a person who is poorly en- dowed with a sense of humour is always liabl3 to quite un- consciously do something which will bring himself or what- ever he may take in hand into ridicule, and I think the experience of most of us will lead us to agree that there is a great deal of truth in this saying. It was also the opinion of Sydney Smith that people who come from beyond the Tweed are so deficient of humour that notbinz, short of a surgical operation is required t) get them to see the point of a joke. I could never agree with this opinion of the witty divine, for some of the very finest humour is Scotch humour, but there is certainly this to justify it, that some Scotchmen are more entirely devoid of this quality than any body else. Now, sir, it would be unhandsome not to admit that our present Mayer has certain personal endow- ments which are considerably above the average, but I think it will be generally conceded that he is short of humour, and that he is indeed just such an one as Sydney Smith, had he lived in these days, would have pointed to as a confirma- tion of the truth of his famous dictum. It may no doubt be said that we do not want a joking Mayor, who, to tell the truth, is one of the worst of infliction!, but there are special reasons why during the coming jubilee year a Mayor should have a keen sense of the humeuroas in order to escape making himself and the town ha is connected with ridiculous. The motives which will prompt the coming local celebrations, so far at least as the bulk of the inhabi- tants are concerned, will be purely sentimental, and senti- ment in England is a rather tender plant, and needs to be handled with a great deal of tact. Let a man gush or in any way got beyond what the "modesty of nature" requires, and instead of making the effect he intended he simply excites derision. The Mayor, therefore, should be particu- larly careful not to connect beforehand the coming War- rington jubilee observances with all sorts of ridiculous associations, or instead of their coming •ff in appropriate fashion they will, to quote the language of an ancient poet, end in "nnextinguishable laughter." As such a result would be deplored by everybody, it is to be hoped that no more of the Mayor's staff will have daughters presented to them during the next twelve months, or at all events if anything of that sort should befall them, that they will have the good sense to "keep it quiet,"—Yours, Warrington, Nov. 17- ADVISER.
-WESLEYAN METHODISM AND THEATRE GOING.

Sir,—My letters have evidently raised a storm in the pot, and touched the dignity of some of these theatricll young men. They have seen fit to throw at tny diminished head several tremendous thunderbolta, which have almost anni- hilated me. I was sorry to read the reply to Mr. J. B. Isaac's letter. Such remarks were entirely uncoiled ter. Any impartial reader, putting the twe side by side, can plainly see that it was not simply theatre going, but per- sonal spite and spleen that would prompt such a vicious letter as that of " Garrick."

I shall tetally ignore the charming epistle from Liver- pool, and turn my attention to Mr. J. E. Richardson, who disposes of the main issues of the question in the most re- markable and summary manner. He sums all up in one statement—that theatre going lies between "God and a man's conscience." Mr. Richardson has evidently read more drama than bible, and studied very little of human nature, or else he would not have adduced such an arela- ment as that. A man's conscience can be made very pli- able, and to acquiesce in almost any fancy he wishes, especially if he has a strong desire pulling him that way. There are many men whose conscience never gives them a pang, being asleep, and others whose conscience being led astray bears approving testimony to them. Conscience is not an infallible guide; it may become seared. To the word of God alone must a Chrietian look in order to be led ' aright. Mr. Richardson questions several of my assertions. First, he insinuates that I was totally wrong in rey statement that "the superintendents were to a man against sucu proceed- ings taking ol ice in the Sunday school." Making inquir- ies, I find that Bold-street superintendents are to a man against it, but that there is one doubtful one at Silver-st., and I am not sure whether he is a member of society or not. Secondly, by a string of figures, lati trys to show that I was altogether wrong in my remarks upon the composi- tion of the Mutual Improvement Class; but I think his figures are rather misleading—he counts "the ladies." I must apologise to them for the omission, and say I did not include them, simply from the fact that they are silent members, therefore only nominal members, and taking that into consideration, he will find I was not far from the mark. Mr. Richardson seems to be grieved and hurt that I did not ventilate the matter before that great assembly, the Mutual Improvement Claes ; but I can assure him I never once entertained such a thought. I do not think that the trustees, stewards. cto , of Methodism, would care to trust the honour of their cause in the hands of a Young Men's Mutual Improvement Class, even though it should be under the direction of such influential and aspiring young men as Messrs. Richardson and Plinston. It was by the " trustees, stewards, leaders, I wished to be heard, and I think I have accomplished my purpose in that direction. Mr. Richardson's remark, "What about the ladies ? " is rather significant. Surely he is joking, or attempting a litt!e " comedy "or " buffoonery." I certainly believe the

LIBERAL CLUB DEBATING SOCIETY. Last evening the second weekly meeting of this society was held at the Liberal Club, Bewsey-street. The President (the Rev. R. Pilcher) took the chair, and there was a large attendance of members. Some preliminary business having been transacted, Mr. S. Kenyon read a paper on "Recreation." He was of opinion that the very large majority of the people in civilised countries had quite enough, and rather' too much, work. They felt that less was desirable for them, and that "all work and no play made Jack a dull boy." On the other hand, there were many of the aristocracy and richer classes suffered from want of serious oc- cupation—of something to string up their facul- ties and unfold their energies. (Hear, hear.) He recommended that gymnasiums should be estab- lished in every large town, so that young men might be benefitted by gymnastic exercises. He also thought it was of the utmost importance to society that girls and young women should have more amusement which involved plenty of physical exercise, for without exercise no one could be healthy. The laws of nature did not accommodate themselves to the ideas en- gendered by custom and folly, vanity, and pride,and it was for every one to live in accordance with na- ture when they would be rewarded with cheerful- ness and peace. (Hear, hear.) He thought ministers of religion were too much separated from the peo- ple in their amusements,. erroneous ideas and cus- toms of society causing' them to refrain from many amusements which they might partake of with advantage. They all knew that innocent amusements were/as ranch a blessing as folly and dissipation were a curse: (Hear, hear.) He con- demned the practice of keeping social gatherings together till late hours, when they were apt to degenerate into dissipation. Referring to horse- racing, he said there was a :great deal of evil con- nected with it, and the fact that it was patronised by the aristocracy was no argument in its favour. Very many were through it led to ruin, while few were benefitted. With regard to most other out- door or indoor modes. of recreation, Mr. Kenyon spoke in favour of a prudent indulgence in them, and remarked that innocent amusements tended to harmonise the human faculties. (Applause.)—A discussion then took place on the paper.—The Chair- man said Mr. Kenyon had indulged in some re- marks which, he had no doubt, shocked them all, for he absolutely had the audacity to think that ministers of religion should be men. (Laughter.) He only wished Mr. Kenyon could convert the , deacons. "Let the galled jade- wince, my withers are unwrung," because there was nothing that his congregation did that he did not do, and. he dare say there was nothing that.he• did that his congre- gation did not dot (Hear, hear,) With regard to betting, he did not think the tendency to evil was in the amusement but in the men who indulged in it. The real evil was not in the betting, but in the secret knowledge which gave a man an unfair advantage, and which made betting an unfair transaction. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Barlow complimented Mr. Kenyon on his paper, and after- wards spoke against horse-racing.—Mr. Dunbobbin having offered a few remarks, Mr. T. Birchall said he considered that a great deal of harm was done by Christian people setting their faces against amusements.—Mr. Duffin was in favour of the Opening of museums, libraries, &c.,on Sundays; and Mr. Bromley considered there was no greater evil in a man backing his opinion in regard to horse- ; racing, than in persons backing their opinions on. the Stock Exchange.—Mr. Holmes strongly con- demned horse-racing on the ground of the cruelty 1 to the animals it caused. The debate was also taken part in by Mr. Stirrup, Mr. Plumpton, Mr. Evans, Air. A. Rathbone, and Mr. Albinson, and after the transaction of some routine business, a very suc- cessful meeting came to a close. Next Friday night a paper will be read by Mr. J. J. Nield on "Thrift and Co-operation."

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. LFROM OUR OW S CORRFSPONDENT. 1 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The release of money following the settlement as caused a general lowering of rates. Money has been abundant in the city during toe past few days, three per cent, being the highest ratecharged for first class paper. A very large arnOunt of business has been done in both Home and American Railways. In the former the southern lines have agiin mo- nopolised most attention, Brighton "A's" being greatly in- quired for. Their continued upward movement bears out my prognos'icttien, and speculators for the rise have to conirratulate thenvi4ivee. Readers will remember how 1 suggested purchise of this Stock when they stood at 113, They Lava now reached 119, and those of my readers who acted upon my advice may think thenaselves well advised. To such I would even now say "hold on." I folly expect ' to see this Stock reach 125, with continued improvement of traffic, and if faith may be placed in a usually well-informed quarter, the price is likely to go to 130. Midland shares, on line other hand, have been largely sold, owing be the unsat- isfactory traffic returns.

In Atnerican Rails I recently predicted a rise in several stocks, which has been fulfilled, especially in the oases of Louisville and Nashville, Eries, and Lake Shores. All of these stocks have considerable improved during the past week.

The mining lever still rages, or has the reputation of do- ing se. It has developed various teudencies and symptoms both new and questionable. Among the latter is the auda- city with which these schemes are" rushed" on the public. A mine is bought out oa Monday, the share lists are elosed on Wednesday, and Saturday's papers announce the shares are at a premium. The public believe in this apparently rapid success, and on the faith of these statements, buy up the shares with which the promoter has meanwhile flooded the country through their private circulars, in which they offer the shares at par, although already quoted at a pre- mium. The unsophisticated investor caught by the bait of a bargais, buys only to find too soon that the shares are valueless.

I am not surprised to find that the inventors of the inge- nious. single Rail Railway exalting so much attention at Westminster that they have gone to the public for support. The practical nature of this invention renders it highly popular in new and difficult countries, and the orders for it will speedily tax the resources of the company, who ask for £200,000. These shares are being taken up largely by sharp-sighted investors, and I should not be surprised to hear great things of the Lartigne Railway Construction Company, which by its very simplicity renders it all the more valuable. Messrs. J. Lewis, Mills, and Co., of Old Broad-street, writing apropos of a reference to them in a previous letter, state trial they do not take half pm. cent. "cover," except in the c Ise of Consols. They point out, and justly, that so small an amount of cover could not but prove more profitable to the broker than the client, therefore it is easy to understand why a respectable firm have no wish to be associated with anything that has the appearance of taking advantage of a client. I wonder bow many of the public are aware of the fact that the Isla of Wight Railway system, comprising 37i. miles, is eerced and managed by no less than six compa- nies Such, however, is the case, and public opinion as well as stock holders will support Mr. William Ab'sott in his endeavour to amalgamate these lines. If any man in spite of strong opposition on the part of those interested in keeping things as they are, can do it, it is Mr. Abbott.

I suppose the lass dragged on a weary existenca till "the ladies" were ntroduced ; since then the class has rapidly grown, the improvement has been truly "mutual," and I am sure it is becoming and gallant of the young gentlemen to walk them home from such a nice matrimonial nursery, to discuss on their way their "mutual improvement" and its ultimate development. div.head: QUEEN'S JUBILEE.-NEW 13A.THS FOll
div.p: THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE.-NEW 13A.THS FOll
WARRINGTON.

Sir,—lt must be a matter of great gratification to her Majesty to notice, as doubtless she has done, the universal desire that exists to celebrate the Jubilee of her accession to the throne Queen Victoria has the proud satisfaction of knowing that the resources of our great Empire have been extended and the material prosperity of the people more greatly increased during her reign than has itten the case during the time of any of her predecessors. From the intimate knowledge we possess ef the keen interest she takes in all objects which are calculated to promote permanently the comforts and conveniences of her people, in my opinion the best way to render memorable the fiftieth anniversary of the Queen's reign, is to erect some institution which shall be capable of conferring a benefit upon the largest possible number of persons. Such an institution would be comprisA in New Public Baths. What is our present posi- tion in regard to this matter? We have a population of nearly 50,000 persons. Of this number probably 20,000 will be children and young people under 21 years of age. For those who may be desirous of learning to swim, or those who, being able to swim already, are wishful to take occasional exercise of that kind, there is positively net a single sheet of water within the whole of the Borough of Warrington where such a pastime may be safely indulged in. Our river, besides being extremely dangerous, is no better than an open sewer ; the c4nals on the Cheshire side are tabooed under strict police surveillance, so that there is no place but the present Legh-street Baths for the youth of our town to learn to swim. Again, it is well known that out of 10,000 inhabited louses in Warrington, there are certainly not more than, at the most, 200, that can boast of possessing bathrooms ; and the working-men of our town. almost without exception, are unable, except by means of the most clumsy expedients, to indulge in that necessary "luxury," a thorough "wash." We have at Legh-street not more than a dozes single bathrooms, the charge for the use of which, for the purpoeekof a warm bath, is 6d, which sum is practically prohibitive to a working-man. In addition, we have two swimming baths, the first-class (?) bath (so-called by courtesy only) is capable of accommodating 20 to 30 persons at a time with a moderate amount of com- fort—it is frequently crammed with 60 or TO, and then pre- sents an appearance more remarkable than pleasant. This bath is supplied with clean water twrce a week, and every person using the bath is charged 61, season ticket holders paying somewhat less. But what do we offer to those who cannot afford 61? lii my opinion our second-class bath is a disgrace to civilisation. To begin with, it is emptied twice a week, and the water which has been previously in use in the first-class bath for at least three days is turned into it. Our twopenny customers never get clean water from year's end to year's end. In addition to this there is not the slightest accommodation for dressing and undress- ing, tits use of bathing drawers is not heisted upon, the bath is very small, so that what with the foulness of the water, the atmosphere beclouded by the steam arising there- from, the entire absence of ventilation, the con- gregating together of seventy sweating specimens of humanity, any person visiting this second-class bath on a warm summer afternoon, as I have often done, cannot help but come away strongly impressed with the necessity for immediate and extensive improvements. The result of this abominable condition of things is that hundreds of men who would gladly avail themselves of the advantages of modern, suitable, and well-managed baths, are kept away altogether by the unsavoury surroundings of Legh-street, and have to go to Liverpool, Manchester, or even Widnes to indulge in the pleasure of a decent swim. Again, it is admitted on all hands that every boy (and girl. too, I think) ought to learn to swim, and probably some day we shall see this included in the" code "adminis- tered in Our public day schools; but what accommodation have we to offer for such a desirable object? At the pre- sent time practically none. The question of Turkish baths is one of great importance, and conid very well be consi- dered, but more of this later on. Now, I believe that the Town Council is prepared to take action in this matter, and that early, too, if it was felt that the ratepayers of War- rington would sanction the necessary expenditure. In con- nection with the Shin C anal scheme, from first to last it has cost Warrington .L 4,000 and by spreading the payment of this sum over two or three years, nobody has felt the tax to be a burdensome one. For a much less sum than that just named, the payment of which coeld be spread ever two, three, roar, or even more years, Warrington could ac- quire commodious and modern baths, which would not only be a credit to.the town but would confer a lasting benefit upon thousands whose life's pleasnres are at present far too limited. May I commend this matter to the serious and earnest consideration of my fellow-townsmen in the hope and belief that their sympathy will be extended to these amongst us who are anxious, if pweible, to carry this matter to a successful issue before next year has expired.— Yours truly, HENRY ROBERTS.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.

- The Duke of Connaught is gazetted to the command of a division of the Bengal army. The Speaker has notified his intention to issue his war- rant for a new writ for B:ighton six days hence. All the great Paris bazaars have agreed, in view of the coming Christmastide aud New Yearl not to buy. any German-made toys.
Very large quantities of herrings were caught off Dover on Friday, and are being sold in the streets of that town at eixty for a shilling. __ _
A- burglar waa shot at Shipton-on-Cherwell, near Oxferd, on Friday morning by a farmer named Parrott. The woun- ded man is in the Oxford Infirmary,

It is stated that unless unforseen 'occurrences prevent an earlier date being fixed, it has been definitely arranged that Parliament shall assemble for its next session on the 17th of January. CABINHT COUNCIL.—A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Otfice at noon on Frid4y. Mr. Arthur Balfour, Secretary for Scotland, who was added to the Cabinet on Thursday, was present. Previous to the Council assembling Lord Ashbourne paid a visit to Sir Michael Hicks-Beach.

TRH POLICE AND TAK SocutisTs,—The following offi- cial notification was issued on Friday afternoon :—The accounts attributed to the Press Association regarding the alleged military and police arrangements for next Sunday are entirely without foundation. We are further authurised to state that no idea has ever been entertained of employing artillery._

LORD SALISBURY AND THE QUEEN.—Lord Salisbury left London for Windsor after the conclusion of the Cabinet council on Friday afternoon. He was met at Slough sta- tion by the royal carriage' in which be proceeded to Wind- sor Castle, and, after an audience of her Majesty, returned to London at 4-35 ia the special train which conveyed the Clue& to the Metropolis. Her Majesty returned to Wind- sor shortly after six o'clock._ _

MARRYING A. CHANCERY WARD.—Mr. Justice North made an order in the Chancery Division on Friday for the com- mittal to prison of Percy Mackenzie. a son of the late well- known actor. Henry Compton, for contempt of court in marrying a ward of the court without the consent of her guardians or the court. The young lady is the danehter of an Indian merchant, and is entitled to a moiety of £20,000. The defendant, it was stated, made her acquaintance at Bright-in last March, and notwithstanding that he had notice of her position as a ward of the court, he married her at St. Mary Abbotts, Kensington, on the 6th inst. The lady is 20 years of age, and Mr. Mackenzie 31.

THE PROPOSED IMPERIAL INSTITUTE IN LONDON. —The sub-committee of the Imperial Institute met on Fri• day afternooh, and conferred with the agents-general for the Colonies. The committee have agreed to advise His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales that it would not be expedient, as part of the scheme of the propoaed Jubilee Memorial Institute, to re-open the present exhibition in the same or similar form next year, and that it would not be practicable at 80 early a date to open a new institute. The committee are now considering what form the proposed memorial should take, but they have at present arrived at no conclusion upon this point, and have not tendered any advice to His Royal Highness upon it.

_ rIAMPTON COURT PALACE IN FLAMES.—A fire broke out at Hampton Court Palace on Friday morning, originating in the apartments of Miss Cappage. in the Tennis Court, and these in spite ef prompt attention were destroyed. The flames then spread to several ether apartments, and a call for assistance was sent round the district. The fire rapidly spread to the westward; and in a short time nearly the wilole story was alight. The roof shortly afterwards fell in, but no one was hurt. Captain Shaw arrived on the scene shottly before three o'clock and was at once able to inspect the building. The dimes had 'then, however, been got entirely under, and the only work of the firemen was to keep playing on the smouldering woodwork. A WOMAN AND THREE CHILDREN SUFFOCATED BY GAS. —On Friday forenoon, at South Toll, Cupar Fife, it was noticed that a strong smell of gas was proceeding from A house occupied by Mrs. Reckie. The door was foond to be locked, but the neighbours succeeded in forcing it open, and on entering they found Mrs. Reckie and her three child- ren lying on the ground evidently suffocated by gas, with which the room was full. The woman and two children were quite dead, but the other child, a boy.was still breath- ing.. Medical assistance was at once procured, but nothing could be done to save the boy, and he died in the course of the afternoon. Mrs. Reckie, whose character was ir- reproachable, was about to start with her family to join her husband in America. It is not known how the escape of gas occurred.

- THE SOUTHPORT MURDER.—On Friday Alfred Smith, the youth who was on Tuesday committed by the coroner's jury for the wilful murder of Maud Hamilton, daughter of Mrs Mary Elizabeth Hamilton, of 94, Seften-street, South• pert, was charged with the murder, before the magistrates, at the Town Hall.—Johanna Pugh, a domestic servant en- gaged by Mrs Hamilton, in giving an account of what happened after hearing the pistol shot, said they lifted her up and put her on the bed. They found the pistol under her. Maud said "Alfred has done it. Once it missed fire, and he fired again and he hurt me." Prisoner had before, in the presence of witness, threatened to shoot himself. They had both said they would die together, but they never gave auy reason for saving so. Once they both took laudanum in her presence, but Dr. Moore was sent for and they re- covered. Prisoner had fired with the pistol many a time in the backyard, and Maud had also a pistol.—Mrs Mary Blackwell said when she SAW Smith she asked him, "Why have you done this ? " He replied, "Mrs Blackwell, I did not know it was loaded. I would not hurt her; I loved her too much." Maud said in the romn, "I love him ; I love him still. Be kind to him when lam gone," He had been asked to leave, but had not done so. Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Assizes on the capital charge.

div.head: CHURCH CONVERSAZIONE AT
div.p: CHURCH CONVERSAZIONE AT

WARRINGTON. On Wednesday evening a Church conversazione was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, and pre- sided over by the Venerable Archdeacon Barber. There was a large attendance, amongst those present being the Mayor (Dr. Mackie), Lady Greenall and the Misses Greenall, Mr. Stanley Leighton, M.P.. Canon Greenall, Canon Blencowe, Canon Heron, Canon Dodd, Rev. J. Whitley, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. G. Allton, Rev. G. F. Roberts; Mr. W..Beamont, Mr. R. Davies, Alderman Harrison, Dr. Watkins, Dr. C. White, Mr. J. White, Mr W. D. Jeans, Mr. J. R. Buckton, Councillor Dixon, &c. In the course of the evening,, a programme of music was admirably rendered by the combined choirs of several churches in the town, under the leadership of Mr. J. White. The solos were sung by Miss Riley, the Rev. T. P. Williamson, and. Mr. Dell. Papers were also read by Mr. Stanley Leighton, and the Rev. Canon Blencowe. The subject of Mr. Leighton's paper was "Church Defence." He said that the more resolute they were now in asserting their intentions, the better it would be not only for their church. but for the peace and welfare of the coun- try. In these days, if people were silent they were supposed to have nothing to say for themselves. Let them take care that judgment did not go by default. Let them clear the ground with regard to the per- sons to whom they were opposed. Separate in their minds the religious Dissenters from the Liber- ationists. They had no quarrel, either as politicians or as citizens with the Nonconformists. But, these Liberationists would take away from Churchmen their freedom, and would rob them of the material means which theyhad themselves for promoting their own religious services. They could make no truce with them. But while they were defending their own church, let it ever be remembered that they were defending at the same time the chapels of the Nonconformists, for the principles of the Libera- tionists, carried to their logical conclusions, ,would root out all definite religious worship and all de- finite religious teaching from the land. And let him remind them that Nonconformity was at this present moment established by law in England, and that Nonconformity had been endowed out of the taxes. All societies or corpora- tions, whether religious or civil, must maintain certain relations with the State. The Nonconfor- mist Churches, 175 in number, were very jealous of this " establishment "by the State, although they avoided using that term, and they were always seeking for some fresh statutory privileges. When he said that the Dissenters were " established by law he meant that for the east two hundredyears, ever since their societies came into existence, Acts of Parliament had been passed conferring upon them privilege, protection, and recognition. Their 16,000 chapels were exempted by statute from the local rates as long as they were used exclusively for public religious services. He could mention scores ' of statutes which illustrate the State establishment of the Dissenters. Nonconformity had not only been established by Act of Parliament, it had also been endowed by the State, and out of the taxes. From the year 1723 and before, to the year 1850, annual grants were voted by Parliament out of the taxes to Protestant Dissenting ministers. An in- teresting return made to the House of Commons showed that between the' years 1830 and 1844 Pro- testant Dissenting ministers received £451,775. (Hear, hear, and applause). Canon Blencowe afterwards read his paper, and a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Leighton and Canon Blencowe.,„ on the motion of Mr. Beamont, seconded by Canon Dodd. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded tile meeting.

BETTING PROSECUTIONS AT WAR- RINGTON.-11EAVY FINE. On Thursday, at the Borough Court at Warring- ton, before Alderman Harrison (ex-Mayor), and Alderman Burgess, John Monks, 4, Ship-yard, War- rington, was charged with allowing his house to be used for the purpose of betting on horse races, and John Mather and James Mather were summoned at the same time for so using the house. The prose- cution was taken up by the police, for whom Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk) appeared. and Mr. Brown (Stockport), appeared for the defence. The informations were laid with respect to the 12th and 26th days of October, but it was decided to take the latter date only, and it was also agreed to first take the charge, against John Mather. A. open- ing the case for tltie prosecution, Mr. Whittle ex- plained the Act under which proceedings were taken, a section of which provided that no house, office, room, or other place, could be opened, kept, or used for the purpose of betting by persons resor- ting thereto. It was not his province to say anything about the subject of betting. The idea of making a fortune at a single stroke was innate in almost everyone. He did not know that there was much sin in betting, either against the divine or the civil law, and there was only one step from the betting house to the stock exchange. The Legislature had been much disinclined to interfere with horse races, but the law prohibited betting houses, and they must deal with the law as they found it. It was true that the houses had a temptation to clerks, apprentices, and servants, who often found themselves involved in losses, and, plunging deeper, were ruined. The defendant was lately, landlord of the Rose and Crown Inn, in Bridge-street, and was now described as a bookmaker. He had lately occupied a room in a common lodging-house, 4, Ship-yard, which was in the occupation of the defendant Mcmks. The room was scantily furnished. containing a table and an easy chair used by Mather. From information that came to the knowledge of the chief constable, he caused inquiries to be made and sent officers to watch the premises, with theresult that a consider- able number of people were seen going in and out. A raid was made on the 26th October by Inspectors Spinks and Cox, and other members of the force, and considerable numbers of people were at various times seen to go in and out of the house. Telegraph boys were also seen, and on the premises being searched a number of racing cards and records were found. Mr. Whittle then called Inspector Spinks, who spoke to visiting the house of Monks on the day in question. Witness said that he went in at the back door, passed through the kitchen into the middle room, just as he was entering which he saw Mr. Mather and his son, Mr. and Mrs Monks, and a son of Monks, who went out of the room into another apartment. Defendant Monks got hold of him and tried to prevent him going in. He (Monks) told him that he had no right there, and demanded to know his business. Witness replied that it was a common lodging-house, and he had a right to enter when he thought proper. Monks said the officer was in his private apartments, and, picking up a poker, threatened to "shift " him when charged with using the house for betting purposes, John Mather said—" John Mather will not be allowed to live in Warrington. If you could pick up a shilling or two easily, you would. You should go up the street, where they are doing more business than I am." The papers produced were found in the room.—lnspector Cox also gave. evidence regarding his visit to the house. Irnsworth, Legh-street, a summoned witness, said that on the 26th October he went to a house in Ship-yard, and put 8s on a horse named Baroness colt. He could not remember what the race was, but the horse won, and he was paid 12s and his 8s back by Mather.—John Pemberton, shop- keeper, Market-place, said that on the 11th October he went to the house in 'Ship-yard kept by the de- fendant Monks, and made a bet with Mather of £33 to £1 on Stone Clink for the Cesarewitch, and £8 to E 1 for a place. The horse won 'the race, and next day witness went for his money, but defendant Mather repudiated the debt, and had not since paid him. Witness told Mather he should pay, and asked his reason for declining.—Mr. Brown objected to this being given in evidence, and said it was merely for the purpose of damaging a person's reputation.—ln defence. Mr. Brown said that if a person used a house for the purposes of betting, and conducted It on a credit systeln„ not taking deposits, he did not come within the law. He only came within the statute when he received deposits to be held by him to abide the event of horse racing. . Mr. Brown ridi- culed the evidence of the police, and said that they bad no right to assume that the persons who visited the house were not lodgers, or that they went to it for the purpose of making a deposit. The zeal Df the police had outrun their discretion, and the evi- dence they had given was useless. Unsworth, he said, proved going to-a house in Ship-yard, but did not conclusively prove that it was the house kept by Monks. Pemberton's evidence did not prove a deposit as required by the Act, and, in fact, none of the witnesses clearly proved that.—Alderman Bur- gess. after the magistrates had consulted with their clerk, said that they had come to the conclusion that the case was proved. John Mather would be fined £25 and costs, or three months' imprisonment in default. The Bench refused to grant a case for the higher court, which Mr. Brown applied for on the ground that it was. not proved that any deposit had been made. The charges against James Mather and John Monks were withdrawn by the prosecut- ing solicitor. After the case was over, Mrs. Mather excitedly accused Chief-constaqe Hunt of driving her husband from his home, and of persecuting him. She advised her husband not to pay the fine. It may be mentioned that summonses that had been issued against Henry Gittens, Stephen Stirrup, and Ellen Butterworth were withdrawn befOre the commencement of the case. :The fineand-costs were afterwards paid by the defendant, Mather.

Yonge will be "Rock of ages cleft for me," and Miss Podmore will sing "Hiding in Thee."

DEATH OF LIEUTENANT ECICEILSLEY.—The death of Lieutenant H. J. F. Eckersley (son of Mr. Eckers- ley, of Standish), late of 3rd South Lancashire Regi- ment, will be read with regret in our obituary column. The deceased gentleman was in Burmah with the 2nd Battalion Somersetsh ire Light Infan- try, which was proceeding to the release of the loyal Woon of Myogyee, when a force of 1,000 rebels was found stockaded there. Lieutenant Eckers'leY, who was leading the advance, was killed during the engagement. ranirma OF EVERY DESCRIPTION, executed by John S. Green, Printer, Bookseller, and Stationer, 34, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt.

HOLY TRINITY LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY. Monday evening, in connection with this society, Mr. W. T. Smithies read a Paper on "Strikes.' The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton presided. A capital debate followed, and the advantages and disadvantages of strikes, their effects upon trade, and employed and unemployed, and other points and matters which. the paper gave rise to, such as the relations of capital and labour, trades unions, &c.,were somewhat fully entered into and discussed. A unanimous vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Smithies at the close of the debate. ALDERMAN CROSFIELD'S CIIRYSAI•ITIIEMUMS.— On Saturday afternoon, at the invitation of Alder- man John Crosfield, some of the members of the Sanitary Committee visited Walton Lea, the resi- dence of that gentleman, and were shown an exceedingly fine collection of chyrsanthemums. The following ladies and gentlemen were the guests of Alderman Cmsfield, viz. :--Alderman and Mrs. Burgess and Miss Burgess, Aldermanicand Mrs. Sutton, Councillor and Mrs. Roberts, Councillor Francomb, Councillor Wright, Mr. Longdin (the borough surveyor), and Mr. W. Owen. The guests were also shown over the grounds and conserva- tories, and spent a very pleasant afternoon. WARRINGTON WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A meeting of this society was held in the School, Bold-street, on Wednesday evening, Mr. G. E. Young, jun., presiding. Mr. S. Beaman read a paper on "John Wesley." The subject was treated in a most instructive and entertaining manner, and frequently drew forth the applause of the audience. The paper consisted of a biographical sketch of "the morning star of the Reformation," with graphic description of the bold stand which he made in behalf of freedom of religious thought and his fearless denunciation of the doctrine which he abhorred. OCCASIONAL COURT. —At an Occasional Court held at the office in Bank-street on Monday, Thomas Moffatt and Thomas Farrington were charged -with sleeping out at Walton Inferior, without an visi- ble means of subsistence. Moffatt was sent to prison for a fortnight, and Farrington was dis- charged. AN EXCITABLE WOMAN. -- At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Nancy Coss- ley, wife of a farmer living at _Rixton, was sum- moned for annoying her husband, from whom she is separated, by being disorderly and turbulent. The parties have several times had their grievances ventilated before the court, and finally, on the ad- vice of the magistrates, a deed of separation was drawn up by which the husband agreed to allow a certain sum per week for the maintenance of his wife. It was alleged that sshe had ince been inthe habit of coming to the front of his house and an- noying him by shouting and praying, and be- . having in a turbulent manner. Defendant, who was very excited, was ordered to find a surety. for her good behaviour, or go to prison for seven days. She declared that the Lord would be with her in prison, and she would 0-o there willingly for years. She read her Bible, she said, and was not afraid of going to prison. No one had come forward to be surety for her when the Court rose. THE VACANCY ON THE TOWN COUNCIL—A va- cancy has been caused on the Town Council by the election of Councillor Thomas Sutton as an Alder- man. Councillor Sutton represented South-West Ward. The election of a successor is fixed for Mon- day, the 29th instant. The nomination papers ; must be delivered at the office of the Town Clerk' ! before five o'clock on the afternoon of Monday ! next, and, if it be necessary, the Mayor (Dr. Mackie) will attend at the town Hall at two ! o'clock on the afternoon of the following day, to hear and decide objections to nomination papers. It is stated that the Conservatives have decided to nominate Mr. R. Heaton, and that the Liberals will not offer opposition. A correspondent, who signs himself " South-West Ward," wishes to know, if politics are to have no place in municipal matters, how it is that the Tories have met and decided to nominate a Tory. He hopes "someone will be ; nominated by the burgesses who has the confidence of the ratepayers." THE KIRKDALB CHARITIES.—In another column an advertisement directs attention to a Christmas ; bazaar to be held in connection with these charities. and help is asked for. The charities to be assisted are the Boys' and Girls' Free Homes, the Major- street Day Industrial and Feeding School, the Girls' ! Home, the Ladies' Charity, the Christian Aid ! Society, the Sick Nurses' Institute, and the Major- street and Christopher-street Missions. Referring ' to the Major-street Schools, a Liverpool contempor- ary says that in them " hundreds of poor children— in many cases destitute, and in some worse than ; destitute—have a thorough education in the three R's, in Bible knowledge, and in the rudiments of handicraft; , they have also three good meals each day, suitable clothing; and, when necessary, they are lodged in clean, wholesome dormitories. There is no finer or more cheering sight in Liverpool than a look into the faces of Canon Lester's children when ! they are receiving the instruction of their teachers. A steady vigilance Of attention and brightness of intelligence is general among them that would sur- prise many acquainted with ordinary elementary ! schools." The institution is one in which orphans and poor children, who are not able to gain an en- ! trance to the local charities, are taken care of to save them from the alternative of being sent to the workhouse.

Between three and four tkousanci people witnessed the game between Lancashire and Cheshire, which was played at Birkenhead on Saturday. The Lancashire men, both for- ward and in the back divlsion, completely overplayed their opponents at all points, and though in the second half Che- shire at times ievaded the Lancastrian quarters, yet they were never really dangerous, and the score of three goals, three tries, and fourteen minors to three minors fairly indi- cates the general play. Runcorn was represented in the Cheshire team by the following players :—T Woods (back), W A Riley (three-quarter back), H Hughes (half back), and J Lewis (forward). The first proseeution for manslaughter in oonnection with fatal accidents at football matches was instituted in Scot- land on Wednesday, against a young man named Hetrick, belonging to Beith, who is charged with having caused tke death of a player by a " charge " at play on Saturday last.
